label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $G$ be a finite $2$-transitive permutation group on a set $\mathcal{P}$ of $v$ points, and write
\[
\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}=\mathcal{T}_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal{T}_r
\]
for the orbit decomposition of $G$ on three-point subsets. For each $i$ choose $\mathcal{O}_i\in\mathcal{T}_i$. The general assertions (1)--(2) below hold for every such $G$; the family-specific data of (3) are asserted only in the ranges explicitly covered by a proof or by a stated computation \textup{(Remarks \ref{rem:proofstatus} and \ref{rem:open})}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The orbit lengths are $|\mathcal{T}_i|=|G|/|G_{\mathcal{O}_i}|$, and the orbit parameter $\lambda_i=6|G|/\bigl(|G_{\mathcal{O}_i}|\,v(v-1)\bigr)$ is a positive integer \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:lambda})}.
\item The setwise stabilizers fit into the exact sequence $1\to G_{({\mathcal{O}_i})}\to G_{\mathcal{O}_i}\to\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}_i}\le S_3\to1$ \textup{(\eqref{eq:ses})}; the stabilizer image is one of $1,C_2,C_3,S_3$.
\item \textbf{The family-by-family data.}  For the families and parameter ranges covered by a proof or by an explicit computation, the orbit decomposition, the stabilizer structure and the orbit parameters $\lambda_i$ are collected in \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}}, each row being proved analytically or verified computationally in its stated range and tagged accordingly; the proof status of each row is recorded in \textup{Remarks \ref{rem:proofstatus} and \ref{rem:open}}.  Rows with a single orbit are precisely the $3$-homogeneous groups \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:3hom})}.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Main classification

label: lem:lambda
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Basic counting

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an unordered pair $P\in\binom{\mathcal{P}}{2}$ and set $b(P)=|\{B\in\mathcal{T}: P\subseteq B\}|$.  Since $G$ is $2$-transitive, for every $Q\in\binom{\mathcal{P}}{2}$ there is $g\in G$ with $g(P)=Q$;  as $\mathcal{T}$ is $G$-invariant, $B\mapsto g(B)$ is a bijection between the blocks of $\mathcal{T}$ through $P$ and those through $Q$, so $b(P)=b(Q)=:\lambda$ is independent of the pair.
(1) is the orbit--stabilizer theorem.
(2) Count the incidences $(P,B)$ with $P\in\binom{\mathcal{P}}{2}$, $B\in\mathcal{T}$, $P\subseteq B$ in two ways:  each block contains $\binom{3}{2}=3$ pairs, and each of the $\binom{v}{2}$ pairs lies in exactly $\lambda$ blocks, hence $\lambda\binom{v}{2}=3|\mathcal{T}|$, i.e.\ $\lambda=3|\mathcal{T}|/\binom{v}{2}=6|\mathcal{T}|/(v(v-1))=6|G|/\bigl(|G_{\mathcal{O}}|\,v(v-1)\bigr)$, an integer.  Simplicity is immediate from $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$.
(3) Distinct $G$-orbits are disjoint as block sets, although the resulting designs may be abstractly isomorphic.

label: def:orbit-ts
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:orbit-ts}
Let $G\leSym(\mathcal{P})$ be $2$-transitive on $\mathcal{P}$.  For $\mathcal{O}\in\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$ we call the $G$-orbit $\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{O})=\mathcal{O}^G$ an \emph{orbit triple system} and write $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{O})=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{O}))$ for the pair consisting of the point set and the orbit as block set.
head: environment
name: Orbit triple system

label: prop:each-orbit
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Every orbit is a triple system

label: prop:union-orbits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:union-orbits}
Let $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}=\mathcal{T}_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal{T}_r$ be the orbit decomposition of $G$ on three-point subsets, and let $\lambda_i$ be the parameter of $\mathcal{T}_i$ \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:each-orbit})}.  For every nonempty $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$ the union $\mathcal{T}_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{T}_i$ defines a simple $G$-invariant $2$-$(v,3,\lambda_I)$ design with
\[
\lambda_I=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i.
\]
Conversely, every nonempty $G$-invariant family of three-point subsets is a union of $G$-orbits, hence is uniquely of the form $\mathcal{T}_I$.
head: environment
name: Unions of orbits are triple systems

title: Proof
body_md: Each $\mathcal{T}_i$ is a $2$-design by \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:each-orbit}}.  For a point pair $\{x,y\}$ the number of blocks of $\mathcal{T}_I$ through it is $\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i$, independent of the pair, because the orbits are disjoint;  simplicity is immediate.  For the converse, if $\mathcal B\subseteq\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$ is nonempty and $G$-invariant, then for every $B\in\mathcal B$ its orbit $B^G$ is contained in $\mathcal B$, so $\mathcal B$ is a union of $G$-orbits;  the orbit decomposition is unique, hence the index set $I$ is unique.

label: cor:all-invariant
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: All $G$-invariant triple systems

label: rem:3hom
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:3hom}
If $G$ is $3$-homogeneous on $\mathcal{P}$, then $r=1$:  the unique orbit $\mathcal{T}$ is $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$ itself, and by \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:each-orbit}} the only $G$-invariant triple system on $\mathcal{P}$ is the complete design $2$-$(v,3,v-2)$, whose blocks are all three-point subsets and whose parameter is therefore fixed, $\lambda=v-2$.  Nontrivial orbit structures, that is, all triple systems other than the complete one, occur only for $2$-transitive groups that are not $3$-homogeneous, and the family-by-family analysis below concentrates on those.  The $3$-homogeneous groups occurring in \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}} are exactly its single-orbit rows:  $Alt(n)$ and $Sym(n)$ \textup{(}$\lambda=n-2$\textup{)}, the Mathieu groups \textup{(}$\lambda=v-2$\textup{)}, $PGL(2,q)$ and $P\string\Gamma L(2,q)$ \textup{(}$\lambda=q-1$\textup{)}, and $PSL(2,q)$ with $q$ even or $q\equiv3\pmod4$ \textup{(}$\lambda=q-1$;  the case $q\equiv3\pmod4$ is $3$-homogeneous but not $3$-transitive, \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psl2}\textup{(}2\textup{)}}\textup{)}.  In addition there are three exceptional affine $1$-dimensional groups, each with a single orbit:  $AGL(1,8)$ and $A\string\Gamma L(1,8)$ on $8$ points, and $A\string\Gamma L(1,32)$ on $32$ points \textup{(}verified directly in \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}:  the setwise stabilizer of every triple is trivial, so the single orbit has the size $\binom{8}{3}=56$ resp.\ $\binom{32}{3}=4960$\textup{)}.  Thus the complete list of $3$-homogeneous groups in the classification is the one just given;  in particular no other $AGL(1,q)$ or $A\string\Gamma L(1,q)$ is $3$-homogeneous (e.g.\ $AGL(1,7)$ has two orbits, \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}).  The computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} confirms that among the primitive groups tested in the stated degree range $3\le v\le200$ the $2$-transitive groups with a single three-point orbit are precisely these.

title: Remark
body_md: When $G$ is sharply $2$-transitive, $|G_{(\mathcal{O})}|=1$ and $G_{\mathcal{O}}\cong\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}$.  In general the kernel $G_{(\mathcal{O})}$ can be large; determining both $G_{(\mathcal{O})}$ and $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}$ \textup{(}hence whether $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ contains elements realizing transpositions, $3$-cycles, or all of $S_3$\textup{)} is the main technical content of this monograph.

label: lem:suborbit
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Suborbit reduction

title: Proof
body_md: The triples in $X^G$ containing $P$ are parametrized by the three two-subsets of a representative triple $X=\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$:  a triple $T\in X^G$ with $P\subseteq T$ has the form $T=g(X)$ with $g^{-1}(P)\subseteq X$, and $g^{-1}(P)$ is one of $\{\alpha,\beta\},\{\alpha,\gamma\},\{\beta,\gamma\}$.  Two such triples $g_1(X),g_2(X)$ lie in the same $G_P$-orbit precisely when some $h\in G_P$ satisfies $hg_1(X)=g_2(X)$;  writing $k=g_2^{-1}hg_1\in G_X$, this holds exactly when $k(g_1^{-1}P)=g_2^{-1}P$ \textup{(since $h(P)=P$)}\textup{)}.  Hence two triples lie in the same $G_P$-orbit precisely when the corresponding two-subsets lie in the same orbit of $\overline{G}_X$ \textup{(the action of $G_X$ on the three two-subsets of $X$ is isomorphic to its action on the three points, via complementation}\textup{)}.  The values $3,2,1,1$ follow by inspecting $H\le S_3$ on the three two-subsets:  a transposition fixes the two-subset complementary to its fixed point and swaps the other two, a $3$-cycle moves all three two-subsets in one cycle, and $S_3$ is transitive.  Surjectivity of the point-to-triple map is recorded above;  the precise bijection criterion and the double-coset form are stated in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:pair-orbits}}, and injectivity must be checked in each family below.
head: environment

label: prop:pair-orbits
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Orbits on triples from the two-point stabilizer

title: Proof
body_md: Well defined:  if $\gamma'=h(\gamma)$ with $h\in G_P$, then $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma'\}=h\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ lies in the same $G$-orbit.  Surjective:  every $3$-subset $T$ contains a pair $\{x,y\}$;  by $2$-transitivity on points $G$ is transitive on unordered pairs, so some $g\in G$ maps $\{x,y\}$ onto $P$, and then $g(T)=\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ for $\gamma=g(z)$, $z=T\setminus\{x,y\}$;  hence $T^{G}=\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}^{G}$.  The fiber statement:  the triples of $X^{G}$ containing $P$ are exactly the sets $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma'\}$ with $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma'\}^{G}=X^{G}$, and $G_P$ acts on this set;  its orbits are precisely the $G_P$-orbits of such $\gamma'$ on $\mathcal{P}\setminus P$.  The double-coset statement is the standard orbit correspondence for the action of $G_P$ on $G/G_X$ (orbit--stabilizer), with $T=g(X)$ corresponding to the coset $gG_X$ and $P\subseteq g(X)$ equivalent to $g^{-1}(P)\subseteq X$.
head: environment

label: rem:pair-orbits
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:pair-orbits}
The bijection of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:pair-orbits}} is \emph{not} automatic:  for $G=AGL(1,5)$ on five points and $P=\{0,1\}$, the setwise stabilizer $G_P\cong C_2$ has two orbits on $\mathcal{P}\setminus P$ \textup{(}$\{2,4\}$ and $\{3\}$\textup{)}, while $G$ has a single orbit $X$ on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$ \textup{(Table \ref{tab:verify}}\textup{)}.  Consistently with \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}}, the induced image of $G_X$ on the representative triple is a transposition, so the fiber over $X$ consists of exactly $2$ $G_P$-suborbits:  the two suborbits are fused by $G$ into the single triple orbit.  One must therefore check injectivity separately in each application;  for $HS$ and $Co_3$ it is confirmed by the suborbit computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}.  Note also that all stabilizers below are \emph{setwise} stabilizers of unordered pairs:  the ordered-pair stabilizer $G_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a subgroup of index $1$ or $2$ in $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$, and the two should not be conflated.
head: environment

label: rem:char
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:char}
The number $r$ of three-point orbits can be obtained without enumerating triples.  For $g\in G$ let $n(g)$ denote the number of $g$-invariant three-point subsets.  A three-point subset is $g$-invariant precisely when it is a union of $g$-cycles of total size $3$;  writing $c_k(g)$ for the number of $k$-cycles of $g$ on $\mathcal{P}$,
\[
n(g)=\binom{c_1(g)}{3}+c_1(g)c_2(g)+c_3(g),
\]
and Burnside's lemma gives $r=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}n(g)$.  The summands depend only on the cycle type of $g$, hence are constant on conjugacy classes;  the fixed-point count $c_1(g)$ is the value of the point permutation character at $g$, and $c_2(g),c_3(g)$ refine it within the same permutation representation \textup{(}available in GAP directly from the cycle types of class representatives\textup{)}.  The formula does not by itself give the structure of $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ (the kernel $G_{(\mathcal{O})}$ and the induced image $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}$ still require the explicit stabilizer analysis of the family sections below), but it is an independent check of the orbit counts, and it is far cheaper than enumerating $\binom{v}{3}$ triples.  Concrete applications of the count are reported in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}.
head: environment
name: Counting the orbits from class functions

label: lem:norm-orbit-fusion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:norm-orbit-fusion}
Let $S\trianglelefteq G$ act on a finite set $\Omega$, and let $\mathcal{O}_S(\Omega)$ denote the set of $S$-orbits.  Then $G/S$ acts naturally on $\mathcal{O}_S(\Omega)$, and the $G$-orbits on $\Omega$ are precisely the unions of the $S$-orbits belonging to one orbit of $G/S$ on $\mathcal{O}_S(\Omega)$.
head: environment
name: Orbit fusion under a normal subgroup

title: Proof
body_md: Let $\Delta\in\mathcal{O}_S(\Omega)$ and choose $x\in\Delta$.  For $g\in G$, the set $\Delta^g=\{y^g:y\in\Delta\}$ is again an $S$-orbit, since $S$ is normal in $G$;  and if $g_1S=g_2S$, then $g_2=sg_1$ for some $s\in S$, so $\Delta^{g_2}=\Delta^{sg_1}=(\Delta^s)^{g_1}=\Delta^{g_1}$.  Hence the action of $G$ on $\mathcal{O}_S(\Omega)$ factors through $G/S$.  Let $\mathcal C=\Delta^{G/S}$ be the orbit of $\Delta$ under the quotient action, and put $U_{\mathcal C}=\bigcup_{\Gamma\in\mathcal C}\Gamma$.  The set $U_{\mathcal C}$ is $G$-invariant and contains the $G$-orbit of every point of $\Delta$.  Conversely, if $y\in U_{\mathcal C}$, then $y=x^g$ for some $x\in\Delta$, $g\in G$;  hence $y\in\Delta^G$.  Thus $\Delta^G=U_{\mathcal C}$.
head: environment

label: lem:sqclass
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sqclass}
Let $q$ be odd and let $s\inPGL(2,q)$ be a permutation of the reference triple $\{0,1,\infty\}$.  Then $\det(s)\in\{1,-1\}$:  the identity and the two $3$-cycles have determinant $1$, and the three transpositions have determinant $-1$.  Consequently, if $g\inPGL(2,q)$ maps $\{0,1,\infty\}$ to $\mathcal{O}$, replacing $g$ by $g\circ s$ \textup{(}where $s$ permutes the reference triple\textup{)} changes the square class of $g$ by the factor $\det(s)$;  for $q\equiv1\pmod4$ ($-1$ a square) the square class is independent of the choice of $s$, while for $q\equiv3\pmod4$ the transpositions $s$ interchange the two classes.
head: environment
name: Well-definedness of the square-class invariant

title: Proof
body_md:
The six elements of $PGL(2,q)_{\{0,1,\infty\}}$ are
\[
\mathrm{id}\ (t\mapsto t),\quad
(0\,1)\ (t\mapsto 1-t),\quad
(0\,\infty)\ (t\mapsto 1/t),\quad
(1\,\infty)\ (t\mapsto t/(t-1)),
\]
\[
(0\,1\,\infty)\ (t\mapsto 1/(1-t)),\quad
(0\,\infty\,1)\ (t\mapsto (t-1)/t),
\]
with matrices $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, of determinants $1,-1,-1,-1,1,1$, respectively.  The claim follows:  $g\circ s$ has determinant $\det(g)\det(s)$, and the square class in $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}/\mathbb{F}_q^{\times2}$ is determined by whether that determinant is a square;  $-1$ is a square exactly for $q\equiv1\pmod4$.
head: environment

label: thm:psl2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:psl2}
Let $S=PSL(2,q)$, $q=p^f$ with $q\ge4$ (the exceptional small cases $q=2,3$ are excluded; the case $q=4$ is covered, with $PSL(2,4)\cong A_5$, see Corollary \ref{cor:psl2-designs}), acting on $\mathcal{P}=\mathrm{PG}(1,q)$, and let $\mathcal{O}$ be a $3$-subset.  Then $S_{(\mathcal{O})}=1$ for every $\mathcal{O}$, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $q$ is even, $PGL(2,q)=PSL(2,q)$ is sharply $3$-transitive on $\mathcal{P}$:  all $3$-subsets form a single orbit and
\[
S_{\mathcal{O}}\cong S_3,\qquad |S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6.
\]
\item If $q\equiv3\pmod4$, $PSL(2,q)$ is $3$-\emph{homogeneous} \textup{(}not $3$-transitive\textup{)} on $\mathcal{P}$:  all $3$-subsets form a single orbit and
\[
S_{\mathcal{O}}\cong C_3,\qquad |S_{\mathcal{O}}|=3.
\]
\item If $q\equiv1\pmod4$, $PSL(2,q)$ has exactly \emph{two} orbits on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$, distinguished by the square class of an element of $PGL(2,q)$ mapping a fixed reference triple to $\mathcal{O}$ \textup{(}i.e.\ by the class in $PGL(2,q)/PSL(2,q)\cong\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}/\mathbb{F}_q^{\times2}$\textup{)}, and on both orbits
\[
S_{\mathcal{O}}\cong S_3,\qquad |S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: $\PSL(2,q)$: three-point stabilizers

title: Proof
head: environment

label: rem:psl2-count
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:psl2-count}
For $q\equiv3\pmod4$, $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=3$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:psl2}(2)}\textup{)};  since $|S|=q(q^2-1)/2$, the orbit size is $q(q^2-1)/6=\binom{q+1}{3}$, the total number of $3$-subsets:  the orbit is all of $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$, i.e.\ $S$ is $3$-homogeneous.  For $q\equiv1\pmod4$, each of the two orbits has stabilizer of order $6$, hence size $q(q^2-1)/12=\frac12\binom{q+1}{3}$, and the two orbits partition $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$.  These counts confirm the orbit structure of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psl2}} directly from $|S|$ and $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|$.
head: environment
name: Counting check for the orbit structure

title: Remark
body_md: For $q$ odd the orbit structure is governed by the square class described in \textup{Section \ref{sec:psl2}} as follows:  for $q\equiv3\pmod4$ the two classes are \emph{fused} by $PSL(2,q)$ \textup{(}the group is $3$-homogeneous\textup{)}, and for $q\equiv1\pmod4$ \emph{both} classes admit the transposition $t\mapsto1-t$ \textup{(}because $-1$ is a square\textup{)}, so both have stabilizer $S_3$.  The statement is verified computationally in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} for $q=5,7,8,9,11$:  $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ \textup{(}two orbits\textup{)}, $3$ \textup{(}one orbit\textup{)}, $6$ \textup{(}one orbit\textup{)}, $6$ \textup{(}two orbits\textup{)}, $3$ \textup{(}one orbit\textup{)}, respectively.

label: cor:psl2-designs
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Designs from $\PSL(2,q)$

title: Proof
body_md: Immediate from \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psl2}} and \eqref{eq:lambda}.  For $q$ even, $|S|=q(q^2-1)$ and $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ give $\lambda=q-1$;  for $q\equiv3\pmod4$, $|S|=q(q^2-1)/2$ and $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=3$ give $\lambda=q-1$ as well;  for $q\equiv1\pmod4$ each of the two $S_3$-orbits has $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ and $\lambda=(q^2-1)/(2(q+1))=(q-1)/2$, an integer.

label: thm:pgl
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: $\PGL(2,q)$, $\PpGL(2,q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) $PGL(2,q)$ is sharply $3$-transitive:  $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ maps onto $S_3$ and fixes no point of $\mathcal{O}$ pointwise (a projective transformation fixing three points is the identity).
(2) $PGL(2,q)\le G$ already realizes all of $S_3$ on $\mathcal{O}$ and is transitive on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$, so $G$ is too.  For the kernel:  an element of $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ is $g=\sigma\circ h$ with $\sigma\in F$, $h\inPGL(2,q)$;  it fixes $\mathcal{O}$ pointwise iff $h(\sigma(x))=x$ for all $x\in\mathcal{O}$.  Since $PGL(2,q)$ is sharply $3$-transitive, for each $\sigma\in F$ there is a unique $h_\sigma$ with $h_\sigma(\sigma(x))=x$ for the three points $x\in\mathcal{O}$, and $h_\sigma\circ\sigma\in G_{(\mathcal{O})}$ (the product lies in $G$ because $h_\sigma\inPGL(2,q)\le G$ and $\sigma\in G$).  Distinct $\sigma$ give distinct kernel elements, and every kernel element arises this way, so $|G_{(\mathcal{O})}|=|F|$.  The image is all of $S_3$ from (1);  the sequence splits since $S_3$ is realized inside $PGL(2,q)\le G$.
head: environment

label: rem:twisted
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:twisted}
By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgl}\textup{(}2\textup{)}} the kernel element for a triple $\mathcal{O}$ is the \emph{twisted} projective transformation $h_\sigma\circ\sigma$, fixing the three points;  only for triples $\mathcal{O}$ lying in the fixed subline \textup{(}e.g.\ $\mathrm{PG}(1,p)$ inside $\mathrm{PG}(1,p^f)$\textup{)} is the kernel element the field automorphism itself.  The computation in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} confirms it:  $|P\string\Gamma L(2,9)_{\mathcal{O}}|=12=6\cdot2$ for \emph{every} $\mathcal{O}$ \textup{(}not $6$ off the subline\textup{)}, and $|P\string\Gamma L(2,25)_{\mathcal{O}}|=12=6\cdot2$ likewise.
head: environment

label: lem:twisted-det
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:twisted-det}
Let $q=p^f$, let $\sigma$ be the field automorphism $t\mapsto t^{p^k}$ of $\mathrm{PG}(1,q)$, and let $\mathcal{O}=g\{0,1,\infty\}$ with $g\inPGL(2,q)$.  The unique $h_\sigma\inPGL(2,q)$ with $h_\sigma(\sigma(x))=x$ for all $x\in\mathcal{O}$ is $h_\sigma=g\circ\sigma(g)^{-1}$, and
\[
\det(h_\sigma)=\delta^{1-p^k},\qquad \delta=\det(g),
\]
which is a square in $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ for every $\delta$:  for $p$ odd, $p^k-1$ is even, so $\delta^{1-p^k}=(\delta^{(1-p^k)/2})^2$;  for $p=2$ every element of $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ is a square.  Hence $h_\sigma\inPSL(2,q)$ for every triple $\mathcal{O}$ and every field automorphism $\sigma$.
head: environment
name: Determinant of the twisted correction

title: Proof
body_md: For $x=g(y)$ with $y\in\{0,1,\infty\}$ one has $\sigma(x)=(\sigma g\sigma^{-1})(y)$, and $(g\circ\sigma(g)^{-1})(\sigma g\sigma^{-1})(y)=g(y)=x$;  as $PGL(2,q)$ is sharply $3$-transitive, the element with this property on the three points is unique.  The determinant is $\det(g)\det(\sigma(g))^{-1}=\delta\,\sigma(\delta)^{-1}=\delta^{1-p^k}$, and the square claim follows.
head: environment

label: thm:psl2-field
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Field overgroups not containing $\PGL(2,q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
Field automorphisms normalize $PSL(2,q)$ and preserve the square class (a square $s$ is mapped to $s^{p^k}$, again a square), so the orbit structure of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psl2}} is unchanged.  The kernel:  as in \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgl}(2)}, for each $\sigma\in F$ there is a unique $h_\sigma\inPGL(2,q)$ with $h_\sigma(\sigma(x))=x$ for $x\in\mathcal{O}$;  by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:twisted-det}}, $\det(h_\sigma)$ is a square for every $\mathcal{O}$ and every $\sigma$, so $h_\sigma\inPSL(2,q)$ and $h_\sigma\circ\sigma\in G_{(\mathcal{O})}$.  Hence $|G_{(\mathcal{O})}|=|F|$ and $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=|F|\cdot|\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}|$ with the image as stated.

(Computed in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}:  $|PSL(2,9)\cdot2_{\mathcal{O}}|=12$ (two orbits), $|PSL(2,25)\cdot2_{\mathcal{O}}|=12$ (two orbits), $|PSL(2,27)\cdot3_{\mathcal{O}}|=9$ (one orbit).)

label: thm:psln
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:psln}
Let $n\ge3$, $S=PSL(n,q)$ acting on $\mathcal{P}=\mathrm{PG}(n-1,q)$, and $\mathcal{O}$ a $3$-subset of $\mathcal{P}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S$ has exactly two orbits on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$:  the \emph{collinear} triples \textup{(}contained in a projective line\textup{)} and the \emph{non-collinear} triples.  Every overgroup $S\le G\leP\string\Gamma L(n,q)$ has the same two orbits.
\item \emph{Collinear triples.}  The image in $S_3$ is all of $S_3$ \textup{(}the line stabilizer induces $PGL(2,q)$, sharply $3$-transitive on its $q+1$ points\textup{)}, and
\[
|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6\,|S_{(\mathcal{O})}|,\qquad
|S_{(\mathcal{O})}|=\frac{(q-1)\,q^{2(n-2)}\,|\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)|}{\gcd(n,q-1)},
\]
\textup{(}with $|\operatorname{SL}(1,q)|=1$;  for $n=3$ this reads $q^2(q-1)/(3,q-1)$\textup{)}.  The pointwise stabilizer consists of the elements acting as a scalar on the line \textup{(}extended with determinant $1$\textup{)}, the unipotent radical with axis the line, and $\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)$ on a complement.
\item \emph{Non-collinear triples.}  The image in $S_3$ is again all of $S_3$ \textup{(}three non-collinear points span a plane;  a permutation $\sigma\in S_3$ of the three points is realized by the permutation matrix composed with a diagonal scalar $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$ with $\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3=\varepsilon(\sigma)^{-1}$, which fixes each of the three points projectively and makes the total determinant $1$;  this works for every $n\ge3$\textup{)}, and
\[
|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6\,|S_{(\mathcal{O})}|,\qquad
|S_{(\mathcal{O})}|=
\begin{cases}
(q-1)^2/(3,q-1), & n=3,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{(q-1)^3\,q^{3(n-3)}\,|\operatorname{SL}(n-3,q)|}{\gcd(n,q-1)}, & n\ge4.
\end{cases}
\]
\textup{(}The pointwise stabilizer fixes the subspace spanned by the three points:  a diagonal part $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$ with $\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3\det B=1$, a triangular part of order $q^{3(n-3)}$, and $B\in\operatorname{GL}(n-3,q)$ on a complement.  The diagonal parameters $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ range freely \textup{(}$(q-1)^2$ choices\textup{)} and $\lambda_3$ is then determined by the determinant condition;  since $|\operatorname{GL}(m,q)|=(q-1)|\operatorname{SL}(m,q)|$, the count $(q-1)^2q^{3(n-3)}|\operatorname{GL}(n-3,q)|$ equals the displayed $(q-1)^3q^{3(n-3)}|\operatorname{SL}(n-3,q)|$.\textup{)}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Three-point stabilizers in $\PSL(n,q)$ on projective space

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Collinearity is preserved by $P\string\Gamma L(n,q)$;  transitivity on collinear triples follows from transitivity on lines (a line is determined by two points) and $3$-transitivity of $PGL(2,q)$ on a line;  transitivity on non-collinear triples follows because three non-collinear points span a plane and $PGL(n,q)$ is transitive on planes and on triangles inside a plane.
(2) The line stabilizer maps onto $PGL(2,q)$ on the line (Levi part), hence onto $S_3$ on $\mathcal{O}$.  For the kernel:  an element fixing the line pointwise has the block form $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda I_2&\ast\\0&B\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $\lambda^2\det B=1$;  counting the choices for $\lambda$, for the unipotent part ($q^{2(n-2)}$ entries) and for $B$ (with $\det B=\lambda^{-2}$, i.e.\ $|\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)|$ choices for each $\lambda$) gives $(q-1)\,q^{2(n-2)}\,|\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)|$ in $\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$, and passage to $PSL(n,q)$ divides by $|\mathbb{Z}(\operatorname{SL}(n,q))|=\gcd(n,q-1)$ \textup{(the stabilizers just counted contain the scalar center $\mathbb{Z}(\operatorname{SL}(n,q))$, which acts trivially on projective points and hence on $\mathcal{O}$)}\textup{)}.
(3) Fixing the three points forces $g$ to fix the spanned $3$-space, with block form $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}D&X\\0&B\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $D=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$, $X\in M_{3\times(n-3)}(\mathbb{F}_q)$, $B\in\operatorname{GL}(n-3,q)$, and determinant condition $\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3\det B=1$.  The entries of $X$ give $q^{3(n-3)}$ choices;  $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ are free ($(q-1)^2$ choices) and $\lambda_3$ is determined by the condition;  $B$ ranges over all of $\operatorname{GL}(n-3,q)$, since any determinant is absorbed into $\lambda_3$.  This yields $(q-1)^2q^{3(n-3)}|\operatorname{GL}(n-3,q)|=(q-1)^3q^{3(n-3)}|\operatorname{SL}(n-3,q)|$ elements of $\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$, and passage to $PSL(n,q)$ divides by $|\mathbb{Z}(\operatorname{SL}(n,q))|=\gcd(n,q-1)$ \textup{(again, the center lies in every counted stabilizer and acts trivially projectively)}\textup{)}, proving (3).  (For $n=3$ there is no $X$ or $B$;  the three non-collinear points form a basis and the count is $(q-1)^2/(3,q-1)$.)  The stabilizer formulas are verified for the five smallest parameter sets in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psl-stab-computed}} \textup{(Chapter \ref{sec:verify})}.
head: environment

label: prop:psl-stab-computed
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:psl-stab-computed}
For the five smallest parameter sets $(n,q)=(3,2),(3,3),(4,2),(4,3),(5,2)$, the stabilizer formulas of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psln}} are verified directly in GAP \textup{(supplementary script \texttt{verify\_psl\_stab.g};  Chapter \ref{sec:verify})}:  the computed collinear setwise stabilizer orders $24,108,576,11664,64512$ and non-collinear ones $6,24,48,648,2304$ agree with the formulas \textup{(as do the pointwise orders $4,18,96,1944,10752$ resp.\ $1,4,8,108,384$)}\textup{)}, in each case with induced image $S_3$ and with $\lambda=q-1$ on the collinear orbit and $\lambda=q^2$ (for $n=3$) resp.\ $v-1-q$ (for $n\ge4$) on the non-collinear one.  In particular $PSL(4,3)$ on $40$ points has kernel $|S_{(\mathcal{O})}|=108=(q-1)^3q^3/\gcd(4,2)$ on the non-collinear orbit, matching \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}.  In addition the script checks the orbit--stabilizer identity $|\mathcal{O}|=|G|/|S_{\mathcal{O}}|$ and that the two orbit sizes sum to $\binom{v}{3}$ \textup{(for $v=40$ the sum equals $\binom{40}{3}=9880$)};  the stabilizer orders and the orbit counts are thus cross-consistent, and not only the $\lambda$-values.  The statement is a finite result for the five listed parameter sets;  no family claim is involved \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:open})}.

label: cor:sp2n-designs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:sp2n-designs}
For $n=3$ the two actions yield the orbit triple systems
\[
2-\mbox{$(28,3,10)$},\quad 2-\mbox{$(28,3,16)$},\quad 2-\mbox{$(36,3,16)$},\quad 2-\mbox{$(36,3,18)$},
\]
and their unions give the complete systems $2$-$(28,3,26)$ and $2$-$(36,3,34)$ \textup{(}\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:union-orbits}}\textup{)}.
For every $n\ge3$ \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:sp2n-triples}} determines the two orbit systems on each half:  on the half of degree $v_s=2^{2n-1}+s2^{n-1}$ ($s=\pm1$) the parameters are $\lambda_0=2^{2n-2}+s2^{n-1}-2$ and $\lambda_1=2^{2n-2}$, and their union is the complete system $2$-\mbox{$(v_s,3,v_s-2)$} \textup{(\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:union-orbits}}\textup{)}}.  For $n\ge4$ the degrees $2^{2n-1}\pm2^{n-1}$ \textup{(}$=120,136,496,528,\dots$\textup{)} lie outside the tested degree range of this monograph, but the classification is supplied by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:sp2n-triples}}.
head: environment
name: Designs from $\Sp(2n,2)$

label: rem:sp2n
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sp2n}
For every $n\ge3$, $Sp(2n,2)$ is $2$-transitive on each half of the nonsingular quadric \textup{(}the point stabilizer $O^s(2n,2)$, $s=\pm1$, is transitive on the remaining points\textup{)}.  On each half the three-point orbits are \emph{exactly two}, and the complete orbit classification with the stabilizer structure and the design parameters is given by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:sp2n-triples}};  for $n=3$ it reduces to \textup{Table \ref{tab:sp62}}.  The following structural formula for higher parabolic subgroups is available as a complement:  if $U$ is a totally isotropic $k$-space and $P_k=\operatorname{Stab}_{Sp(2n,2)}(U)$, then
\[
P_k=Q_k\rtimes\bigl(\operatorname{GL}(k,2)\timesSp(2n-2k,2)\bigr),
\qquad
|Q_k|=2^{\,2k(n-k)+\binom{k+1}{2}},
\]
so $|P_k|=2^{\,2k(n-k)+\binom{k+1}{2}}\,|\operatorname{GL}(k,2)|\,|Sp(2n-2k,2)|$.  This formula concerns higher parabolic subgroups;  it is retained for completeness and is not needed for \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:sp2n-triples}}, which determines the three-subset stabilizers directly.
head: environment

label: thm:sp2n-triples
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sp2n-triples}
Let $n\ge3$, let $V$ be a $2n$-dimensional symplectic space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and let
\[
G=Sp(V)=Sp(2n,2).
\]
For $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{F}_2$, let $\Omega_\varepsilon$ be the set of quadratic forms on $V$ polarizing to the symplectic form and having Arf invariant $\varepsilon$.  Put
\[
s=(-1)^\varepsilon,
\qquad
v_s=|\Omega_\varepsilon|
   =2^{2n-1}+s2^{n-1}.
\]
Then $G$ is $2$-transitive on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ and has exactly two orbits
\[
\mathcal{T}_0,\mathcal{T}_1
\]
on $\binom{\Omega_\varepsilon}{3}$.

For $X=\{Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\}$, the orbit containing $X$ is determined by
\[
\delta(X)
=
\operatorname{Arf}(Q_1+Q_2+Q_3)+\varepsilon
\in\mathbb{F}_2;
\]
namely $X\in\mathcal{T}_{\delta(X)}$.  The corresponding orbit triple systems have parameters
\[
\lambda_0=2^{2n-2}+s2^{n-1}-2,
\qquad
\lambda_1=2^{2n-2}.
\]
In particular,
\[
\lambda_0+\lambda_1=v_s-2.
\]

For every $X\in\mathcal{T}_\delta$, the induced action of $G_X$ on $X$ is $S_3$.  More precisely,
\[
G_X\cong
\begin{cases}
U\rtimes
 \bigl(\operatorname{GL}(2,2)\times O^s(2n-4,2)\bigr),\quad |U|=2^{\,4n-7},
 &\delta=0,\\[2mm]
S_3\times O^s(2n-2,2),
 &\delta=1,
\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
G_{(X)}\cong
\begin{cases}
U\rtimes O^s(2n-4,2),
 &\delta=0,\\[2mm]
O^s(2n-2,2),
 &\delta=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus
\[
|\mathcal{T}_\delta|
=
\frac{v_s(v_s-1)\lambda_\delta}{6},
\qquad
|G_X|
=
\frac{6|G|}{v_s(v_s-1)\lambda_\delta}.
\]
head: environment
name: Three-subset orbits of $\Sp(2n,2)$

title: Proof
body_md:
The $2$-transitivity of $G$ on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ is standard:  $Sp(2n,2)$ is transitive on the quadratic forms polarizing to the symplectic form and having a fixed Arf invariant (the forms of the prescribed Arf invariant form a single affine orbit of size $2^{2n-1}\pm2^{n-1}$), and the stabilizer $O^s(2n,2)$ is transitive on the remaining forms --- equivalently, fixing $Q\in\Omega_\varepsilon$, $O(Q)$ is transitive on the nonzero $Q$-singular vectors, which parametrize the other forms of the same Arf type by $Q_a\longmapsto a$;  this is what allows the reduction below to the classification of the ordered pairs $(a,b)$.
Fix $Q\in\Omega_\varepsilon$.  Every quadratic form polarizing to the fixed symplectic form is uniquely of the form
\[
Q_a(x)=Q(x)+B(x,a)
\]
for $a\in V$, and
\[
\operatorname{Arf}(Q_a)=\operatorname{Arf}(Q)+Q(a).
\]
Consequently, after fixing the first point, an ordered triple of distinct elements of $\Omega_\varepsilon$ has the form
\[
(Q,Q_a,Q_b),
\]
where $a,b$ are distinct nonzero $Q$-singular vectors.

Since
\[
Q+Q_a+Q_b=Q_{a+b},
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{Arf}(Q+Q_a+Q_b)+\varepsilon
=Q(a+b)=B(a,b).
\]
By Witt's lemma, $O(Q)$ is transitive on the ordered pairs of distinct nonzero singular vectors having a prescribed value of $B(a,b)$.  Hence the two values $B(a,b)=0,1$ give exactly two orbits, and the displayed Arf invariant is a complete invariant.

Fix a nonzero singular vector $a$.  The form induced on $a^\perp/\langle a\rangle$ has dimension $2n-2$ and type $s$.  It follows that
\[
|\{b:Q(b)=0,\ B(a,b)=0\}|
=
2^{2n-2}+s2^{n-1}.
\]
After deleting $b=0,a$, this gives
\[
\lambda_0=2^{2n-2}+s2^{n-1}-2.
\]
The total number of singular vectors is $v_s$, so
\[
\lambda_1
=
v_s-(2^{2n-2}+s2^{n-1})
=
2^{2n-2}.
\]

Put $R=Q_1+Q_2+Q_3$.  The three differences $Q_i+R$ correspond to the three nonzero vectors of a $2$-space $W$.  If $\delta=0$, then $W$ is totally singular for $R$, and its stabilizer is
\[
U\rtimes
 \bigl(\operatorname{GL}(2,2)\times O^s(2n-4,2)\bigr),
\qquad |U|=2^{\,4n-7},
\]
where $U$ is the unipotent radical of the stabilizer of the totally singular $2$-space $W$;  $U$ is \emph{not} elementary abelian:  fixing a Witt decomposition $V=W\oplus E\oplus W'$ with $\dim E=2n-4$, the transformations of $U$ moving the two directions of $W$ are parametrized by $a,b\in E$, and their commutator is governed by $B_E(a,b)$;  since $E$ is nondegenerate and $n\ge3$, one may choose $B_E(a,b)=1$, giving a nontrivial commutator.  The factor $\operatorname{GL}(2,2)\cong S_3$ permutes the three nonzero vectors of $W$.  If $\delta=1$, then $W$ is a nondegenerate minus-type plane and
\[
V=W\perp W^\perp,
\qquad
O(W)\cong O^-(2,2)\cong S_3,
\]
while $W^\perp$ has type $s$.  This gives
\[
G_X\cong S_3\times O^s(2n-2,2).
\]
Taking the kernels of the actions on the three points gives the stated pointwise stabilizers.  The orbit-size and design-parameter formulas now follow from orbit--stabilizer and double counting.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The two descriptions of the $Sp(2n,2)$-actions are the same family:  fixing $Q\in\Omega_\varepsilon$, the bijection $Q_a\longmapsto a$ identifies $\Omega_\varepsilon$ with the set of $Q$-singular vectors of $V$, so $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ have $v_+=2^{2n-1}+2^{n-1}$ and $v_-=2^{2n-1}-2^{n-1}$ elements, matching the two halves of the nonsingular quadric in \textup{(4.2)};  the point stabilizer of the action on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ is the orthogonal group $O^s(2n,2)$, $s=(-1)^\varepsilon$.  For $n=3$ the parameters of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:sp2n-triples}} reduce to $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1)=(10,16)$ for $v=28$ and $(18,16)$ for $v=36$, and the setwise stabilizers $Sp(6,2)_X$ computed in \textup{Table \ref{tab:sp62}}, namely $1152=2^5\,|\operatorname{GL}(2,2)|\,|O^-(2,2)|=32\cdot6\cdot6$ and $720=6\,|O^-(4,2)|=6\cdot120$ for $v=28$, and $384=2^5\,|\operatorname{GL}(2,2)|\,|O^+(2,2)|=32\cdot6\cdot2$ and $432=6\,|O^+(4,2)|=6\cdot72$ for $v=36$, agree with the two cases $\delta=0,1$ of the theorem.

label: lem:unital
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unital}
Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the Hermitian unital in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^2)$, $q\ge3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every line of $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^2)$ meets $\mathcal{U}$ in $1$ point \textup{(}tangent\textup{)} or $q+1$ points \textup{(}secant block\textup{)};  every pair of points of $\mathcal{U}$ lies on a unique block;  there are $q^2(q^2-q+1)$ blocks, each of size $q+1$, and each point lies on $q^2$ blocks.  In particular, no $3$-subset with two points on a block and the third off it exists:  a $3$-subset is either \emph{collinear} \textup{(}contained in a block\textup{)} or \emph{non-collinear}.
\item There is no pair of distinct isotropic points $u
\ne v\in\mathcal{U}$ with $u\perp v$ (orthogonality taken with respect to the standard Hermitian form $x^{q+1}+y^{q+1}+z^{q+1}$ on the underlying $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^3$):  such a pair would span a totally singular $2$-space $W$ (both vectors are isotropic and mutually orthogonal, so $W\subseteq W^{\perp}$, and $\dim W=2$ forces equality), contradicting the fact that the Hermitian form has Witt index $1$ \textup{(its maximal totally singular subspaces are the $1$-spaces of the unital}\textup{)}.  Consequently no ``self-polar'' or ``pairwise orthogonal'' triples exist.
\item $|S|=q^3(q^3+1)(q^2-1)/d$;  $S$ is $2$-transitive on $\mathcal{U}$;  the point stabilizer $S_{\alpha}$ has order $q^3(q^2-1)/d$ and is transitive on $\mathcal{U}\setminus\{\alpha\}$ \textup{(}an imprimitive quotient of $\operatorname{SU}(2,q)$-type on the $q^3$ remaining points with blocks the $q^2$ blocks through $\alpha$\textup{)}.
\item Two-point stabilizer:  for distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{U}$,
\[
|S_{\alpha,\beta}|=\frac{q^2-1}{d},\qquad
S_{\alpha,\beta}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{(q^2-1)/d}
\]
\textup{(}a cyclic group;  on the block through $\alpha,\beta$ it acts transitively on the remaining $q-1$ points, and off the block it has the $qd$ regular orbits of length $(q^2-1)/d$\textup{)}.  Three-point pointwise stabilizer:
\[
S_{(\mathcal{O})}\cong
\begin{cases}
\mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/d}, & \mathcal{O}\ \text{collinear},\\
1, & \mathcal{O}\ \text{non-collinear},
\end{cases}
\]
\textup{(}for non-collinear triples the pointwise stabilizer is trivial for every $q$:  it is contained in $S_{\alpha,\beta}$, which acts regularly off the block by (4)\textup{)}.
\item Block stabilizer:  if $B$ is a block, $S_B$ induces on $B$ the group $PGL(2,q)$ \textup{(sharply $3$-transitive on the $q+1$ points of $B$}\textup{)}:  the block stabilizer in $PGU(3,q)$ maps onto $PGL(2,q)$ with kernel the cyclic pointwise stabilizer $\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}$ of $B$ (a classical result of Mitchell \cite{mitchell1911}, used here as input and not reproved), and the image of $S_B=PGU(3,q)_B\cap S$ is then all of $PGL(2,q)$.  Indeed $|PGU(3,q)_B|=(q+1)|PGL(2,q)|$;  the index $[PGU(3,q)_B:S_B]$ equals $d=(3,q+1)$;  for $d=1$ there is nothing to prove, and for $d=3$ the diagonal element $\delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,\zeta)$, $\zeta^{q+1}=1$, $\zeta
\ne1$, fixes pointwise the block $B_0=\{z=0\}\cap\mathcal{U}$ and maps onto a generator of $PGU(3,q)/S\cong C_3$, while $PGU(3,q)$ is transitive on blocks \textup{($S$ is $2$-transitive on $\mathcal{U}$, and blocks are the pairs of unital points}\textup{)}, so the index is $d$ for every block;  and $|S_B\cap\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}|=(q+1)/d$.  Hence $|S_B|=(q+1)|PGL(2,q)|/d$, the pointwise stabilizer $S_{(B)}$ of the block in $S$ has order $|S_B\cap\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}|=(q+1)/d$, and the image of $S_B$ in $PGL(2,q)$ has order $|S_B|/|S_{(B)}|=|PGL(2,q)|$, so it is the whole group.  In particular every $3$-cycle of $S_3$ on a collinear triple is realizable in $S$ and lifts to an element of $S_{\mathcal{O}}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Geometry of the unital

title: Proof
body_md:
(1),(2) standard facts on Hermitian varieties (e.g.\ \cite{mitchell1911});  the Witt index is $1$, giving (2).
(3) $|PSU(3,q)|=q^3(q^3+1)(q^2-1)/d$ and $2$-transitivity is classical \cite{huppert1967,mitchell1911}.
(4) The two-point stabilizer is a cyclic group (the classical Singer-type subgroup of the unitary group;  see \cite{mitchell1911});  the pointwise stabilizer statements follow by restricting to a block (on which the relevant group is a subgroup of $PGL(2,q)$ fixing $3$ points, hence trivial) or from the two-point case.
(5) That the block stabilizer in $PGU(3,q)$ maps onto $PGL(2,q)$ with kernel $\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}$ is a classical theorem of Mitchell \cite{mitchell1911} on the ternary linear groups \textup{(the automorphism group of the Hermitian curve in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^2)$)}\textup{)};  the displayed order count then shows that the image of $S_B$ is all of $PGL(2,q)$.

label: thm:collinear
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:collinear}
Let $\mathcal{O}=\{x,y,z\}$ be a collinear $3$-subset of $\mathcal{U}$ \textup{(}contained in a block $B$\textup{)}, and $S=PSU(3,q)$, $d=\gcd(3,q+1)$.  Then
\[
S_{\mathcal{O}}\cong \mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/d}\rtimes S_3,
\qquad |S_{\mathcal{O}}|=\frac{6(q+1)}{d},
\qquad S_{(\mathcal{O})}=\mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/d},
\]
and the image of $S_{\mathcal{O}}$ on $\mathcal{O}$ is all of $S_3$.
head: environment
name: Collinear triples

title: Proof
body_md: Using the classical input of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:unital}(4),(5)} \textup{(cf.\ \cite{mitchell1911})}:  the pointwise stabilizer of $\mathcal{O}$ is cyclic of order $(q+1)/d$;  the block stabilizer induces $PGL(2,q)$, sharply $3$-transitive on $B$, so the setwise stabilizer of $\mathcal{O}$ maps onto $S_3$;  a preimage of each permutation is obtained inside $S_B$.  The kernel of $S_{\mathcal{O}}\to S_3$ is $S_{(\mathcal{O})}$, and the sequence splits because $S_3$ is realized inside $S_B$ (a $3$-cycle and a transposition of the three points, cf.\ (5)).  Hence $S_{\mathcal{O}}=\mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/d}\rtimes S_3$, of order $6(q+1)/d$.

label: thm:main-psu
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-psu}
Let $q\ge3$, $d=\gcd(3,q+1)$, and let $S=PSU(3,q)$ act on the Hermitian unital $\mathcal{U}$ with $|\mathcal{U}|=q^3+1$.  For a pair $\alpha
\ne\beta\in\mathcal{U}$ let $B$ be the block through $\alpha,\beta$, $T=S_{\alpha,\beta}$ the pointwise stabilizer of the pair, and $\tau\in S$ an element interchanging $\alpha$ and $\beta$;  by the classical normalizer structure \textup{(\cite{mitchell1911,huppert1967})} $\tau$ can always be chosen of order $2$ \textup{(verified for every $q\le27$ in \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}})}.  Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S$ is $2$-transitive on $\mathcal{U}$;  $T\cong\mathbb{Z}_{(q^2-1)/d}$ is cyclic and acts regularly on $\mathcal{U}\setminus B$, so the $T$-orbits off $B$ are the $qd$ regular orbits of length $(q^2-1)/d$.  The setwise stabilizer is $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}=\langle T,\tau\rangle$ with $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}/T\cong C_2$, and $\tau$ normalizes $T$ by the automorphism
\[
\tau\,t\,\tau^{-1}=t^{-q}\qquad(t\in T).
\]
\item \emph{Fixed-orbit number.}  Let $k$ be the number of regular $T$-orbits off $B$ fixed by $\tau$ as a set.  Then
\[
k=\begin{cases}
0, & q\ \text{even},\\
d, & q\ \text{odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ has, off $B$, $k$ orbits of length $(q^2-1)/d$ and $(qd-k)/2$ orbits of length $2(q^2-1)/d$.
\item \emph{Orbit number.}  The stabilizer image on a non-collinear triple is one of $S_3,C_3,1$ \textup{(trivial pointwise stabilizer, Lemma \ref{lem:psu-pointwise})};  by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}} each $S_3$- or $C_3$-suborbit contributes one triple orbit, while the trivial suborbits fuse three-to-one \textup{(the three $2$-subsets of the triple form one orbit under $S_3$ and $C_3$, three singleton orbits under the trivial image)}\textup{)}.  With the $C_3$- and trivial-suborbit multiplicities of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}} \textup{(theoretical in the $d=1$ rows, proved for every $q$ with $3\mid q+1$ in the odd-$d=3$ rows \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd})} and for every $q=2^{2m+1}$ in the even-$d=3$ rows \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even})};  the pattern is proved for all $q$ in the $d=1$ rows and verified for $q\le27$ in \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}}}\textup{)}:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_3(S,\mathcal{U})
&=1+\#\textup{(S}_3\textup{-orbits)}+\#\textup{(C}_3\textup{-orbits)}\\
&\qquad+\tfrac13\#\textup{(trivial suborbits)}\\
&=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{q+3}{2}, & q\ \text{odd},\ d=1,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{5q+11}{6}, & q\ \text{odd},\ d=3\ \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd})},\\[4pt]
1+\dfrac q2, & q\ \text{even},\ d=1,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{5q+2}{6}, & q\ \text{even},\ d=3\ \textup{(}q=2^{2m+1}>2,\ \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}\textup{)},
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
\textup{in particular $\sigma_3(PSU(3,8),\mathcal{U})=7$ and $\sigma_3(PSU(3,32),\mathcal{U})=27$;  for $q$ even with $d=3$, equivalently $q=2^{2m+1}>2$, the $C_3$- and trivial-suborbit multiplicities are proved for every $q$ in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}:  $(q-2)/2$ and $(q+1)/3$, respectively.}
\item \emph{Stabilizer structure.}  The block orbit consists of the collinear triples, with setwise stabilizer $\mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/d}\rtimes S_3$ of order $6(q+1)/d$ and $\lambda=q-1$ \textup{(\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:collinear}}\textup{)}}.  Every non-collinear triple has trivial pointwise stabilizer \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:psu-pointwise})}.  The remaining stabilizer refinement, namely the setwise stabilizer on the $k$ fixed
regular orbits having order $6$ and image $S_3$, is proved for $d=1$ and, for
the odd-$d=3$ case, by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-odd-fixed}};  the $C_3$-/trivial-
image distribution on the merged orbits is proved theoretically for $d=1$ and for
$d=3$ in \textup{Propositions \ref{prop:psu-odd} and \ref{prop:psu-even}}
\emph{(}the even-$d=3$ values in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}, the
odd-$d=3$ values in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}}\emph{)}, while
\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}} records the small-$q$ computational
refinement.  The $\lambda$-values then follow:  $\lambda=(q^2-1)/d$ on the fixed
orbits, and $\lambda=2(q^2-1)/d$ or $6(q^2-1)/d$ on the merged $C_3$- or
trivial-orbits.
\end{enumerate}
For $q=3^a$ \textup{(}$a\ge1$, $d=1$\textup{)} the theorem reduces to the previously stated classification \textup{(one fixed orbit with stabilizer $6$, $(q-1)/2$ merged orbits with stabilizer $3$, $\sigma_3=(q+3)/2$;  moreover in this range the field automorphism $\sigma\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x^q:y^q:z^q]$ fixes every $S$-orbit as a set, so no fusion occurs under $A=P\string\Gamma U(3,q)$ and $\sigma_3(A)=\sigma_3(S)$, as recorded in \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgu}(2),(3)}}).
head: environment
name: Unitary two-point suborbits and the three-point orbit number

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) $2$-transitivity and the cyclic two-point stabilizer are classical \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:unital}(3),(4));  cf.\ \cite{mitchell1911,huppert1967}}.  The regularity off the block follows exactly as in the $q=3^a$ case:  an element of $T$ fixing $x
\notin B$ fixes $\{\alpha,\beta,x\}$ pointwise, which contradicts the classical Singer-type action of $T$ \textup{(cf.\ \cite{mitchell1911})};  hence the $qd$ regular $T$-orbits off $B$, each of length $|T|=(q^2-1)/d$.  The extension $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}=\langle T,\tau\rangle$ with $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}/T\cong C_2$ is the classical normalizer of the (toroidal) two-point stabilizer \textup{(\cite{mitchell1911,huppert1967})}:  $T$ is the Singer cycle, and its normalizer in $PSU(3,q)$ is $\langle T,\tau\rangle$ with $\tau$ an involutory unitary reflection interchanging $\alpha,\beta$ and acting on $T$ by the anti-toroidal automorphism
\[
\tau\,t\,\tau^{-1}=t^{-q}\qquad(t\in T),
\]
the standard structure of the torus normalizer (cf.\ \cite{mitchell1911,huppert1967});  the identity is verified computationally for every $q\le27$ in \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}}, and the existence of an order-$2$ representative interchanging $\alpha,\beta$ is confirmed there and in \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}.
\smallskip

(2) We first determine the fixed points of $\tau$, taken of order $2$ (which exists for every $q$ by (1)).  Since $\tau$ is an isometry of order $2$ of a $3$-dimensional nondegenerate Hermitian space $V$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ with Witt index $1$:
\emph{if $q$ is odd}, $\tau$ has eigenvalues $\{1,1,-1\}$ with an eigenvalue-$1$ plane $L_\tau$ and an eigenvalue-$(-1)$ line $p_\tau$, and $V=L_\tau\perp p_\tau$ is an orthogonal direct sum.  Since $\tau$ interchanges $\alpha$ and $\beta$, neither $\alpha$ nor $\beta$ lies on $L_\tau\cup p_\tau$, and $L_\tau
\ne B$;  moreover $\alpha+\beta\in B$ is a fixed vector of $\tau$ (in projective notation $\tau(\alpha+\beta)=\alpha+\beta$), and it is anisotropic:  $h(\alpha+\beta,\alpha+\beta)=2h(\alpha,\beta)$, and $h(\alpha,\beta)
\ne 0$ because the polar line of the isotropic point $\alpha$ in the hyperbolic plane $B$ is the tangent $\langle\alpha\rangle$ (cf.\ \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:unital}(2)}), so $\beta
\notin\alpha^{\perp}$.  Hence $\alpha+\beta\in B\cap(L_\tau\cup p_\tau)$, and the point $w_0=L_\tau\cap B$ is anisotropic:  if $w_0$ were isotropic then $w_0\in B\cap\mathcal{U}$ would be a $\tau$-fixed unital point, and the remaining fixed point of the involution $\tau|_B$ on the projective line $B$ would lie on $p_\tau$, forcing $\tau(\alpha+\beta)=-(\alpha+\beta)$ (as $p_\tau$ is the eigenvalue-$(-1)$ line), contradicting $\tau(\alpha+\beta)=\alpha+\beta$;  so $w_0
\notin\mathcal{U}$.  Also $L_\tau$ cannot be anisotropic:  the Witt index is additive over the orthogonal direct sum, $1=\mathrm{WI}(L_\tau)+\mathrm{WI}(p_\tau)$, and $p_\tau$ has $\mathrm{WI}=0$, forcing $\mathrm{WI}(L_\tau)=1$.  Hence $L_\tau$ is a hyperbolic plane and $L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}$ consists of $q+1$ points, all off $B$ (as $w_0
\notin\mathcal{U}$);  $p_\tau$ is anisotropic (again by the Witt-index sum), so $p_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}=\varnothing$.  Consequently $\tau$ fixes exactly $q+1$ points off $B$ and none on $B$.
\emph{If $q$ is even}, $\tau$ is an isometric transvection (all eigenvalues $1$):  it fixes a plane $L_\tau$ pointwise, $L_\tau$ is degenerate with radical $w_0\in\mathcal{U}$, and $w_0\in B$ (the restriction $\tau|_B$ fixes a point of the line $B$, which lies in $L_\tau\cap B=\{w_0\}$).  Hence $\tau$ fixes the single unital point $w_0\in B$ and no point off $B$.
\smallskip

Now let $O=T\cdot x$ be a regular $T$-orbit off $B$.  Since $\tau T\tau^{-1}=T$, $\tau(O)$ is again a regular $T$-orbit, and $\tau(O)=O$ holds exactly when $O$ meets the fixed-point set $L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}$:  if $y\in O\cap(L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U})$, then $\tau(y)=y\in\tau(O)\cap O$, so $\tau(O)=O$;  conversely, if $\tau(O)=O$ and $q$ is odd, write $x\in O$, $\tau(x)=t_0x$, $t_0\in T$;  the map $tx\mapsto\tau(tx)=\tau t\tau^{-1}\tau(x)=t^{-q}t_0x$ has a fixed point iff $t^{-q}t_0=t$ for some $t$, i.e.\ iff $t_0\in T^{q+1}$, where $T^{q+1}=\{u^{q+1}:u\in T\}$ is a subgroup of index $\gcd(q+1,|T|)$ in the cyclic group $T$;  the inclusion $t_0\in T^{q+1}$ is equivalent to $O$ containing a $\tau$-fixed point \textup{(the points $y\in O$ with $\tau(y)=y$ are exactly those of the form $t x$ with $t^{q+1}=t_0$, of which there are $\gcd(q+1,|T|)$ provided one exists;  one always exists by the first part, applied to the hyperbolic line $L_\tau$)}.  Hence
\[
k=\#\{T\text{-orbits meeting }L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}\}
=\frac{|L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}|}{\gcd(|T|,q+1)}.
\]
Since $\gcd(|T|,q+1)=\gcd((q^2-1)/d,q+1)=(q+1)/d$ \textup{($d\mid q+1$ and $\gcd(q-1,d)=1$)} and $|L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}|=q+1$ for $q$ odd, $k=d$;  for $q$ even there are no fixed points off $B$, and any $\tau$-fixed $T$-orbit $O$ has odd length $|T|=(q^2-1)/d$ on which $\tau$ acts as an involution, hence would contain a $\tau$-fixed point off $B$, contradiction;  so $k=0$.  The values $k=1$ for $q=3,9$ (where the classical normalizer still contains order-$2$ representatives) are contained in the uniform statement and verified in \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}}.
\smallskip

The formula of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(3)} follows from \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}} and (2):  off the block, $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ has the $k$ fixed orbits of length $|T|$ (image $S_3$, one triple orbit each) and the $(qd-k)/2$ merged pairs of length $2|T|$, each merged pair carrying either image $C_3$ (one triple orbit) or trivial image (three suborbits fusing into one triple orbit);  the block orbit contributes the collinear triples \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:collinear}}).  The closed forms of (3) are then obtained from the multiplicity data of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}}:  for $d=1$ the counts are proved for every $q$ (one fixed $S_3$-orbit together with $(q-1)/2$ resp.\ $q/2$ $C_3$-merged orbits and no trivial suborbit), and for $d=3$ the counts $(q-5)/2$ and $(q+1)/3$ of $C_3$-orbits and $q+1$ of trivial suborbits hold for $q$ odd \textup{(computed values for $q\le49$;  verified for $q\le27$ in \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}}}\textup{)}, while for $q$ even (equivalently $q=2^{2m+1}$ when $d=3$) the $C_3$- and trivial-suborbit multiplicities are proved for every $q$ in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}} \textup{(}$(q-2)/2$ and $(q+1)/3$ respectively\textup{)}.
\smallskip

(3) By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-pointwise}} the pointwise stabilizer of a non-collinear triple is trivial, so $S_{\mathcal{O}}$ maps injectively into $S_3$ with stabilizer image $C_3$, $S_3$ or trivial.  On a fixed regular orbit $O$ \textup{(q odd;  for $q$ even there are none, by (2))} choose, by (2), a point $x\in O\cap(L_\tau\cap\mathcal U)$ fixed by $\tau$;  then $\tau(x)=x$, so $\tau$ permutes $\{\alpha,\beta,x\}$ as the transposition $(\alpha\,\beta)$ and lies in $S_{\{\alpha,\beta,x\}}$, whence the stabilizer image contains a transposition and $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\in\{2,6\}$.  By contrast, for $q$ even \textup{(equivalently $q=2^{2m+1}$ when $d=3$)} there are no fixed orbits by (2), and the even-$d=3$ closed forms of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}} account for every non-collinear orbit with stabilizer image $C_3$ or trivial, so no non-collinear stabilizer image contains a transposition;  a transposition-bearing stabilizer image $S_3$ among the non-collinear triples occurs only for $q$ odd, on the fixed orbits.  The value $6$ \textup{(image $S_3$)} on every fixed orbit is established in
\textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-odd-fixed}} for $q$ odd with $3\mid q+1$, the
occurrence of an order-$3$ element cyclically permuting $\{\alpha,\beta,x\}$ for
$x\in L_\tau\cap\mathcal U$, forced by the symmetry $\tau(x)=x$;  this is part of
the computed census for $q=3,9,27$ \textup{(Table \ref{tab:psu-pgu};  Chapter
\ref{sec:verify})};  for $q$ even there are no fixed orbits by (2).  With
$|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ on the fixed orbits, \eqref{eq:lambda} gives
$\lambda=6(q^2-1)/(d\cdot6)=(q^2-1)/d$.  On a merged orbit $\{\alpha,\beta,x\}$ the image is $C_3$ precisely when some order-$3$ element permutes the three points cyclically;  the numbers of such orbits in each congruence class of $q$ are the integers listed in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}}, obtained from \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}} for $q\le49$ (and, for the $C_3$-counts, confirmed by the class analysis of the order-$3$ elements of $PSU(3,q)$:  the $C_3$-orbits correspond to the $3$-cycles of the order-$3$ elements with one fixed point, cf.\ the remark below).  The $\lambda$-values follow from \eqref{eq:lambda}.

label: prop:psu-diag
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Diagonal-overgroup orbit number of $\PGU(3,q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}} the suborbit map in $PGU(3,q)$ is a bijection on those triple orbits whose induced image contains a $3$-cycle \textup{(sufficient condition of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}}}\textup{)}.  The collinear orbits carry the full $S_3$ from $PGL(2,q)$.  For the non-collinear orbits the image is $C_3$ or $S_3$:  the diagonal element $\delta$ of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgu}(1b)} supplies a $3$-cycle on every non-collinear orbit that meets a $\delta$-cycle, and the order-$3$ elements already in $S$ act likewise on the remaining non-collinear orbits.  That every non-collinear $PGU(3,q)$-orbit is covered in this way, equivalently that the induced image of every non-collinear triple orbit contains a $3$-cycle, is established for every $q$ by the independent coordinate proof below \textup{(the order-$3$ diagonal element of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgu}(1b)} cyclically permutes the three points of a non-collinear triple, so \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}} applies)}\textup{)}.  By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}}, $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q),\mathcal{U})=1+\#\{$orbits of $G^{\mathrm{PGU}}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ off $B\}$, where $G^{\mathrm{PGU}}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ is the setwise stabilizer of the pair in $PGU(3,q)$, of order $2(q^2-1)$ \textup{(the cyclic torus $T^{\mathrm{PGU}}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{q^2-1}$ together with $\tau$)}.  The cyclic part acts regularly off $B$ (of length $q^2-1$), giving $q$ regular $T^{\mathrm{PGU}}$-orbits;  $\tau$ fixes as sets exactly the orbits meeting the hyperbolic line $L_\tau$ of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(2)}, and their number is
\[
\#\{T^{\mathrm{PGU}}\text{-orbits meeting }L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}\}
=\frac{|L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}|}{\gcd(|T^{\mathrm{PGU}}|,q+1)}
=\frac{q+1}{q+1}=1
\qquad(q\ \text{odd}),
\]
while for $q$ even $\tau$ has no fixed point off $B$ by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(2)}, so no regular orbit is fixed.  Hence $G^{\mathrm{PGU}}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ has, off $B$, $1+(q-1)/2$ orbits for $q$ odd and $q/2$ orbits for $q$ even, giving $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))=(q+3)/2$ and $(q+2)/2$ respectively.  Equivalently, for $q$ odd the $q$ regular $T^{\mathrm{PGU}}$-orbits pair up under $\tau$ with the single fixed orbit, and the $d=3$ diagonal element $\delta$ realizes this fusion inside $PGU(3,q)$ (cf.\ (1b) of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgu}}).  The case $q=2$ gives $\sigma_3(PGU(3,2))=2$, in agreement with the formula $(q+2)/2$ \textup{(Table \ref{tab:psu-general})}.

\smallskip
\emph{Independent coordinate proof of the orbit number (every $q$).}  Let $K=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, $\bar x=x^q$, and let $h(x_0,x_1,x_2)=x_0\bar x_2+x_1\bar x_1+x_2\bar x_0$ be the standard Hermitian form, so that $\mathcal{U}=\{\langle(x_0,x_1,x_2)\rangle:h(x_0,x_1,x_2)=0\}$.  Put $P=\langle(1,0,0)\rangle$ and $Q=\langle(0,0,1)\rangle$.  As $PGU(3,q)$ is $2$-transitive on $\mathcal{U}$, every three-subset is $\{P,Q,R\}$ for a third point $R$;  off the block $PQ$ write $R=R(x,y)=\langle(x,y,1)\rangle$ with $y
\ne 0$, the isotropy condition being $x+\bar x+y\bar y=0$.  Set $u=y\bar y\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ and $z=x/u$;  then $z\in\mathcal{Z}:=\{z\in K:z+\bar z=-1\}$, and the trace map $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{F}_q}$ has kernel of size $q$, so $|\mathcal{Z}|=q$.  An element of the ordered two-point stabilizer $G_{(P,Q)}$ is diagonal $D=\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)$ with $a\bar c=b\bar b=c\bar a$, so with $t=a/c$, $s=b/c$ it acts as $R(x,y)\mapsto R(tx,sy)$, where $t=s\bar s\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$;  hence $u\mapsto tu$ and $x\mapsto tx$, so $z$ is fixed, and conversely any two points with the same parameter $z$ are joined by $\operatorname{diag}(t,s,1)$ with $s=y'/y$.  Thus $G_{(P,Q)}$ acts transitively on the points of parameter $z$, and its non-collinear orbits are parameterised by $z\in\mathcal{Z}$.  The matrix
\[
w=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
interchanges $P,Q$, preserves $h$, has $\det w=-1$, and sends $R(x,y)$ to $R(x^{-1},y/x)$, whence $z\mapsto\bar z=-1-z$.  So $G_{\{P,Q\}}=G_{(P,Q)}\rtimes\langle w\rangle$ has, off $B$, the orbit space $\mathcal{Z}/\langle\iota\rangle$ with $\iota\colon z\mapsto-1-z$.  The fixed points of $\iota$ solve $2z=-1$:  for $q$ odd there is the unique fixed point $z=-1/2$ and $|\mathcal{Z}/\langle\iota\rangle|=(q+1)/2$ by Burnside;  for $q$ even, $2=0$ gives no fixed point and $|\mathcal{Z}/\langle\iota\rangle|=q/2$.  The points of the block $PQ$ other than $P,Q$ are $\langle(x,0,1)\rangle$ with $x\in T:=\{x\in K:x+\bar x=0\}$, a one-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-space on which the diagonal elements $t\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ act regularly, so all collinear triples form a single $PGU(3,q)$-orbit.  Therefore $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q),\mathcal{U})=1+(q+1)/2$ for $q$ odd and $1+q/2$ for $q$ even, as stated.
head: environment

label: rem:psu-diag-dist
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:psu-diag-dist}
For $q$ odd with $3\mid q+1$ ($d=3$), the fusion of the $S$-orbits under the diagonal overgroup $G=PGU(3,q)$ is recorded in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag}}:  $\sigma_3(G)=(q+3)/2$.  The setwise stabilizer distribution behind this count is as follows:  on the blocks there is a single orbit, of setwise stabilizer order $6(q+1)$ (the full cyclic torus $T^{\mathrm{PGU}}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}$ together with $S_3$);  off the blocks there is $1$ orbit of order $6$ (image $S_3$, the three $S$-fixed orbits of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}} fused by the order-$3$ diagonal element $\delta$) together with $(q-1)/2$ orbits of order $3$ (image $C_3$).  Indeed $\delta$ cyclically permutes the three points of every non-collinear $S$-orbit on which it acts, so the $C_3$-orbits and the trivial orbits of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}} merge into the $(q-1)/2=(q-5)/6+(q+1)/3$ order-$3$ orbits of $G$, and no orbit of trivial image survives in the overgroup.  This distribution is verified in GAP for $q=5,11,17,23$:  collinear order $6(q+1)$;  non-collinear order $6$ (once) and order $3$ ($(q-1)/2$ times);  $\sigma_3=(q+3)/2$.  The count $\sigma_3(G)=(q+3)/2$ follows for general $q$ from the suborbit argument of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag}};  the stabilizer-order distribution is verified computationally as stated.
head: environment
name: The diagonal-overgroup stabilizer distribution

label: lem:psu-pointwise
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psu-pointwise}
Let $S=PSU(3,q)$, $q\ge3$, act on the Hermitian unital $\mathcal{U}$, and let $T$ be a triple of points not contained in a block.  Then the pointwise stabilizer $S_{(T)}$ is trivial.
head: environment
name: Trivial pointwise stabilizers of non-collinear triples

title: Proof
body_md: Fix two points $\alpha,\beta$ of $T$ and put $B$ for the block through them.  Any element of $S_{(T)}$ fixes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ pointwise, hence lies in the pointwise two-point stabilizer $T=S_{\alpha,\beta}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{(q^2-1)/d}$;  it also fixes the third point $x\in T\setminus\{\alpha,\beta\}$, which lies off $B$.  By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(1)} $T$ acts regularly on $\mathcal{U}\setminus B$, so no non-identity element of $T$ fixes $x$.  Hence $S_{(T)}=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:psu-c3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psu-c3}
Let $q\ge3$ with $d=\gcd(3,q+1)=3$ (equivalently $q=2^{2m+1}>2$, or $q$ odd with
$3\mid q+1$), and write $K=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, $F=\mathbb{F}_q$,
$K^1=\{a\in K^{\times}:a^{q+1}=1\}$.  Let $S=PSU(3,q)$ act on $\mathcal{U}$, fix
$\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{U}$ with block $B$ through them, and write the third point as
$\gamma=(1,u,z)$ in the coordinates $\alpha=e_1$, $\beta=e_2$, so that
$\gamma\in\mathcal{U}\setminus B$ iff $u
\notin F^{\times}$ and $z
\ne 0$ satisfy
$\mathrm{Tr}_{K/F}(u)+N_{K/F}(z)=0$.  Then the image of $S_{\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}}$
in $S_3$ contains a $3$-cycle if and only if
\[
\frac{\bar u}{u}\in (K^1)^3.
\]
head: environment
name: The $C_3$-criterion on the unital

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v_1=\alpha$, $v_2=\beta$, $v_3=\gamma$ and let
$\Gamma=\bigl(h(v_i,v_j)\bigr)_{i,j}$ be the Gram matrix of the triple, namely
\[
\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&\bar u\\1&0&1\\u&1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
An element $g\inPGU(3,q)$ inducing the cycle $\sigma=(123)$ on $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$
is a similarity of $\Gamma$:  $g(v_i)=\lambda_i\,v_{\sigma(i)}$ with
$\lambda_i\in K^{\times}$ and
$\lambda_i\lambda_j^q\,\Gamma_{\sigma(i)\sigma(j)}=
u\,\Gamma_{ij}$ for some
$
u\in F^{\times}$.  This system reduces to
\[
\lambda_1\lambda_2^q=
u,\quad \lambda_1\lambda_3^q=
u\bar u,\quad
\lambda_2\lambda_3^q\,u=
u,\quad \lambda_3\lambda_1^q=
u u,
\]
and admits a solution in $K^{\times}$ for every $u
\ne 0$ (e.g.\
$\lambda_2=\lambda_1/N(u)$, $\lambda_3=
u u/\lambda_1^q$ with $\lambda_1$ chosen so
that $N(\lambda_1)=
u N(u)$).  Hence a $3$-cycle is realized in $PGU(3,q)$ for
every $u
\ne 0$.  Its class in $PGU(3,q)/PSU(3,q)\cong C_3$ is computed as follows.  Let $g$ be the matrix of the cycle in the basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$:  $g(v_1)=\lambda_1v_2$, $g(v_2)=\lambda_2v_3$, $g(v_3)=\lambda_3v_1$, so $\det g=\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3$.  From the four equations $\lambda_2=\lambda_1/N(u)$, $\lambda_3=
u u/\lambda_1^q$ and $N(\lambda_1)=
u N(u)$, whence
\[
\det g=\frac{\lambda_1^3\,u}{N(u)^2},
\]
and in particular $\det g^{q+1}=
u^3$, as for every unitary similitude of multiplier $
u$.  Since $PGU(3,q)=\operatorname{GU}(3,q)/\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ and $PSU(3,q)=\operatorname{SU}(3,q)/\mu_3$, an element represented by a similitude $A$ with multiplier $
u_A$ lies in $PSU(3,q)$ iff some $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ satisfies $N(c)
u_A=1$ and $c^3\det A=1$;  as $N(c)=c^2$ for $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$, this is equivalent to $\det A^2=
u_A^3$, the condition $\det A\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ being automatic ($\det A^{q+1}=
u_A^3$ and $\det A^2=
u_A^3$ force $\det A^{q-1}=1$).  For our cycle,
\[
\det g^2=
u^3 \iff \frac{\lambda_1^6u^2}{N(u)^4}=\frac{N(\lambda_1)^3}{N(u)^3}
\iff u^{q-1}=(\lambda_1^{q-1})^{-3},
\]
using $N(\lambda_1)=
u N(u)$;  as $\lambda_1^{q-1}\in K^1$ and $(K^1)^3$ is closed
under inversion, this is equivalent to $u^{q-1}=\bar u/u\in(K^1)^3$.  Hence a determinant-$1$ representative exists in $PSU(3,q)$ (equivalently $S_{\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}}$ contains a $3$-cycle) precisely when $\bar u/u\in(K^1)^3$, and the criterion is independent of the choice of $\lambda_1$.  The criterion, together with its
consequences in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}, is verified for $q=8,32$
in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}};  the proof uses only the Gram determinant
class modulo $(K^1)^3$ and the identification $PGU(3,q)/PSU(3,q)\cong C_3$, and
hence holds verbatim for odd $q$ with $3\mid q+1$ \textup{(supplemented by the
verification for $q=5,11,17,23$ in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}})}.
head: environment

label: prop:psu-even
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: The even-$d=3$ unitary case: closed forms

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(2)}, $k=0$ for $q$ even, so off $B$ the
group $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ has $(qd-k)/2=3q/2$ merged suborbits of length
$2|T|=2(q^2-1)/3$, none fixed by $\tau$ as a set.
(2) For $\gamma=(1,u,z)$ with $u
\notin F^{\times}$, $z
\ne 0$, the criterion of
\textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-c3}} says that $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ is of $C_3$-type
iff $\bar u/u\in(K^1)^3$.  The map $uF^{\times}\mapsto\bar u/u$ identifies
$K^{\times}/F^{\times}\cong K^1$;  $|K^1|=q+1$ and $(K^1)^3$ has index $3$ inside
$K^1$ (as $\gcd(3,q+1)=3$).  The collinear coset ($u\in F^{\times}$) corresponds to
$\bar u/u=1\in(K^1)^3$, so the number of non-collinear $C_3$-type cosets is
$|(K^1)^3|-1=(q+1)/3-1=(q-2)/3$.  Each coset carries $q-1$ values of $u$, and for
each such $u$ the $q+1$ values $z
\ne 0$ with $\mathrm{Tr}_{K/F}(u)+N_{K/F}(z)=0$;
hence the $C_3$-type non-collinear points number
$\frac{q-2}{3}(q-1)(q+1)$.  Since $T=S_{\alpha,\beta}$ acts regularly on
$\mathcal{U}\setminus B$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(1))}, these split into
\[
\frac{\frac{q-2}{3}(q-1)(q+1)}{(q^2-1)/3}=q-2
\]
regular $T$-suborbits, which by (1) pair under $\tau$ into $(q-2)/2$ merged
$C_3$-suborbits;  each yields one $C_3$-orbit of $S$ \textup{(Lemma
\ref{lem:suborbit})}.  Thus $m_{C_3}=(q-2)/2$, and by \eqref{eq:lambda}
$\lambda=6(q^2-1)/(d\cdot3)=2(q^2-1)/3$.
(3) By (1) and (2) the trivial merged suborbits number $3q/2-(q-2)/2=q+1$.  A
$C_3$-orbit contributes one merged suborbit, while a trivial orbit (trivial setwise
stabilizer) contributes exactly three:  its three $2$-subsets are singletons under the
trivial image, and $\hat T=G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ of order $2(q^2-1)/3$ acts freely on
the $\lambda=2(q^2-1)$ blocks through $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ of that orbit (the block
stabilizer is $S_{\mathcal{O}}\cap\hat T=1$), splitting them into
$\lambda/|\hat T|=3$ suborbits.  Hence $m_1=(q+1)/3$, $\lambda=2(q^2-1)$, and
\[
\sigma_3(S,\mathcal{U})=1+\frac{q-2}{2}+\frac{q+1}{3}=\frac{5q+2}{6}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:psu-odd-fixed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psu-odd-fixed}
Let $q$ be odd with $d=\gcd(3,q+1)=3$, and let $S=PSU(3,q)$ act on the unital
$\mathcal{U}$.  Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{U}$ be a pair on a block $B$, let
$\tau\in S_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ be the order-$2$ involutory unitary reflection fixing
the hyperbolic plane $L_\tau$ pointwise, and let $x\in L_\tau\cap\mathcal{U}$.  Then
the image of $S_{\{\alpha,\beta,x\}}$ in $S_3$ is the full $S_3$;  in particular
$|S_{\{\alpha,\beta,x\}}|=6$.
head: environment
name: Fixed orbits carry the full $S_3$ image

title: Proof
body_md:
Take coordinates $\alpha=e_1$, $\beta=e_2$ with $h(\alpha,\beta)=1$ and $e_3$
anisotropic and orthogonal to $\mathrm{Span}\{\alpha,\beta\}$, normalized so that
$\tau(\alpha)=\beta$ and $\tau(\beta)=\alpha$.  By \textup{Theorem
\ref{thm:main-psu}(2)}, $L_\tau\cap B$ is the anisotropic point $w_0
\notin\mathcal{U}$,
so $x
\notin B$ and $x$ is not collinear with $\alpha,\beta$.  The first coordinate of
$x$ is nonzero:  otherwise $x\in\mathrm{Span}\{e_2,e_3\}$ with $x_1=0$, and
$h(x,x)=x_3x_3^q=|x_3|^2=0$ forces $x_3=0$, so $x\in\mathrm{Span}\{e_2\}\subseteq B$, a
contradiction.  Normalize $x_1=1$ and write $x=(1,u,z)$.
Since $\tau$ fixes $L_\tau$ pointwise, $\tau(x)=x$;  and $\tau$ being an isometry
fixing $\alpha,\beta$ up to interchange gives $\tau(e_1)=e_2$, $\tau(e_2)=e_1$, while
$\tau(e_3)\perp\mathrm{Span}\{\tau(e_1),\tau(e_2)\}=\mathrm{Span}\{e_1,e_2\}$, hence
$\tau(e_3)=s\,e_3$ with $s^2=1$.  Comparing components of
$\tau(x)=\tau(x_1e_1+x_2e_2+x_3e_3)=x_1e_2+x_2e_1+x_3se_3=x_1e_1+x_2e_2+x_3e_3$
gives $x_2=x_1$, whence $u=x_2/x_1=1$.  By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-c3}} the image
contains a $3$-cycle, since $\bar u/u=1\in(K^1)^3$.  Together with the transposition
$(\alpha\,\beta)$ induced by $\tau$, the image is the full $S_3$.  By \textup{Lemma
\ref{lem:psu-pointwise}} the pointwise stabilizer is trivial, so
$|S_{\{\alpha,\beta,x\}}|=6$.
head: environment

label: prop:psu-odd
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: The odd-$d=3$ unitary case: closed forms

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(2)} $k=d=3$, so there are $3$ fixed regular
$T$-orbits off $B$;  by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-odd-fixed}} each carries the full
$S_3$ image, giving $m_{S_3}=3$ and, by \eqref{eq:lambda},
$\lambda=6(q^2-1)/(d\cdot6)=(q^2-1)/3$.
(2) By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-c3}}, a non-collinear $\gamma=(1,u,z)$ is of
$C_3$-type iff $\bar u/u\in(K^1)^3$.  As in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}(2)},
the number of non-collinear $C_3$-type cosets is $|(K^1)^3|-1=(q-2)/3$, each carrying
$q-1$ values of $u$ and $q+1$ values $z
\ne 0$;  hence the $C_3$-type non-collinear
points number $\frac{q-2}{3}(q-1)(q+1)$, which split under the regular action of
$T=S_{\alpha,\beta}$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(1))} into
$\frac{\frac{q-2}{3}(q-1)(q+1)}{(q^2-1)/3}=q-2$ regular $T$-suborbits.  The $3$
fixed orbits satisfy the criterion (their image $S_3$ contains a $3$-cycle), so they
lie among these $q-2$ suborbits;  the remaining $q-5$ contain no $\tau$-fixed point
and pair under $\tau$ into $(q-5)/2$ merged $C_3$-suborbits, each giving one
$C_3$-orbit of $S$ \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit})}.  Thus $m_{C_3}=(q-5)/2$.
(3) By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(2)}, $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ has, off $B$,
$k+(qd-k)/2=3+(3q-3)/2=(3q+3)/2$ suborbits.  A $C_3$-orbit contributes one merged
suborbit, an $S_3$-orbit one, and a trivial orbit three (its three $2$-subsets are
singletons under the trivial image);  hence
$3+m_{C_3}+3m_1=(3q+3)/2$, giving $3m_1=(3q+3)/2-3-(q-5)/2=q+1$, so
$m_1=(q+1)/3$.  Consequently
\[
\sigma_3(S,\mathcal{U})=1+3+\frac{q-5}{2}+\frac{q+1}{3}
=1+3+\frac{3q-15+2q+2}{6}=\frac{5q+11}{6}.
\]

label: prop:psu-computed
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Computed stabilizer refinement for $q\le49$

label: rem:psu-general-computation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:psu-general-computation}
The geometric content of the proof of (2) is the following.  For $q$ odd the involution $\tau$ fixes the hyperbolic plane $L_\tau$ pointwise and the anisotropic line $p_\tau$ pointwise;  $L_\tau\cap B=\{w_0\}$ is an anisotropic point (proved via $\alpha+\beta$, which is $\tau$-fixed and anisotropic, not lying in $p_\tau$), so the $q+1$ isotropic points of $L_\tau$ are exactly the fixed points of $\tau$ off the block, and $\tau$ fixes none of the block points.  For $q$ even the transvection $\tau$ fixes the tangent plane through $w_0\in B\cap\mathcal{U}$ pointwise, so it has no fixed point off $B$.  This is confirmed by the computed values $\operatorname{fix}(\tau;\mathcal{U}\setminus B)=q+1$ ($q$ odd) and $0$ ($q$ even) of \textup{Table \ref{tab:psu-general}}.
\smallskip

The $C_3$-stabilizer orbits are the non-collinear three-cycles of the order-$3$ elements of $PSU(3,q)$:  an order-$3$ element $g$ fixes a set $F$ of unital points with $|F|\equiv q^3+1\pmod3$, where $|F|=1$ precisely when $3\mid q$ (then the remaining $q^3$ points split into $q^3/3$ three-cycles), while $|F|\in\{0,3\}$ when $3\mid q+1$;  and a non-collinear triple whose setwise stabilizer contains a $C_3$ is a three-cycle of \emph{exactly one} such element (two order-$3$ elements sharing a non-collinear three-cycle differ by an element fixing that triple pointwise, hence agree by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(4)});  the collinear three-cycles are the blocks, already accounted for in the block orbit.  The distribution of the $C_3$-orbits among the merged orbits is read off from \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}} for $q\le49$ and recorded in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}};  the pattern stated there is the observed one and is proved in the $d=1$ rows and in the $d=3$ rows \emph{(}the odd-$d=3$ rows in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}}, the even-$d=3$ rows in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}\emph{)}.  On the fixed orbits the required $3$-cycle, an order-$3$ element cyclically permuting $\{\alpha,\beta,x\}$ with $x\in L_\tau\cap\mathcal U$, is proved for every $q$ odd with $3\mid q+1$ in \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-odd-fixed}}:  the symmetry $\tau(x)=x$ forces the second coordinate $u$ of the normalized point $x=(1,u,z)$ to be $1$, whence $\bar u/u=1\in(K^1)^3$ and the criterion of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-c3}} applies;  the order-$6$ values of the fixed-orbit column of \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}} therefore no longer rest on computational input but follow from \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:psu-odd-fixed}}.
head: environment
name: The fixed line of $\tau$; the order-$3$ elements

label: rem:psu-types
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:psu-types}
For the theoretically settled cases ($d=1$) \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}} gives, in addition to the collinear orbit $(\lambda=q-1)$, the non-collinear orbits with stabilizer $S_3$ (the $k$ fixed orbits, $k=1$) and the $(q-1)/2$ merged orbits with stabilizer $C_3$, together with the closed forms $\sigma_3(PSU(3,q))$ and $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))$.  For $q=3^a$ this reduces to one non-collinear orbit with stabilizer $S_3$ and $\lambda=q^2-1$ plus $\frac{q-1}{2}$ orbits with stabilizer $C_3$ and $\lambda=2(q^2-1)$;  for $q$ even with $d=1$ the $(q/2)$ merged orbits all have image $C_3$.  For the remaining cases the stabilizer types and multiplicities are proved in \textup{Propositions \ref{prop:psu-odd} and \ref{prop:psu-even}} \textup{(the odd-$d=3$ case in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}}, the even-$d=3$ case in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}})}), with the small-$q$ computational refinement recorded in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}} and \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}.

name: The non-collinear types

title: Remark
body_md: For $q=3$ \textup{(}$a=1$\textup{)} the unital has $28$ points and $S=PSU(3,3)$ of order $6048$;  \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}} gives the three systems $2$-$(28,3,2)$, $2$-$(28,3,16)$ and $2$-$(28,3,8)$ \textup{(}collinear, and non-collinear with stabilizers $3,6$\textup{)}, in agreement with \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}.  For $q=2$ \textup{(}excluded from the theorem but included in the tables\textup{)} the stabilizers are $1$ \textup{(}non-collinear\textup{)} and $6$ \textup{(}collinear\textup{)}:  $|\mathcal{U}|=9$, $|S|=72$.
