label: cor:psu-designs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:psu-designs}
The distinct triple systems with point set the unital and automorphism group containing $PSU(3,q)$ correspond to the orbits in \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}.  Since $|S|=q^3(q^3+1)(q^2-1)/d$ and $v=q^3+1$,
\[
\lambda = \frac{6|S|}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\,v(v-1)}
=\frac{6\,q^3(q^3+1)(q^2-1)/d}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\,(q^3+1)q^3}
=\frac{6(q^2-1)}{d\,|S_{\mathcal{O}}|},
\]
and $\lambda$ is an integer for every orbit that occurs \textup{(}\textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}, \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}\textup{)}.  In particular, for a collinear triple, $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6(q+1)/d$ \textup{(}\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:collinear}}\textup{)} gives
\[
\lambda=\frac{6(q^2-1)}{d\cdot 6(q+1)/d}=q-1,
\]
an integer for every $q$:  the collinear orbit yields the triple system $2$-\mbox{$(q^3+1,3,q-1)$}.  By \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:union-orbits}}, every nonempty union of these orbit designs is a $PSU(3,q)$-invariant triple system whose parameter is the corresponding subset sum of the orbit parameters.  \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(4)} and \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-computed}} determine the complete non-collinear $\lambda$-list:  the $k$ fixed orbits ($|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$) give $\lambda=(q^2-1)/d$, the $C_3$-orbits give $\lambda=2(q^2-1)/d$, and the orbits with trivial stabilizer give $\lambda=6(q^2-1)/d$, with the multiplicities
{\small
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
& q\ \text{odd},\ d=1 & q\ \text{odd},\ d=3 & q\ \text{even} \\ \hline
\lambda=(q^2-1)/d & 1 & 3\ \text{(proved)} & 0 \\
\lambda=2(q^2-1)/d & \tfrac{q-1}{2} & \tfrac{q-5}{2}\ \text{(proved)} & \tfrac{q}{2}\ \text{(d=1)},\ \tfrac{q-2}{2}\ \text{(d=3,\ proved)} \\
\lambda=6(q^2-1)/d & 0 & \tfrac{q+1}{3}\ \text{(proved)} & 0\ \text{(d=1)},\ \tfrac{q+1}{3}\ \text{(d=3,\ proved)}
\end{array}
\]
}
with the odd-$d=3$ entries proved for every $q$ with $3\mid q+1$ in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-odd}} and the even-$d=3$ entries proved for every $q=2^{2m+1}$ in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-even}}.
Thus, for instance:  $q=3^a$ ($d=1$, odd):  one system $2$-\mbox{$(q^3+1,3,q^2-1)$} and $\frac{q-1}{2}$ copies of $2$-\mbox{$(q^3+1,3,2(q^2-1))$} (e.g.\ $q=3$:  $2$-$(28,3,2)$, $2$-$(28,3,16)$, $2$-$(28,3,8)$;  $q=9$:  $2$-$(730,3,8)$, $2$-$(730,3,80)$ and four copies of $2$-$(730,3,160)$);  $q=5$ ($d=3$):  three systems $2$-$(126,3,8)$ and two systems $2$-$(126,3,48)$, no $C_3$-orbits \textup{($\tfrac{q-5}{2}=0$;  the three fixed $S_3$-orbits give $\lambda=8$ and the $(q+1)/3=2$ trivial orbits give $\lambda=48$, see \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}})};  $q=4$ ($d=1$):  $\lambda=3$ (collinear) and $30$ (non-collinear);  $q=8$ ($d=3$):  $\lambda=7$ (collinear), $42$ (three $C_3$-orbits) and $126$ (three trivial orbits);  $q=2$ ($d=3$):  $\lambda=1$ (collinear, the affine plane $\mathrm{STS}(9)$) and $6$ (the unique non-collinear orbit).  All values are listed in \textup{Section \ref{sec:params}}.

name: Design parameters for the unitary family

label: thm:pgu
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Overgroups of $\PSU(3,q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
(1a) As in \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:collinear}}, with the pointwise stabilizer now of order $q+1$:  the block stabilizer has shape $\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}\rtimesPGL(2,q)$-type (a quotient of the full unitary point stabilizer), and its kernel on a collinear triple is the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}$ (a direct coordinate computation with the standard Hermitian form;  cf.\ \cite{mitchell1911});  the diagonal element $\delta$ of order $3$ acts with $3$-cycles on the unital and does \emph{not} fix the triple pointwise, so the kernel is the cyclic part, not the diagonal.
(1b) In the standard coordinates of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:unital}}, the diagonal element is $\delta\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x:y:\zeta z]$ with $\zeta^{q+1}=1$, $\zeta
\ne1$, of order $3$ when $3\mid q+1$.  A unital point satisfies $x^{q+1}+y^{q+1}+z^{q+1}=0$;  since $(\zeta z)^{q+1}=z^{q+1}$, the three points $[x:y:z]$, $[x:y:\zeta z]$, $[x:y:\zeta^2 z]$ all lie on the unital, and they are distinct precisely when $z
\ne 0$.  Hence $\delta$ permutes the unital points with $3$-cycles on the set $z
\ne 0$ and fixes pointwise the sub-unital $z=0$;  in particular a triple of the stated form is a $3$-cycle for $\delta$, so $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ contains $\delta$ and the image contains $C_3$.  A transposition of the three points is not realized by $\delta$.
(2) In the standard coordinates a field automorphism is $\sigma\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x^{p^k}:y^{p^k}:z^{p^k}]$;  it fixes precisely the points of the sub-unital $\mathcal{U}'$ over the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{p^{f/f'}}$ \textup{(those with coordinates in $\mathbb{F}_{p^{f/f'}}$}\textup{)} pointwise, it preserves the Hermitian equation \textup{(the form is defined over $\mathbb{F}_p$}\textup{)}, collinearity is preserved, and orbit types are preserved because $\sigma$ normalizes $S$.
head: environment

label: prop:psu-field-nofusion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:psu-field-nofusion}
Let $q\ge3$, let $S=PSU(3,q)\le G=PGU(3,q)$ act on the Hermitian unital $\mathcal{U}$, and let $\sigma\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x^q:y^q:z^q]$ be the field conjugation of order $2$ \textup{(the field automorphism fixing $\mathbb{F}_q$ pointwise}\textup{)}.  Then $\sigma$ fixes every $G$-orbit on three-subsets of $\mathcal{U}$ as a set, and consequently
\[
\sigma_3(\langle G,\sigma\rangle,\mathcal{U})=\sigma_3(G,\mathcal{U}),
\]
so the field conjugation causes no additional fusion beyond the diagonal fusion of $G$, for every $q\ge3$.  \textup{(The full field-automorphism group is analysed separately in \textup{Remark \ref{rem:psu-field}}:  it fuses certain $G$-orbits, e.g.\ for $q=8$ and $q=25$}\textup{)}.
head: environment
name: The field conjugation causes no fusion for general $q$

title: Proof
body_md:
The automorphism $\sigma$ fixes pointwise the sub-unital over $\mathbb{F}_q$ \textup{(the points with coordinates in $\mathbb{F}_q$}\textup{)}, preserves the Hermitian equation and collinearity, and normalizes $G$, so it sends $G$-orbits to $G$-orbits and preserves their setwise stabilizer orders and induced images in $S_3$.  The collinear orbit is unique \textup{(the blocks}\textup{)} and is preserved;  it remains to show that $\sigma$ preserves every non-collinear orbit.

Fix the base pair $\{\alpha,\beta\}=[e_1],[e_2]$ with block $B$, and write $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}=\langle T,\tau\rangle$, where $T\cong\mathbb{Z}_{(q^2-1)/d}$ acts regularly off $B$ and $\tau$ is an order-$2$ element interchanging $\alpha,\beta$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(1);  for $d=3$ the full torus $T^{\mathrm{PGU}}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{q^2-1}$ of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag}}}\textup{)}.  By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:suborbit}} every non-collinear $G$-orbit on triples is represented by $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ with $\gamma\in\mathcal{U}\setminus B$ \textup{(the suborbit map is surjective, and bijective when the induced image contains a $3$-cycle}\textup{)}.  Write $\gamma=(1,u,z)$, so that $\gamma\in\mathcal{U}\setminus B$ iff $u
\notin\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$ and $z
\ne 0$, and set $a=\overline{u}/u\in K^1$, where $K=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ and $K^1=\{w\in K^{\times}:w^{q+1}=1\}$.  Since $\tau\in G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ interchanges $\alpha$ and $\beta$, it acts on the parameters $a$ of the off-$B$ points by reversal $a\mapsto a^{-1}$ \textup{(the pairing $t\mapsto t^{-q}$ of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag}} is exactly this reversal on $K^1$;  cf.\ \textup{Remark \ref{rem:psu-diag-dist}}\textup{)}};  hence every non-collinear $G$-orbit, being represented by $\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ and by $\{\alpha,\beta,\tau(\gamma)\}$, contains points with parameters $a$ and $a^{-1}$;  the orbit is reversal-closed.  Now $\sigma$ sends $\gamma=(1,u,z)$ to $(1,u^q,z^q)$, hence maps the parameter $a$ to $\overline{u^q}/u^q=(\overline{u}/u)^q=a^q=a^{-1}$ \textup{(as $a\in K^1$}\textup{)}.  Thus $\sigma$ maps the reversal-closed parameter set of a non-collinear orbit to itself;  since the non-collinear $G$-orbits are parameterised by their reversal classes \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag} for $d=3$;  Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu}(3) for $d=1$}\textup{)}, $\sigma$ fixes every non-collinear orbit as a set.  Every $G$-orbit on triples is therefore fixed by $\sigma$ as a set;  since $\sigma$ normalizes $G$, every $\langle G,\sigma\rangle$-orbit on triples is a union of $G$-orbits, and fixing each $G$-orbit forces the two orbit sets to coincide, so $\sigma_3(\langle G,\sigma\rangle,\mathcal{U})=\sigma_3(G,\mathcal{U})$.
head: environment

label: rem:psu-field
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:psu-field}
For $q=3,9,27$ the field conjugation $\sigma\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x^q:y^q:z^q]$ of order $2$ fixes every $S$-orbit on three-subsets as a set \textup{(verified in GAP, Table \ref{tab:psu-pgu}:  cycle type $1^{q+1}2^{q(q^2-1)/2}$ on the $q^3+1$ points, with every $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$-suborbit fixed as a set}\textup{)}.  By \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-field-nofusion}} this no-fusion conclusion for the conjugation holds for every $q\ge3$:  $\sigma$ fixes every $PGU(3,q)$-orbit on three-subsets as a set, so $\sigma_3(\langlePGU(3,q),\sigma\rangle)=\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))$;  it reproduces the odd-$d=3$ statement of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-field-nofusion}} and the verified values $q=3,9,27$, and was checked directly in GAP for $q=5,11$ \textup{($\sigma$ added as a permutation on the $q^3+1$ points yields no new three-subset orbits}\textup{)}.  The full field part $P\string\Gamma U(3,q)/PGU(3,q)\cong C_{2f}$ is generated by the Frobenius automorphism $\sigma_p\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[x^p:y^p:z^p]$ ($p$ the characteristic), of which the conjugation $\sigma_q$ is the $f$-th power, $\sigma_q=\sigma_p^f$ (its unique order-$2$ element).  This generator structure explains the dichotomy:  $\sigma_q$ maps the parameter $a$ to $a^q=a^{-1}$, hence fixes every reversal-closed class and never fuses (Proposition~\ref{prop:psu-field-nofusion}, for every $q\ge3$), whereas $\sigma_p$ maps $a$ to $a^p$ and does fuse certain $PGU(3,q)$-orbits whenever $f>1$.  In the coordinate parameterization of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:psu-diag}}, the non-collinear $PGU(3,q)$-orbits are the classes $Z/\langle\iota\rangle$ with $Z=\{z\in K:z+\bar z=-1\}$ and $\iota\colon z\mapsto-1-z$, and $\sigma_p$ acts on these classes by $z\mapsto z^p$;  hence $\sigma_p$ fixes a $PGU(3,q)$-orbit precisely when $z^p=z$ or $z^p=-1-z$ for its representative $z$.  The number of such classes depends on the arithmetic of $q=p^f$ and is not given by a single closed form, so the full field part remains a computed value for the four cases $q=8,9,25,27$ rather than a family-wide statement.  Concretely, it is checked in GAP that $\sigma_3(P\string\Gamma U(3,q))=3$ for $q=8$ (even $d=3$;  $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))=(q+2)/2=5$), $=4$ for $q=9$ (odd $d=1$;  $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))=(q+3)/2=6$), $=8$ for $q=25$ (odd $d=1$, $f=2$;  $\sigma_3(PSU(3,q))=(q+3)/2=14$) and $=7$ for $q=27$ (odd $d=1$;  $\sigma_3(PGU(3,q))=15$), whereas the conjugation $\sigma_q$ alone leaves $\sigma_3$ unchanged in each case.  For $q=3$ ($f=1$) the field part is generated by $\sigma_p=\sigma_q$ alone and causes no fusion.  The orbit classification of the socle $PSU(3,q)$ and of the diagonal overgroup $PGU(3,q)$ is unaffected \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:main-psu};  Theorem \ref{thm:pgu}(1),(2))}.

label: thm:sz
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Three-point stabilizers for the Suzuki group

title: Proof
body_md:
The following classical facts are due to Suzuki \cite{suzuki1962} and are used as input.  Key facts:  the point stabilizer $S_{\alpha}$ is a Frobenius group of order $q^2(q-1)$ acting transitively on the remaining $q^2$ points;  the two-point stabilizer is cyclic of order $q-1$ (the split torus $S_{u,v}\cong C_{q-1}$) and acts semiregularly on the remaining $q^2-1$ points (Zassenhaus);  hence fixing three points forces the identity.  The dichotomy ``an involution swapping $x,y$ and fixing $z$ exists precisely for the circle triples'' is part of the classical Suzuki ovoid geometry (cf.\ \cite{suzuki1962});  it is used here as input and is verified computationally for $q=8$ \textup{(Table \ref{tab:verify})}.  The circles are the blocks of the classical $2$-$(q^2+1,q+1,1)$ design carried by the Suzuki ovoid (cf.\ \cite{suzuki1962}):  any two points lie on a unique circle.  The circle class is a single $S$-orbit:  given circles $B,B'$ and $x,y\in B$, $x',y'\in B'$, the $2$-transitivity of $S$ supplies $g$ with $g\{x,y\}=\{x',y'\}$, and $g(B)$ is the unique circle through $g(x),g(y)$, hence $g(B)=B'$.  To see that the non-circle stabilizer is trivial, let $X=\{x,y,z\}$ be a three-subset not contained in a circle.  Since $3
\nmid|S|$, the image of $S_X$ in $Sym(X)\cong S_3$ contains no element of order $3$;  by (1) the kernel of $S_X\toSym(X)$ is trivial, so the image is trivial or a $C_2$ generated by a transposition.  If the image were nontrivial, some $g\in S_X$ would interchange two points of $X$ and fix the third;  then $g^2$ fixes $X$ pointwise, so $g^2=1$ by (1), and $g$ is an involution of the type excluded by the dichotomy for non-circle triples.  Hence $S_X=1$ for every non-circle triple.  The orbit--design parameters follow in \textup{Corollary \ref{cor:sz-designs}}.

name: The Suzuki orbit number

title: Proof
head: environment

label: cor:sz-designs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:sz-designs}
Since $|S|=q^2(q^2+1)(q-1)$ and $v=q^2+1$, the formula \eqref{eq:lambda} gives
\[
\lambda=\frac{6|S|}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\,v(v-1)}
=\frac{6\,q^2(q^2+1)(q-1)}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\,(q^2+1)q^2}
=\frac{6(q-1)}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|}.
\]
For a circle triple $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=2$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(2))}, giving $\lambda=3(q-1)$;  for a non-circle triple $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=1$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(2))}, giving $\lambda=6(q-1)$.  Thus the complete list of $Sz(q)$-orbit parameters is
\[
3(q-1),\quad\underbrace{6(q-1),\ldots,6(q-1)}_{(q-2)/6\ \text{times}},
\]
i.e.\ the circle system $2$-$(q^2+1,3,3(q-1))$ and $(q-2)/6$ copies of $2$-$(q^2+1,3,6(q-1))$ \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(4)}\textup{)}.  For $q=8$ this gives the two systems $2$-$(65,3,21)$ and $2$-$(65,3,42)$, whose union has $\lambda=63$ \textup{(Proposition \ref{prop:union-orbits});  Proposition \ref{prop:sz8-computed};  Table \ref{tab:verify})}.

name: Designs from $\Sz(q)$

label: rem:sz-field
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sz-field}
$\operatorname{Aut}(Sz(q))=Sz(q)\cdot(2m+1)$ \textup{(}field automorphisms of odd order $2m+1$\textup{)}.  Field automorphisms preserve the circle orbit \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:sz-field-reduction}(1)}\textup{)};  the quotient action on the generic class is the Frobenius action $[\lambda]\mapsto[\lambda^{2^c}]$ on the parameter space $(\mathbb F_q\setminus\{0,1\})/H$, and the number $\sigma_3(Sz(q)\cdot f')$ is given by the closed form of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:suzuki-field-final}} for every field quotient $C_{f'}\le C_{2m+1}$ \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:suzuki-bluher-count})}.  The pointwise kernel inside a fused triple stabilizer remains an orbit-by-orbit invariant of the extension:  for $G=Sz(q)\cdot f'$, whether the twisted elements $h_\sigma\circ\sigma$ fix a given triple pointwise or permute it depends on the individual orbit.  The case $Sz(8)\cdot3$ is computed in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} \textup{(\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:sz8-computed}};  \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}\textup{)}}:  $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=3$ \textup{(}kernel $1$, image $C_3$, $\lambda=42$\textup{)} on the generic orbit and $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ \textup{(}kernel $3$, image $C_2$, $\lambda=21$\textup{)} on the circle orbit.  \textup{(}This is a genuine difference from the projective-line case of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:pgl}\textup{(}2\textup{)}}, where a twisted kernel element exists for every triple.\textup{)}
head: environment
name: Field automorphisms

label: thm:sz-field-reduction
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sz-field-reduction}
Let $S=Sz(q)$, $q=2^{2m+1}$, and let $S\le A\le\operatorname{Aut}(S)=S\cdot(2m+1)$ with $F=A/S\le C_{2m+1}$.  Let $\mathcal G_q$ denote the set of the $\frac{q-2}{6}$ non-circle $S$-orbits on three-subsets \textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(4)}\textup{)}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The circle orbit is fixed by $F$.
\item The action of $A$ on the non-circle three-subset orbits is exactly the induced action of $F$ on $\mathcal G_q$.  If the $F$-orbits on $\mathcal G_q$ are $\mathcal C_1,\ldots,\mathcal C_t$, then
\[
\sigma_3(A,\mathcal{O})=1+t.
\]
\item If $\mathcal C_i$ has size $e_i$, then the corresponding $A$-orbit on triples is the union of $e_i$ generic $S$-orbits and has design parameter
\[
\boxed{\;\lambda_i=6e_i(q-1)\;}
\]
\textup{(}orbit size $e_i|Sz(q)|$, since every generic $S$-orbit has stabilizer $1$\textup{)};  the circle orbit has parameter $3(q-1)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Suzuki field extensions: reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) The circle property is defined geometrically (a Suzuki sub-ovoid) and is preserved by every automorphism of the ovoid, so $F$ fixes the circle orbit.  (2) Since $S\trianglelefteq A$, the quotient $A/S$ acts on the set of $S$-orbits on three-subsets, and by the normal-subgroup fusion lemma \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:norm-orbit-fusion};  Proposition \ref{prop:ree-ext-reduction})} the $A$-orbits are precisely the unions of the $S$-orbits belonging to one $F$-orbit;  the circle orbit contributes one $A$-orbit.  (3) A generic $S$-orbit has size $|S|$ (trivial stabilizer, Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(2)), so an $F$-orbit of size $e_i$ gives an $A$-orbit of size $e_i|S|$;  its parameter is
\[
\lambda_i=\frac{6e_i|S|}{v(v-1)}=\frac{6e_i\,q^2(q^2+1)(q-1)}{(q^2+1)q^2}=6e_i(q-1),
\]
and the circle orbit has $\lambda=6(q-1)/2=3(q-1)$.
head: environment

label: lem:suzuki-bluher-count
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:suzuki-bluher-count}
Let $q=2^a$ with $a$ odd, let $\sigma_b\colon x\mapsto x^{2^b}$ be a field automorphism of $\mathbb F_q$, put
\[
d=(a,b),\qquad q_0=2^d,\qquad n=a/d,
\]
and let
\[
H=\left\{\,x,\ x+1,\ x^{-1},\ (x+1)^{-1},\ x(x+1)^{-1},\ (x+1)x^{-1}\,\right\}\cong S_3
\]
be the six M\"obius transformations of $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)$ permuting $\{0,1,\infty\}$.  The group $H$ acts freely on $\Lambda_q=\mathbb F_q\setminus\{0,1\}$.  For $h\in H$ put
\[
N_b(h)=\left|\left\{x\in\Lambda_q:\sigma_b(x)=h(x)\right\}\right|.
\]
Then
\[
N_b(1)=q_0-2,
\]
\[
N_b(h)=0\qquad\text{for every transposition }h\in H,
\]
and
\[
N_b(h)=\begin{cases}q_0+1,&3\mid n,\\0,&3
\nmid n\end{cases}\qquad\text{for every $3$-cycle }h\in H.
\]
Consequently, since $H$ acts freely on $\Lambda_q$ and the six equations $\sigma_b(x)=h(x)$ have disjoint solution sets,
\[
\left|\operatorname{Fix}_{\Lambda_q/H}(\sigma_b)\right|=\frac16\sum_{h\in H}N_b(h)=
\begin{cases}\dfrac{2^d-2}{6},&3
\nmid a/d,\\[3mm]2^{d-1},&3\mid a/d,\end{cases}
\]
where in the first case integrality uses $d$ odd, so $2^d\equiv2\pmod6$.
head: environment
name: The complete finite-field count

title: Proof
body_md:
The free action of $H$ on $\Lambda_q$:  the transposition $x\mapsto x+1$ has no fixed point, $x\mapsto x/(x+1)$ fixes only $0$, the involution $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ fixes only $1$, and the two $3$-cycles fix exactly the roots of $x^2+x+1=0$, which lie in $\mathbb F_4\setminus\mathbb F_2$;  since $a$ is odd, $\mathbb F_4
\not\subseteq\mathbb F_{2^a}=\mathbb F_q$, so none lies in $\Lambda_q$.  Counting $N_b(h)$:  the identity equation $x^{2^b}=x$ has as solutions exactly the fixed field $K=\mathbb F_{q_0}$, hence $N_b(1)=q_0-2$.  For a transposition, write $T=h\circ\sigma_b$;  since $h$ is defined over $\mathbb F_2$ it commutes with $\sigma_b$, and $h^2=1$ gives $T^n=h^n\,\sigma_b^n=h$, because $n$ is odd.  If $x^{2^b}=x+1$ then $T(x)=x$ and $x=T^n(x)=x+1$, a contradiction;  if $x^{2^b}=x^{-1}$ then $T^n(x)=x^{-1}=x$ forces $x=1$ (or the projective degenerations $0,\infty$), outside $\Lambda_q$;  the third transposition is conjugate to the first two in $H$.  For a $3$-cycle $c(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ the matrix $C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ satisfies $C^3=I$ in characteristic $2$, so $T=c\circ\sigma_b$ satisfies $T^n=c^n\,\sigma_b^n=c^n$.  If $3
\nmid n$, then $c^n$ is a nontrivial $3$-cycle;  a fixed point of $c$ or $c^2$ satisfies $x=(x+1)^{-1}$, i.e.\ $x^2+x+1=0$, whose roots lie in $\mathbb F_4\setminus\mathbb F_2
\not\subset\mathbb F_q$, so $N_b(c)=N_b(c^2)=0$.  If $3\mid n$, then $T^n=c^n=1$;  by Galois descent for semilinear maps, $T$ is conjugate in $\mathrm{P}\Gamma\mathrm{L}(2,q)$ to the pure Frobenius $\sigma_b$, hence $|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)}(T)|=|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)}(\sigma_b)|=|\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_{q_0})|=q_0+1$.  The points $0,1,\infty$ are not among them ($x^{2^b}(x+1)=1$ fails at $0$ and $1$, and $c(\infty)=0
\neq\infty$), so all $q_0+1$ fixed points lie in $\Lambda_q$, giving $N_b(c)=q_0+1$;  the other $3$-cycle $c^2$ is conjugate to $c$ in $H$.  The Burnside average over the free action of $H$ gives the displayed fixed-orbit count.
head: environment

label: thm:suzuki-field-final
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:suzuki-field-final}
Let $q=2^a$ with $a=2m+1$ odd, let $S=Sz(q)$, and let
\[
A=S\rtimes\langle\sigma_c\rangle\le\operatorname{Aut}(S)=Sz(q)\cdot(2m+1),
\]
where $\sigma_c\colon x\mapsto x^{2^c}$ is the field automorphism.  Put $d_0=(a,c)$ and $e=a/d_0$, so $|A/S|=e$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The set of generic $S$-orbits is parametrized by $\mathcal G_q\cong(\mathbb F_q\setminus\{0,1\})/H$ \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:suzuki-bluher-count})}, and $\sigma_c$ acts on this parameter space by
\[
[\lambda]\longmapsto[\lambda^{2^c}].
\]
\item The number of $A$-orbits on three-subsets is
\[
\boxed{\;\sigma_3(A)=1+\frac1e\sum_{r\mid e}\varphi\!\left(\frac er\right)
\begin{cases}\dfrac{2^{d_0r}-2}{6},&3
\nmid e/r,\\[3mm]2^{d_0r-1},&3\mid e/r,\end{cases}\;}
\]
where the first term is the invariant circle orbit.
\item If an $A$-orbit fuses $r_i$ generic $S$-orbits, then its design parameter is $\lambda_i=6r_i(q-1)$ and its setwise stabilizer has order $|A_X|=e/r_i$;  the circle orbit has parameter $3(q-1)$ and setwise stabilizer of order $2e$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Three-subset orbits of Suzuki field extensions

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) This is the classical affine parametrization of the generic orbits together with Lemma \ref{lem:suzuki-bluher-count};  the field automorphism acts by raising the parameter to the corresponding $2$-power.  (2) For $0\le j<e$ we have $\sigma_c^j=\sigma_{cj}$ with $(a,cj)=d_0(e,j)$;  writing $r=(e,j)$, the element $\sigma_c^j$ fixes, by Lemma \ref{lem:suzuki-bluher-count},
\[
\varepsilon_j=\begin{cases}\dfrac{2^{d_0r}-2}{6},&3
\nmid e/r,\\[2mm]2^{d_0r-1},&3\mid e/r\end{cases}
\]
generic $S$-orbits.  By Burnside's lemma on the parameter space $\mathcal G_q$ (the circle orbit contributes the first term $1$;  Theorem \ref{thm:sz-field-reduction}(2)),
\[
t_F=\frac1e\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}\varepsilon_j=\frac1e\sum_{r\mid e}\varphi\!\left(\frac er\right)
\begin{cases}\dfrac{2^{d_0r}-2}{6},&3
\nmid e/r,\\[2mm]2^{d_0r-1},&3\mid e/r,\end{cases}
\]
after merging the divisors $r$ of $e$ (there are $\varphi(e/r)$ elements of order $e/r$ in $\langle\sigma_c\rangle$).  (3) A fused $A$-orbit is the union of $r_i$ generic $S$-orbits of size $|S|$ (Theorem \ref{thm:sz}(2)), so its orbit size is $r_i|S|$ and, by (2),
\[
\lambda_i=\frac{6\,r_i|S|}{v(v-1)}=6r_i(q-1),\qquad |A_X|=\frac{|A|}{r_i|S|}=\frac{e}{r_i},
\]
and the circle orbit has $\lambda=3(q-1)$ and $|A_X|=|A|/(|S|/2)=2e$.

label: ex:ree-q3
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:ree-q3}
The smallest value $q=3^{2m+1}$ with $m=0$ gives ${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$ acting on the $28$ points of the Ree unital \textup{($|{}^2G_2(3)|=1512=3^3\cdot28\cdot2$)}.  The three-point orbit data, recorded in \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}, consist of six orbits with replication parameters
\[
\lambda=6,\ 4,\ 6,\ 2,\ 6,\ 2,
\]
i.e.\ three orbits with setwise stabilizer of order $2$ \textup{($\lambda=6=3(q-1)$)}, one orbit of order $3$ \textup{($\lambda=4=2(q-1)$)}, and the collinear and non-collinear orbits of order $6$ \textup{($\lambda=2=q-1$)};  there is no orbit with trivial stabilizer ($N_1=0$).  These values instantiate \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}(2)} at $q=3$, namely $(N_1,N_2,N_3,N_6)=(0,3,1,2)$, and serve as the small-case check on which the analysis for $q>3$ does not rely \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:ree-remark2})}.

label: thm:ree
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Ree reduction

title: Proof
body_md: The action of $S_{\mathcal{O}}$ on $\mathcal{O}$ gives a homomorphism $S_{\mathcal{O}}\longrightarrow S_3$ whose kernel is the pointwise stabilizer.  Therefore the image is one of the subgroups $1$, $C_2$, $C_3$, $S_3$.  If the pointwise stabilizer is trivial, the stabilizer itself is isomorphic to one of these four groups.  The occurrence and number of the corresponding orbits require an independent Ree-specific orbit calculation and are not inferred merely from this embedding;  the computed values are listed in \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}.

label: rem:ree-remark2
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ree-remark2}
For the smallest simple case $q=27$ the GAP suborbit computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} determines the collinear triple stabilizer explicitly:  the three points of a block of $\mathcal R$ form one $S$-orbit with setwise stabilizer of order $6$, pointwise stabilizer of order $2$ and induced image $C_3$ on the three points, hence $\lambda=q-1=26$.  For arbitrary $q>3$ the same conclusion follows from the classical block stabilizer $C_2\timesPSL(2,q)$ of the Ree unital \textup{\cite{luneburg1966}} together with \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}(3)} below, which only needs the order of the two-point stabilizers and the occurrence of one collinear orbit.  The general formula $\lambda=6|S|/\bigl(|S_{\mathcal{O}}|\,v(v-1)\bigr)$ \textup{(Corollary \ref{cor:ree-designs})} then gives $\lambda=q-1$ for the collinear orbit and the values $6(q-1)$, $3(q-1)$, $2(q-1)$, $q-1$ for the four families of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}}.

label: lem:ree-classes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ree-classes}
Let $S=Ree(q)={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act on $\Omega$ with $|\Omega|=q^3+1$, and write $f(g)=\operatorname{fix}_\Omega(g)$ for the number of fixed points of $g\in S$.  The non-identity conjugacy class types of $S$, together with their fixed-point numbers, centralizer orders and numbers of classes, are as follows \textup{\cite{bradley2014}, Lemma 3.5.2 and Table 3.5}:
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{0.95}{1.1}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
class type & $f(g)$ & $|C_S(g)|$ & number of classes \\
\midrule
$J$ (involution) & $q+1$ & $q(q+1)(q-1)$ & $1$ \\
$X$ (order $3$, in the centre of a Sylow $3$-subgroup) & $1$ & $q^3$ & $1$ \\
$T$, $T^{-1}$ (order $3$) & $1$ & $2q^2$ & $1$ each \\
$Y$, $YT$, $YT^{-1}$ (order $9$) & $1$ & $3q$ & $1$ each \\
$JT$, $JT^{-1}$ (order $6$) & $1$ & $2q$ & $1$ each \\
$R^a
\neq1$, order $m\mid(q-1)/2$ & $2$ & $q-1$ & $(q-3)/2$ \\
$S^a
\neq1$, order $m\mid(q+1)/4$ & $0$ & $q+1$ & $(q-3)/2$ \\
$JR^a
\neq R^a$ & $2$ & $q-1$ & $(q-3)/2$ \\
$JS^a
\neq S^a$ & $0$ & $q+1$ & $(q-3)/2$ \\
$V$ (order $m\mid q+1-\sqrt{3q}$) & $0$ & $q+1-\sqrt{3q}$ & $(q-\sqrt{3q})/6$ \\
$W$ (order $m\mid q+1+\sqrt{3q}$) & $0$ & $q+1+\sqrt{3q}$ & $(q+\sqrt{3q})/6$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Together with the identity class ($f= q^3+1$), these give the $q+8$ conjugacy classes of $S$ \textup{\cite{bradley2014}, Lemma 3.5.1}.  The cycle types needed below are
\begin{gather*}
\pi_J=1^{q+1}2^{(q^3-q)/2},\qquad
\pi_X=\pi_T=\pi_{T^{-1}}=1^13^{q^3/3},\\
\pi_{JT}=\pi_{JT^{-1}}=1^13^{q/3}6^{(q^3-q)/6},
\end{gather*}
and $\pi_Y=\pi_{YT}=\pi_{YT^{-1}}=1^19^{q^3/9}$ \textup{\cite{bradley2014}, Proposition 3.5.3, with the entries for the $JT$-classes corrected to the GAP-verified form $1^13^{q/3}6^{(q^3-q)/6}$ of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}}.  Every element of the remaining class types fixes at most two points and has no cycle of length $2$ or $3$.
head: environment
name: Ree class input

label: lem:eta3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:eta3}
Let $g$ be a permutation of a finite set $\Omega$, let $f=\operatorname{fix}_\Omega(g)$, and let $c_2(g)$, $c_3(g)$ be the numbers of $2$- and $3$-cycles of $g$.  The number of $3$-subsets of $\Omega$ fixed setwise by $g$ is
\[
\eta_3(g)=\binom{f}{3}+c_3(g)+f\,c_2(g).
\]
head: environment
name: Three-subsets fixed by a permutation

title: Proof
body_md: A $3$-subset $X$ satisfies $X^g=X$ if and only if $X$ is a union of $g$-cycles of length at most $3$:  either three fixed points, or one $3$-cycle, or one $2$-cycle together with one fixed point.  These three alternatives are disjoint and give the displayed count.
head: environment

label: lem:ree-pointwise
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ree-pointwise}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act on the Ree unital, and let $T=\{u,v,x\}$ be a triple of points not contained in a block.  Then the pointwise stabilizer $S_{(T)}$ is trivial.
head: environment
name: Pointwise stabilizers of non-collinear triples

title: Proof
body_md: By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}}, every non-identity element of $S$ outside the involution class $J$ fixes at most two points in the degree-$(q^3+1)$ action \textup{(the order-$3$ classes $X,T,T^{-1}$ and the order-$6$ classes $JT,JT^{-1}$ fix one point, as do the order-$9$ classes $Y,YT,YT^{-1}$;  the classes $R^a$ and $JR^a$ fix two;  the classes $S^a,JS^a,V,W$ fix none)};  an element of the involution class $J$ fixes exactly the $q+1$ points of one block.  Hence an element fixing $u,v,x$ pointwise must belong to $J$, and the block it fixes pointwise contains the triple $T$, making $T$ collinear, contrary to the hypothesis.  Thus $S_{(T)}=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:ree-dihedral
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ree-dihedral}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act $2$-transitively on the $q^3+1$ points of the Ree unital $\mathcal R$, and fix two points $u
\ne v$.  The setwise two-point stabilizer has order $2(q-1)$ and is a dihedral group $D_{2(q-1)}$, acting on the remaining $q^3-1$ points with orbit lengths
\[
q-1,\quad (q+1)\times(q-1),\quad \frac{q^2-1}{2}\times 2(q-1),
\]
namely one orbit of the $(q-1)$ points of the block $L_{uv}$ through $u,v$, the $q+1$ invariant orbits carried by the $q+1$ points of the block $L'$ fixed pointwise by the transposition $\tau\in S$ exchanging $u$ and $v$ \textup{(the $J$-involution whose fixed block is $L'$;  the $q-1$ transpositions of $S_{\{u,v\}}$ fix pairwise distinct blocks, and $L'$ is the one through no point of $\{u,v\}$)}, and the $\frac{q^2-1}{2}$ paired orbits of the remaining points.
head: environment
name: Dihedral two-point stabilizer and its suborbits

title: Proof
body_md:
The pointwise two-point stabilizer $S_{u,v}$ is cyclic of order $q-1$ \textup{(Zassenhaus group, \cite[pp.~256--259]{luneburg1966})}.  The transposition $\tau\in S$ exchanging $u$ and $v$ exists because the number of involutions exchanging a given pair is $(q^3-q)/2$ \textup{(from the $J$-class data of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}}:  $|S|/|C_S(J)|$ involutions, each swapping $(q^3-q)/2$ pairs)}.  The involution $\tau$ is of type $J$ and fixes pointwise the $q+1$ points of a block $L'
\ne L$;  in particular $u,v
\notin L'$.

By the standard Zassenhaus normalizer structure of the Ree action \textup{\cite[pp.~256--259]{luneburg1966}}, the setwise stabilizer of two distinct points $u,v$ is
\[
S_{\{u,v\}}\cong C_{q-1}\rtimes C_2,
\]
where the cyclic factor is the pointwise two-point stabilizer $S_{u,v}$ and the involution $\tau$ acts on $C_{q-1}$ by inversion;  equivalently $\tau c\tau=c^{-1}$ for every $c\in S_{u,v}$.  Hence, with $c$ a generator of $S_{u,v}$,
\[
S_{\{u,v\}}=\langle c,\tau\rangle\cong D_{2(q-1)}.
\]
That is, by the cited normalizer structure the setwise two-point stabilizer is $S_{\{u,v\}}=\langle S_{u,v},\tau\rangle\cong D_{2(q-1)}$;  in particular its order is $|S_{\{u,v\}}|=2(q-1)$.
(We record that the weaker observation that $\tau$ does \emph{not} centralize $S_{u,v}$ is not sufficient for this conclusion:  the automorphism of $C_{q-1}$ induced by $\tau$ could in general be $c\mapsto c^r$ for any $r$ with $r^2\equiv1\pmod{q-1}$, and for composite $q-1$ these need not be $\pm1$.  The dihedral conclusion is therefore taken from the cited normalizer structure rather than from an ad hoc argument.)

\emph{Suborbits.}  On the block $L\setminus\{u,v\}$ ($q-1$ points) the stabilizer of $x\in L\setminus\{u,v\}$ inside $S_{u,v}$ has order $2$ (the unique involution of $S_{u,v}$ fixes the block pointwise), so $S_{u,v}$ has one orbit of length $(q-1)/2$ there;  $\tau$ permutes this orbit with the orbit of $\tau(x)$, giving one $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbit of length $q-1$.  On $\Omega\setminus L$ the action of $S_{u,v}$ is free \textup{(the pointwise stabilizer of a non-collinear triple is trivial by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-pointwise}}, so no non-identity element of $S_{u,v}$ fixes a third point off $L$)};  hence $q(q+1)$ free orbits of length $q-1$.  The transposition $\tau$ fixes pointwise exactly the $q+1$ points of $L'$, one on each of $q+1$ free $S_{u,v}$-orbits, and has no fixed point on any other free orbit:  on a free orbit $O$, $\tau$ reverses the $c$-action, so a fixed point $x$ would satisfy $c^kx=\tau$-fixed for every $k$, forcing $O$ to contain the $q+1$ fixed points of $\tau$, i.e.\ $O$ is an invariant orbit through a point of $L'$.  Thus $\tau$ fixes $q+1$ free orbits and pairs the remaining $q(q+1)-(q+1)=q^2-1$ free orbits, giving $(q^2-1)/2$ paired $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits of length $2(q-1)$.
head: environment

label: thm:ree-triples
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ree-triples}
Let $S=Ree(q)={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}$, act $2$-transitively on the $q^3+1$ points of the Ree unital.  Then the number of $S$-orbits on three-subsets is
\[
\sigma_3(S)=\frac{(q+3)^2}{6}.
\]
In particular $\sigma_3(Ree(3))=6$, $\sigma_3(Ree(27))=150$, and $\sigma_3(Ree(243))=10086$.  The value $6$ agrees with the direct enumeration of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}} for ${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$;  the value $150$ is independently confirmed by the class computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}.
head: environment
name: Three-subset orbit number of $\Ree(q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
By Burnside's lemma $\sigma_3(S)=\frac1{|S|}\sum_{g\in S}\eta_3(g)$, and by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:eta3}} it suffices to know, for each class, the fixed-point number and the numbers of $2$- and $3$-cycles.  Using \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}} and summing over the conjugacy classes, the identity class and the $J$-, $(X,T,T^{-1})$-, $(JT,JT^{-1})$-families give
\begin{align*}
\sigma_3(S)
&=\frac{1}{q^3(q^3+1)(q-1)}\binom{q^3+1}{3}
 +\frac{1}{q^3-q}\Bigl(\binom{q+1}{3}+(q+1)\frac{q^3-q}{2}\Bigr)\\
&\quad+\frac{q+1}{q^3}\cdot\frac{q^3}{3}
 +\frac{1}{q}\cdot\frac{q}{3},
\end{align*}
and every other class contributes $0$:  the $Y$-family has $\eta_3(\pi_Y)=0$ since $\pi_Y$ has no $2$- or $3$-cycle, and the remaining types fix at most two points and have no $2$- or $3$-cycle.  Here the coefficient $\frac1{q^3-q}$ is $1/|C_S(J)|$, the coefficient $\frac{q+1}{q^3}$ is $\frac1{q^3}+\frac1{2q^2}+\frac1{2q^2}$ for the three order-$3$ classes, and the coefficient $\frac1q$ is $2\cdot\frac1{2q}$ for the two order-$6$ classes.  Simplifying,
\[
\frac{q^2+q+1}{6}+\frac{3q+4}{6}+\frac{q+1}{3}+\frac13
=\frac{q^2+6q+9}{6}=\frac{(q+3)^2}{6},
\]
where the first term is $\binom{q^3+1}{3}/\bigl(q^3(q^3+1)(q-1)\bigr)$ and the second is $\bigl[\binom{q+1}{3}+(q+1)(q^3-q)/2\bigr]/(q^3-q)$.  Since $q=3^{2m+1}\equiv3\pmod6$, we have $q+3=6k$ with $k=(3^{2m}+1)/2\in\mathbb N$, so $(q+3)^2/6=6k^2$ is an integer.  For $q=3$ the class input of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}} requires $q>3$ \textup{\cite{bradley2014}};  the value $6$ for ${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$ is taken from the direct enumeration of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}, and it agrees with the formula.  The value for $q=27$ ($150$) and the class count of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} give an independent check of the $q>3$ case.
head: environment

label: lem:ree-count
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Counting of transpositions and $3$-cycles

label: eq:ree-star1
title: Proof
body_md:
We first record a uniformity fact.  Let $\mathcal R_3=\{r\in S:\mathrm{ord}(r)=3\}$;  by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}} $|\mathcal R_3|=(q^3+1)(q^2-1)$, every $r\in\mathcal R_3$ fixes exactly one point and acts on the remaining $q^3$ points as a product of $q^3/3$ three-cycles.  Counting pairs $(r,(u,v))$ with $r(u)=v$:  each $r$ contributes $3\cdot q^3/3=q^3$ ordered pairs, so the total is $q^3(q^3+1)(q^2-1)$;  since $S$ is $2$-transitive, the distribution over the $(q^3+1)q^3$ ordered pairs $(u,v)$ is uniform, and therefore
\[
\bigl|\{r\in S:\mathrm{ord}(r)=3,\ r(u)=v\}\bigr|=q^2-1.
\]
Fix $(u,v)$ and put $L=L_{uv}$;  write $\mathcal R=\{r:\mathrm{ord}(r)=3,\ r(u)=v\}$ and $x=r(v)$.  Then $x\ne u,v$, and $r$ cyclically permutes $\{u,v,x\}$, so $x$ is of $3$-cycle type and the map $r\mapsto x$ is injective \textup{(the order-$3$ elements of $S_{\{u,v,x\}}$ are $r$ and $r^{-1}$, of which exactly one sends $u$ to $v$)}.  Hence the orbit counts of the lemma are recovered below from the cardinalities of the parts of $\mathcal R$ with $x$ of the respective kinds, divided by the length of one orbit of the corresponding kind.

\emph{Collinear part.}  For $x\in L\setminus\{u,v\}$ the block stabilizer acts as $PSL(2,q)$ on the projective line $L$, which is $3$-transitive;  the two order-$3$ elements of $S_{\{u,v,x\}}$ cyclically permute the three points, exactly one of them sending $u$ to $v$.  Hence exactly $|L\setminus\{u,v\}|=q-1$ elements of $\mathcal R$ have $x\in L\setminus\{u,v\}$.

\emph{Two independent counts.}  \textup{(i) \emph{$3$-cycles.}}  Write $n_3^i$ and $n_3^p$ for the numbers of invariant resp.\ paired orbits of $3$-cycle type.  The elements of $\mathcal R$ with third point $x$ of $3$-cycle type number $n_3^i(q-1)+2n_3^p(q-1)$ \textup{(an invariant orbit has length $q-1$, a paired orbit $2(q-1)$, and every point of such an orbit is of $3$-cycle type, the property being $S_{\{u,v\}}$-invariant)}\textup{)}.  Together with the collinear part,
\begin{equation}
q^2-1=(q-1)+n_3^i(q-1)+2n_3^p(q-1),\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad 2n_3^p+n_3^i=q.
\label{eq:ree-star1}
\end{equation}
\textup{(ii) \emph{Transpositions.}}  The same uniformity with the transposition class $J$ \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}:  $|J|=q^2(q^3+1)/(q+1)$, each transposition fixing $q+1$ points)} gives
\[
\bigl|\{\tau'\in J:\tau'(v)=v\}\bigr|
=\frac{|J|(q+1)}{q^3+1}=q^2,
\]
and a transposition fixing both $u$ and $v$ pointwise fixes the block $L$ pointwise:  the pointwise two-point stabilizer $S_{u,v}$ is cyclic of order $q-1$ \textup{(Zassenhaus;  cf.\ \cite{luneburg1966}, as in Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral})}, and its unique involution $c^{(q-1)/2}$ lies in the unique involution class $J$ of $S$ \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:ree-classes}:  every involution of $S$ is of class $J$)};  the members of $J$ fix pointwise the $q+1$ points of a block \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral})}, and since $c^{(q-1)/2}$ fixes $u$ and $v$, that block is the block $L$ through $u,v$.  Hence
\[
\bigl|\{\tau'\in J:\tau'(u)=u,\ \tau'(v)=v\}\bigr|=1.
\]
The remaining $q^2-1$ transpositions fix $v$ and move $u$;  each realizes a $(13)$-type permutation of $\{u,v,\tau'(u)\}$, and symmetrically for $(23)$.  The map $\tau'\mapsto\tau'(u)$ is injective on them \textup{(if two such transpositions agreed on $u$, their product would fix $\{u,v,\tau'(u)\}$ pointwise, forcing the identity by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-pointwise}}, the trivial pointwise stabilizer of a non-collinear triple)}, so the $(13)$-type points number $q^2-1=(q-1)(q+1)$;  such a point is necessarily non-collinear \textup{(a collinear triple lies on a block fixed pointwise by the block involution, so its pointwise stabilizer is nontrivial, and its induced image is $C_3$, whence no transposition fixes one of its points and swaps the other two; see the block-stabilizer computation in the proof of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral}})}\textup{)}.  A paired orbit whose stabilizer contains a transposition has length $2(q-1)$ and contains exactly $q-1$ points of $(13)$-type and $q-1$ of $(23)$-type \textup{(the involution $\tau$ conjugates $(13)$ to $(23)$)};  the $n_3^i$ invariant orbits of $3$-cycle type contain $q-1$ points of $(13)$-type each \textup{(their stabilizer has image $S_3$)}.  Hence, $t$ denoting the number of paired transposition orbits,
\begin{equation}
\bigl(t+n_3^i\bigr)(q-1)=(q-1)(q+1),\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad t+n_3^i=q+1.
\label{eq:ree-star2}
\end{equation}

\emph{The orbit number.}  To pin down $n_3^i$ we combine the two counts above with the fusion rule for unordered pairs, recorded here:  an $S$-orbit of a non-collinear triple meets the set of triples containing $\{u,v\}$ in $3$, $2$, $1$ or $1$ of the $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits according as its setwise stabilizer has order $1,2,3$ or $6$ \textup{(the three unordered pairs of a triple lie in one $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbit exactly when the induced image contains a $3$-cycle, and in two exactly when the image is $\langle(12)\rangle$, since $S$ is transitive on the relevant pairs)}.  Of the $q+1$ invariant orbits, $n_3^i$ carry a $3$-cycle \textup{(image $S_3$)} and the remaining $q+1-n_3^i$ have image $\langle(12)\rangle$;  the latter fuse two-to-one with the $t=q+1-n_3^i$ paired transposition orbits \textup{(by \eqref{eq:ree-star2})} into $N_2=q+1-n_3^i$ $S$-orbits, while the $n_3^p$ paired orbits of $3$-cycle type give $N_3=n_3^p$ \textup{(no fusion)}.  With $N_1=q(q-3)/6$ free orbits \textup{(three-to-one fusion)} and $N_6=2$, the total $\sigma_3(S)=(q+3)^2/6$ of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-triples}} gives
\[
\frac{q(q-3)}6+\bigl(q+1-n_3^i\bigr)+\frac{q-n_3^i}{2}+2=\frac{(q+3)^2}{6},
\]
where $n_3^p=(q-n_3^i)/2$ is substituted from \eqref{eq:ree-star1};  the left-hand side equals $\frac{q^2}{6}+q+3-\frac32n_3^i$ and the right-hand side $\frac{q^2}{6}+q+\frac32$, whence $n_3^i=1$.  This proves (3) \textup{(an invariant orbit of $3$-cycle type contains exactly one point of $L'$, by the suborbit structure of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral}};  equivalently exactly one $x\in L'$ carries a $3$-cycle)}\textup{.}  Substitution back into \eqref{eq:ree-star1} and \eqref{eq:ree-star2} gives $n_3^p=(q-1)/2$ and $t=q$, proving (2) and (1).

All three counts are confirmed for $q=27$ by the computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}:  the suborbit distribution $393=1+28+364$ of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify-ree}} splits as $[1,324],[2,54],[3,14],[6,1]$, i.e.\ $324/3=108$ free, $54/2=27$ transposition (paired and invariant fused two-to-one), $14-1=13$ paired $3$-cycle and $1$ invariant $3$-cycle orbits, in agreement with the three formulas.
head: environment

label: thm:ree-structure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ree-structure}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act $2$-transitively on the $q^3+1$ points of the Ree unital $\mathcal R$, and let $N_j$ denote the number of $S$-orbits on three-subsets whose setwise stabilizer has order $j$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The setwise two-point stabilizer of $S$ is a dihedral group $D_{2(q-1)}$ of order $2(q-1)$, with the suborbit decomposition of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral}}:  one orbit of the $q-1$ points of the block $L_{uv}$ through $u,v$, the $q+1$ invariant orbits of length $q-1$ carried by the $q+1$ points of the block $L'$ fixed pointwise by the transposition $\tau$ exchanging $u$ and $v$, and the $\frac{q^2-1}{2}$ paired orbits of the remaining points.
\item The occurring setwise stabilizer orders are $1,2,3,6$, with multiplicities
\[
N_1=\frac{q(q-3)}6,\qquad N_2=q,\qquad N_3=\frac{q-1}{2},\qquad N_6=2.
\]
\item The orbit of $N_6=2$ is split into one \emph{collinear} orbit (the $b$ triples lying on blocks;  pointwise stabilizer $C_2$, induced image $C_3$, hence setwise stabilizer $6$) and one \emph{non-collinear} orbit (trivial pointwise stabilizer, induced image $S_3$, setwise stabilizer $6$).  Every non-collinear triple has trivial pointwise stabilizer.
\end{enumerate}
In particular $N_1+N_2+N_3+N_6=(q+3)^2/6$, and the orbit-size identity $N_1+N_2/2+N_3/3+N_6/6=(q^2+q+1)/6$ holds.  For $q=27$ the four values are $(108,27,13,2)$, verified by the direct suborbit computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}};  for $q=3$ ($^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$) the same formulas give $(0,3,1,2)$, matching the six orbits with $\lambda=6,4,6,2,6,2$ of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}.
head: environment
name: Three-subset orbit structure of $\Ree(q)$

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S$ is $2$-transitive, fix two points $u,v$ and put $L=L_{uv}$.  By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-dihedral}} the setwise two-point stabilizer is $S_{\{u,v\}}=\langle c,\tau\rangle\cong D_{2(q-1)}$, with $S_{u,v}=\langle c\rangle$ cyclic of order $q-1$ and $\tau$ the transposition exchanging $u$ and $v$, and its action on the remaining $q^3-1$ points has exactly the suborbits of item (1).  This proves (1).

\emph{Stabilizer orders.}  For a representative $T=\{u,v,x\}$ with $x$ in the block-orbit, $S_T$ has order $6$:  the pointwise part is $C_2$ (the block involution) and the induced image is $C_3$, the latter following from the classical block stabilizer $C_2\timesPSL(2,q)$ acting on the block as $PSL(2,q)$ on the projective line \textup{\cite{luneburg1966}} (for $q=27$ verified directly in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}).  For non-collinear $x$ the pointwise stabilizer is trivial by \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-pointwise}}, so $|S_T|$ equals the order of the induced image, i.e.\ $1$, $2$ or $3$ according as $S_T$ contains no transposition, a transposition but no $3$-cycle, or a $3$-cycle;  the image is $S_3$ exactly when both occur, giving order $6$.

On the $q+1$ invariant orbits (the points of $L'$), the transposition $\tau$ is present, so $|S_T|\ge2$.  The counting Lemma \ref{lem:ree-count} shows that exactly one of these $q+1$ orbits carries a $3$-cycle (equivalently, a third-point $x\in L'$ for which some order-$3$ element of $S$ cyclically permutes $\{u,v,x\}$), and that among the $(q^2-1)/2$ paired orbits exactly $q$ carry a transposition and $(q-1)/2$ carry a $3$-cycle, the remaining $q(q-3)/2$ being free.  Since a $3$-cycle together with $\tau$ generates $S_3$, the distribution (2) follows at the level of $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits:  one orbit of order $6$ (collinear), $q+1$ of order $2$ (the invariant orbits without a $3$-cycle), one of order $6$ (the invariant orbit with a $3$-cycle, image $S_3$), $q$ of order $2$ and $(q-1)/2$ of order $3$ among the paired orbits, and $q(q-3)/2$ of order $1$.

\emph{Fusion.}  It remains to pass from $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits to $S$-orbits.  Let $O$ be the $S$-orbit of a non-collinear $T=\{u,v,x\}$, and consider the elements of $O$ containing $u,v$ as a subset.  For $A\in\binom{T}{2}$ let $O_A$ be the set of $gT$ with $g^{-1}\{u,v\}=A$, i.e.\ $g(A)=\{u,v\}$.  The three sets $O_{\{u,v\}}$, $O_{\{u,x\}}$, $O_{\{v,x\}}$ are $S_{\{u,v\}}$-invariant, mutually disjoint, and by the transitivity of $S$ on the relevant pairs they form three $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits when $|S_T|=1$ (free case):  indeed $S_{\{u,v\}}$ acts transitively on the representatives $g$ with $g(A)=\{u,v\}$, and the map $g\mapsto gT$ is then $S_{\{u,v\}}$-equivariant.  When $|S_T|=2$ with image $\langle(12)\rangle$, the $3$-cycle-free transposition $g$ realising $A=\{u,x\}$ or $A=\{v,x\}$ is conjugate into the image, so exactly two of the three sets survive as distinct $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits;  when the image is $C_3$ (respectively contains a $3$-cycle), the three $2$-subsets of $T$ lie in one orbit, giving a single $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbit.  Therefore the $S$-orbit of a non-collinear triple contains $3$, $2$, $1$, $1$ of the $S_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits according as $|S_T|=1,2,3,6$.  Combining with the suborbit counts:  the $q(q-3)/2$ free orbits fuse three-to-one into $N_1=q(q-3)/6$;  the $q$ transposition orbits of order $2$ among the paired orbits fuse two-to-one with $q$ of the $q+1$ invariant orbits of order $2$ into $N_2=q$ (one invariant orbit is left, the one with the $3$-cycle);  the $(q-1)/2$ orbits of order $3$ do not fuse, giving $N_3=(q-1)/2$;  the collinear orbit and the order-$6$ invariant orbit give $N_6=2$.  This proves (2) and (3).
head: environment

label: cor:ree-designs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:ree-designs}
Since $|S|=q^3(q^3+1)(q-1)$ and $v=q^3+1$, the general formula is
\[
\lambda=\frac{6(q-1)}{|S_{\mathcal{O}}|}.
\]
By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-triples}} the number of orbit systems is $(q+3)^2/6$, and by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}} the occurring stabilizer orders and their multiplicities are known for every $q>3$:  $q(q-3)/6$ orbits with $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=1$ give $2$-$(q^3+1,3,6(q-1))$, $q$ orbits with $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=2$ give $2$-$(q^3+1,3,3(q-1))$, $(q-1)/2$ orbits with $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=3$ give $2$-$(q^3+1,3,2(q-1))$, and the two orbits with $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6$ (one collinear, one non-collinear) give $2$-$(q^3+1,3,q-1)$.
For the computed case $q=3$ \textup{(${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$ on $28$ points)}, \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}} records six orbits with $\lambda=6,4,6,2,6,2$, and the formulas $N_1=0,N_2=3,N_3=1,N_6=2$ of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}} evaluated at $q=3$ give exactly this:  the three orbits with $\lambda=6=3(q-1)$ have stabilizer order $2$, the single orbit with $\lambda=4=2(q-1)$ has stabilizer order $3$, and the two orbits with $\lambda=2=q-1$ have stabilizer order $6$;  no orbit of stabilizer order $1$ (which would have $\lambda=12$) occurs, matching $N_1=0$.  For $q=27$ the distribution is $(108,27,13,2)$ with $\lambda=156,78,52,26$ respectively \textup{(verified, Chapter \ref{sec:verify})};  in particular the $150$ orbit systems consist of $108$ copies of $2$-$(19684,3,156)$, $27$ copies of $2$-$(19684,3,78)$, $13$ copies of $2$-$(19684,3,52)$ and two copies of $2$-$(19684,3,26)$.

name: Designs from $\Ree(q)$

label: lem:ree-ext-cycles
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ree-ext-cycles}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q_0^3)$ and let $\sigma$ be the field automorphism of order $3$ fixing the sub-unital $\mathcal U_0\cong{}^2G_2(q_0)$ on $q_0^3+1$ points. Put
\[
R_0=|{}^2G_2(q_0)|=q_0^3(q_0^3+1)(q_0-1).
\]
Then $\sigma$ fixes exactly
\[
a=\frac{q_0^2+2q_0+3}{2}
\]
$S$-orbits on three-subsets, namely $(q_0+3)^2/6$ subfield orbits and $q_0^2/3$ free cycle-type orbits (with $S$-setwise stabilizer $1$).
head: environment
name: Fixed orbits for the cubic field extension

title: Proof
body_md:
The automorphism $\sigma$ fixes the $q_0^3+1$ rational points and permutes all other points in $3$-cycles, and its centralizer is $C_S(\sigma)={}^2G_2(q_0)$, of order $R_0$.

On a block (a projective line over $\mathbb{F}_{q_0^3}$) the field automorphism $\sigma$ fixes exactly the $q_0+1$ points of $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb{F}_{q_0})$. Hence a $\sigma$-invariant block contains precisely $q_0+1$ rational points and is one of the sub-unital blocks, whose number is
\[
b_0=q_0^2(q_0^2-q_0+1).
\]
Each such block carries $(q_0^3-q_0)/3$ non-rational $\sigma$-cycles, so the number of collinear $\sigma$-cycles is
\[
b_0\frac{q_0^3-q_0}{3}
 =\frac{q_0^3(q_0^3+1)(q_0-1)}{3}
 =\frac{R_0}{3}.
\]
The total number of non-rational $\sigma$-cycles is $(q_0^9-q_0^3)/3$, and therefore the number of non-collinear $\sigma$-cycles is
\[
N=\frac{q_0^9-q_0^3}{3}-\frac{R_0}{3}
 =\frac{q_0^4(q_0-1)(q_0+1)(q_0^3+1)}{3}.
\]

We next determine how many of these fixed three-subsets lie on subfield orbits. Let $\mathcal O$ be a subfield orbit with $S$-setwise stabilizer $H$ of order $m$, which $\sigma$ centralizes (so $H\leq C_S(\sigma)$), and write $G_T=H\rtimes\langle\sigma\rangle$ for the stabilizer of a representative $T$. A point $sH$ of $\mathcal O$ is fixed by $\sigma$ precisely when $s^{-1}\sigma s\in G_T$. Double-counting gives
\[
|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathcal O}(\sigma)|=\frac{n_T R_0}{m},
\]
where $n_T$ is the number of elements of $G_T$ conjugate to $\sigma$ in $S$: each such element is $s^{-1}\sigma s$ for exactly $R_0$ elements $s$, and each fixed point accounts for $m$ representatives. An element $h\sigma$ with $h\in H$ has order $3$ exactly when $h$ has order $1$ or $3$, and is then conjugate to $\sigma$ by the Lang--Steinberg theorem (the Lang map of the defining field automorphism is surjective on the connected Ree group); when $h$ is an involution, $h\sigma$ has order $6$ and its fixed points are $\operatorname{Fix}(h)\cap\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma)$, namely the $q_0+1$ points fixed by $h$ on the sub-unital. Thus
\[
n_T=1+\#\{\text{elements of order }3\text{ in }H\}.
\]

By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}} applied to the sub-unital group ${}^2G_2(q_0)$, the subfield orbits comprise $q_0(q_0-3)/6$ with $H=1$, $q_0$ with $H\cong C_2$, $(q_0-1)/2$ with $H\cong C_3$, and two with $H\cong S_3$ (one collinear, one non-collinear). Subtracting the all-fixed rational triples ($R_0/m$ per orbit) from $|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathcal O}(\sigma)|$, the $\sigma$-cycles on subfield orbits total
\[
\frac{q_0-1}{2}\cdot\frac{2R_0}{3}
   +2\cdot\frac{2R_0}{6}
 =\frac{R_0(q_0+1)}{3},
\]
of which $R_0/3$ are collinear and $R_0q_0/3$ are non-collinear. Hence the number of non-collinear $\sigma$-cycles on free orbits is
\[
N-\frac{R_0q_0}{3}
 =\frac{q_0^5(q_0-1)(q_0^3+1)}{3}.
\]
On a free orbit ($H=1$) the centralizer $C_S(\sigma)$ acts freely, and the fixed triples are one $C_S(\sigma)$-orbit of length $R_0$; hence the number of free cycle-type orbits is
\[
\frac{1}{R_0}\cdot\frac{q_0^5(q_0-1)(q_0^3+1)}{3}
 =\frac{q_0^2}{3}.
\]
Together with the $(q_0+3)^2/6$ subfield orbits this gives
\[
a=\frac{(q_0+3)^2}{6}+\frac{q_0^2}{3}
 =\frac{q_0^2+2q_0+3}{2},
\]
as claimed.
head: environment

label: thm:ree-ext
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ree-ext}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act on the Ree unital, and let $G=Ree(q)\cdot 3$ with $\langle\sigma\rangle=G/S$, $\sigma$ of order $3$;  put $q_0=3^{(2m+1)/3}$.  The field automorphism $\sigma$ fixes exactly the $q_0^3+1$ rational points of the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}$ pointwise and acts on the remaining points in cycles of length $3$.  A $\sigma$-invariant three-subset $S$-orbit contains either a three-subset of rational points \textup{(``subfield type'')} or a subset $\{x,\sigma x,\sigma^2x\}$ carried by one $3$-cycle \textup{(``cycle type'')}, and the $G$-orbits on three-subsets are precisely the $\sigma$-closures of the $S$-orbits \textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:norm-orbit-fusion})}.  Hence
\[
\sigma_3(G)=a+\frac{\sigma_3(S)-a}{3},\qquad
\sigma_3(S)=\frac{(q+3)^2}{6},
\]
where the number $a$ of $\sigma$-fixed $S$-orbits is
\[
a=\frac{q_0^2+2q_0+3}{2}
\qquad\textup{(Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles})}.
\]
For $q=27$, $f'=3$ \textup{($q_0=3$)}:  $a=9$, consisting of $6$ subfield-type orbits \textup{(the $6$ orbits of ${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$ on $28$ points, lifted)} and $3$ cycle-type orbits (all with trivial socle stabilizer), so
\[
\sigma_3(Ree(27){:}3)=9+\frac{150-9}{3}=56,
\]
and the $56$ orbits of $Ree(27){:}3$ have setwise stabilizer orders distributed as $1^{35},2^8,3^7,6^3,9^1,18^2$ and pointwise stabilizer orders as $1^{50},3^5,6^1$ \textup{(all computed independently in Chapter \ref{sec:verify})}.

title: Proof
body_md: The description of the fixed points of $\sigma$ is classical (the cycle type $1^{28}3^{6552}$ on the $19684$ points of the Atlas representation of $Ree(27){:}3$ is verified in Chapter \ref{sec:verify}). A three-subset fixed setwise by $\sigma$ is a union of $\sigma$-cycles of length at most $3$, i.e.\ three fixed points or one $3$-cycle; hence a $\sigma$-fixed $S$-orbit contains such a triple, and conversely. By Lemma \ref{lem:norm-orbit-fusion} the $G$-orbits are the orbits of $\langle\sigma\rangle$ on the $S$-orbits: $a$ fixed orbits and $(\sigma_3(S)-a)/3$ orbits of size $3$, giving the displayed formula. The fixed-orbit number $a=(q_0^2+2q_0+3)/2$ is the content of Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles}. For $q=27$, $q_0=3$, the computation of Chapter \ref{sec:verify} constructs $Ree(27){:}3$ from the Atlas generators, reads off $\sigma$ (order $3$, $28$ fixed points), and computes the $A_{\{u,v\}}$-orbits ($137$ suborbits) and their fusion in $A$: $56$ orbits with the stated stabilizer distributions and the split $a=9=6+3$, in agreement with Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles}.

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Galois descent and the fixed-orbit count for the Ree socle

title: Proof
body_md:
For $f'=1$ there is nothing to prove.  For $f'=3$ the assertions are \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles}}.  Assume $f'\ge5$.  We use three elementary facts.  Write $\sigma=F|_S$ for a Steinberg endomorphism $F$ of the connected algebraic group $\mathbf G$ with $S=\mathbf G^{F^{f'}}$ \textup{(the field quotient is cyclic, so we may choose $F$ to generate the same cyclic group as $\sigma$;  for the twisted Ree root datum this is allowed by the standard form of $F$)}.

\emph{(1)  A semilinear element of the correct order is conjugate to $\sigma$.}  Let $x\in S\sigma$ with $x^{f'}=1$, and write $x=sF$ with $s\in S$.  By Lang's theorem \cite{lang1956,steinberg1968} there is $u\in\mathbf G$ with $s=u^{-1}F(u)$;  then $x=u^{-1}Fu$ and
\[
x^{f'}=(u^{-1}Fu)^{f'}=u^{-1}F^{f'}(u)\,F^{f'},
\]
so $x^{f'}=1$ forces $F^{f'}(u)=u$, i.e.\ $u\in\mathbf G^{F^{f'}}=S$.  Hence $x=u^{-1}Fu=u^{-1}\sigma u$ with $u\in S$.

\emph{(2)  Every $\sigma$-invariant $S$-orbit contains a $\sigma$-fixed triple.}  The collinear orbit is unique and contains a triple of the fixed subfield $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}$ (a subfield line carries $q_0+1\ge4$ points), so it is $\sigma$-invariant and contains a $\sigma$-fixed triple.  Let $O$ be a non-collinear $\sigma$-invariant $S$-orbit and choose $T\in O$.  Since $O=\sigma(O)=T^S$, there is $s\in S$ with $\sigma(T)=s(T)$;  put $\delta=s^{-1}\sigma\in S\sigma$.  Then $\delta(T)=T$, and the image of $\delta$ in $G/S\cong C_{f'}$ is $\sigma S
\ne S$, so $\delta
\ne1$.  Let $m\in\{1,2,3\}$ be the order of the permutation induced by $\delta$ on $T$.  If $m\mid f'$, then $\delta^{f'}\in S$ fixes $T$ pointwise, so $\delta^{f'}\in S_{(T)}=1$ (Theorem \ref{thm:ree-structure}:  the pointwise three-point stabilizer of the Ree socle is trivial), and $\delta$ is an $f'$-th power-free element of order dividing $f'$ with $\delta^{f'}=1$;  by (1) $\delta$ is $S$-conjugate to $\sigma$, whence $\sigma(u(T))=u(T)$ for some $u\in S$:  the orbit contains a $\sigma$-fixed triple.  If $\gcd(m,f')=1$ (which covers $m=2$ since $f'$ is odd, and $m=3$ exactly when $3
\nmid f'$), choose $k\equiv1\pmod{f'}$, $k\equiv0\pmod m$;  then $y=\delta^k\in S\sigma$ fixes $T$ pointwise, so $y^{f'}\in S_{(T)}=1$ and, by (1), $y$ is $S$-conjugate to $\sigma$, giving again a $\sigma$-fixed triple in $O$.  The only remaining case is $m=3$ with $3\mid f'$, which is the case $m\mid f'$ treated first:  $\delta$ is $S$-conjugate to $\sigma$, and $u(T)$ is a $\sigma$-fixed triple of cycle type $\{x,\sigma x,\sigma^2x\}$.  Thus (i) holds in all cases.

\emph{(3)  Rigidity of subfield triples.}  Let $\tau$ be a field automorphism of odd order $d$ and let $T,U$ be triples with all points fixed by $\tau$;  if $s(T)=U$ for $s\in S$, then $s\in C_S(\tau)$.  Indeed, put $c=s^{-1}\tau(s)$;  since $\tau(U)=U$ and $s(T)=U$, the element $c$ fixes $T$ pointwise, so $c\in S_{(T)}$.  If $T$ is non-collinear, $S_{(T)}=1$ and $c=1$.  If $T$ is collinear, $S_{(T)}\cong C_2$ is normalized by $\tau$, which acts trivially on it (odd order), and $1=c\,\tau(c)\cdots\tau^{d-1}(c)=c^{d}$, so $c=1$ again.  Hence $\tau(s)=s$.

\emph{(4)  The fixed-orbit count.}  If $3
\nmid f'$, the non-rational $\sigma$-cycles have length $f'\ge5$, so a $\sigma$-fixed triple consists of fixed points and lies in $\mathcal{P}(q_0)$.  By (3) with $\tau=\sigma$, subfield triples are $S(q_0)$-equivalent exactly when they are $S$-equivalent, so by (2) the $\sigma$-fixed $S$-orbits are precisely the subfield orbits, and $A(f')=\sigma_3(Ree(q_0))=(q_0+3)^2/6$.  If $3\mid f'$, then $\sigma^3$ fixes every $\sigma$-fixed triple pointwise \textup{(the induced permutation on the three points has order $1$ or $3$)}, so every $\sigma$-fixed triple lies in $\mathcal{P}(q_0^3)$;  by (3) with $\tau=\sigma^3$ \textup{(order $f'/3$, odd)} the $S(q)$-equivalence on such triples coincides with the $S(q_0^3)$-equivalence, and by (2) the $\sigma$-fixed $S$-orbits are in bijection with the $\sigma$-fixed $S(q_0^3)$-orbits.  The latter are counted by the cubic case $f'=3$ of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles}} with base field $\mathbb{F}_{q_0^3}$:  $A(q_0^3,3)=(q_0^2+2q_0+3)/2$.  This proves (ii).

label: rem:ree-descent-status
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ree-descent-status}
The Galois-descent assertion (i) and the closed form (ii) of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:ree-descent}} are proved unconditionally for every $f'\mid 2m+1$, without any hypothesis.  The cycle-type orbits mentioned in (i) are exactly the triples $\{x,\sigma x,\sigma^2x\}$ with $x\in\mathcal{P}(q_0^3)$ not in $\mathcal{P}(q_0)$ \textup{(they can occur only when $3\mid f'$;  for $f'=3$ they are the $3$ orbits giving $a=9=6+3$ and $\sigma_3(Ree(27){:}3)=56$, verified in Chapter \ref{sec:verify})}.  Their number is absorbed in the closed form (ii):  for $3\mid f'$ every $\sigma$-fixed triple lies in $\mathcal{P}(q_0^3)$, the $S(q)$-equivalence on $\mathcal{P}(q_0^3)$ coincides with the $S(q_0^3)$-equivalence \textup{(rigidity step (3) of the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:ree-descent}, applied to $\tau=\sigma^3$)}, and (ii) counts the $\sigma$-fixed $S(q_0^3)$-orbits by the cubic closed form $A(q_0^3,3)=(q_0^2+2q_0+3)/2$.  In particular the previously open instances $f'=9,27$ are now closed:  $\sigma_3(Ree(3^9)\cdot9)=7\,176\,734$ (degree $q^3+1=3^{27}+1$;  $\operatorname{Out}(Ree(3^9))\cong C_9$, so $f'=27$ does not occur for $q=3^9$;  the $f'=27$ case occurs only for $3^{27}\mid q$, i.e.\ $f'=27\mid 2m+1$).

name: Status of the Ree descent

label: prop:ree-ext-noncubic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ree-ext-noncubic}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, act on the Ree unital, let $f'\mid 2m+1$ with $f'\ge5$, and let $G=Ree(q)\cdot f'$ with $\langle\sigma\rangle=G/S$, $\sigma$ of order $f'$.  By \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:ree-descent}} the $\sigma$-fixed $S$-orbits are counted by $A(f')$ of (ii), and by the orbit-fusion principle the $G$-orbits on three-subsets are the orbits of $\langle\sigma\rangle$ on the $S$-orbits.  Burnside's lemma applied to this finite quotient action gives the closed form, for every $f'\mid 2m+1$,
\[
\sigma_3(G)=\frac1{f'}\sum_{d\mid f'}\varphi(d)\,A\!\left(3^{(2m+1)/d},d\right),
\qquad
A(Q,d)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{(Q+3)^2}{6},&3
\nmid d,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{Q^2+2Q+3}{2},&3\mid d,
\end{cases}
\]
where $d$ is the order of $\sigma^j$ in the sum over $j=0,\ldots,f'-1$ ($\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$;  a field automorphism of order $d$ fixes exactly the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{3^{(2m+1)/d}}$ and, by (ii), fixes $A(3^{(2m+1)/d},d)$ of the $S$-orbits).  For example
\[
\sigma_3(Ree(27){:}3)=\tfrac13\bigl(\sigma_3(S)+2A(3,3)\bigr)=\tfrac13(150+2\cdot9)=56,
\]
\[
\sigma_3(Ree(243)\cdot5)=\tfrac15\bigl(\sigma_3(S)+4A(3,5)\bigr)=\tfrac15(10086+4\cdot6)=2022,
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_3(Ree(3^9)\cdot9)&=\tfrac19\bigl(\sigma_3(S)+2A(27,3)+6A(3,9)\bigr)\\
&=\tfrac19(64\,589\,766+2\cdot393+6\cdot9)=7\,176\,734
\end{aligned}
\]
(degrees $19684,14348908,3^{27}+1$ respectively).  The first two values agree with the computations of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}.

name: Extension formula for every field quotient

label: rem:ree-field
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ree-field}
For a field automorphism $\sigma$ of order $f'\mid 2m+1$ acting on the Ree unital, the Galois-descent assertion (i) and the fixed-orbit count (ii) of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:ree-descent}} are proved unconditionally for every $f'$:  \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:ree-ext-cycles}} covers $f'=3$ ($a=(q_0^2+2q_0+3)/2$, and $\sigma_3(Ree(27){:}3)=56$ is verified in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}, Table \ref{tab:verify-ree}}), and the proof of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:ree-descent}} covers every $f'\ge5$ by the Lang-conjugation step (1), the fixed-triple step (2) and the rigidity step (3) there, without any intermediate-subfield hypothesis.  Hence \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:ree-ext-noncubic}} is unconditional for every $f'\ge5$, e.g.\ $\sigma_3(Ree(243)\cdot5)=2022$ and $\sigma_3(Ree(3^9)\cdot9)=7\,176\,734$;  the previously open instances $f'=9,27$ are closed by the cubic reduction of \textup{Remark \ref{rem:ree-descent-status}} ($\operatorname{Out}(Ree(3^9))\cong C_9$, so $f'=27$ requires $27\mid 2m+1$).

\label{prop:ree-ext-reduction}
Let $S={}^2G_2(q)\trianglelefteq G\le\operatorname{Aut}(S)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, with $S$ acting on the point set $\mathcal{P}$ and $\Omega=\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$.  If the $S$-orbits on $\Omega$ are $\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_r$, then the $G$-orbits on $\Omega$ are exactly the sets

\Delta_{\mathcal C}=\bigcup_{\Delta_i\in\mathcal C}\Delta_i
\]
as $\mathcal C$ runs over the orbits of $G/S$ on $\{\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_r\}$;  in particular $|\Delta_{\mathcal C}|=\sum_{\Delta_i\in\mathcal C}|\Delta_i|$.

title: Proof
body_md: For $\mathcal{O}=\{x,y,z\}$, the pointwise stabilizer in $Alt(n)$ is $Alt(n-3)$ (order $(n-3)!/2$), and in $Sym(n)$ is $Sym(n-3)$ (order $(n-3)!$).  The image on $\mathcal{O}$:  for every $\sigma\in S_3$ there is an even permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ inducing $\sigma$ on $\mathcal{O}$ and fixing the other points (for $n\ge5$:  use $\sigma$ on $\mathcal{O}$ together with a transposition of two of the remaining $n-3$ points to adjust the sign);  hence the image is $S_3$ and $S_{\mathcal{O}}=Alt(n-3)\rtimes S_3$ with $|S_{\mathcal{O}}|=6\cdot(n-3)!/2=3(n-3)!$.  The $n=4$ case is immediate ($Alt(4)$ acts as the tetrahedral group on $4$ points;  the stabilizer of a $3$-subset is the stabilizer of its complement, of order $3$).

body_md: The transitivity degrees of the Mathieu actions are classical \textup{(cf.\ \cite{curtis1976,cameron1999})}:  the actions used here are at least $3$-transitive:  $M_{11}$ (deg 11) is $4$-transitive, $M_{11}$ (deg 12) is $3$-transitive, $M_{12}$ is $5$-transitive, $M_{22}$ is $3$-transitive, $M_{23}$ is $4$-transitive, $M_{24}$ is $5$-transitive, and the extensions $M_{12}.2$, $M_{22}.2$ act $3$-transitively on the same $12$ resp.\ $22$ points \textup{(an overgroup of a $3$-transitive group is $3$-transitive in the same action;  the degrees and actions are those of the natural Mathieu representations, checked against the GAP rows of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}}\textup{)}. label: thm:spor-fw
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:spor-fw}
Let $G\in\{HS,Co_3\}$ in its $2$-transitive action, and $\mathcal{O}$ a $3$-subset.  Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is $2$-transitive:  $|G_{\alpha,\beta}|=|G|/(v(v-1))$ equals $1440$ \textup{(}for $HS$\textup{)} and $6531840$ \textup{(}for $Co_3$\textup{)} \textup{(here $G_{\alpha,\beta}$ is the ordered-pair stabilizer}\textup{)}.
\item Fix an unordered pair $P=\{\alpha,\beta\}$ with setwise stabilizer $G_P=G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$.  By \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:pair-orbits}} the map $\gamma^{G_P}\mapsto\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}^{G}$ is a well-defined surjection from the $G_P$-orbits on $\mathcal{P}\setminus P$ onto the $G$-orbits on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$;  for $HS$ and $Co_3$ the suborbit computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} shows that it is a bijection \textup{(}3 resp.\ 2 orbits\textup{)}.  For $\mathcal{O}=\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ with $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}\setminus P$, writing $G_{P,\gamma}=G_P\cap G_{\gamma}$ and $C_2(P)=\{\mathrm{id},(\alpha\,\beta)\}\leSym(\mathcal{O})$,
\[
|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=\frac{|G_P|}{|\gamma^{G_P}|}\cdot\frac{|\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}|}{|\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}\cap C_2(P)|},
\qquad
|G_P|=|G_{\alpha,\beta}|\cdot[G_P:G_{\alpha,\beta}],
\]
where the index $[G_P:G_{\alpha,\beta}]$ is $1$ or $2$, and equals $2$ precisely when some element of $G$ swaps $\alpha,\beta$ \textup{(}the case for $HS$ and $Co_3$\textup{)}.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Framework for $HS$ and $Co_3$

label: rem:spor-correction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:spor-correction}
The two-point stabilizers of $HS$ and $Co_3$ have orders $1440$ and $6531840$, respectively \textup{(}Atlas data, \cite{conway1985,wilson1996}\textup{)};  in particular $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ is not the trivial group.  The analysis uses the framework of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:spor-fw}}:  it requires the suborbit structure of $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$, which is a finite computation carried out in GAP and recorded in \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}.  For $HS$ the two-point stabilizer has order $1440$, and it acts on the remaining $174$ points with suborbits of sizes $12,72,90$;  the three-point setwise stabilizers are $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ of orders $720$ \textup{(}kernel $120$\textup{)}, $120$ \textup{(}kernel $20$\textup{)} and $96$ \textup{(}kernel $16$\textup{)}, all with image $S_3$, giving $\lambda=12,72,90$;  with $|G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}|=2880$ and $|\gamma^{G_P}|=12,72,90$ these orders match the formula of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:spor-fw}(2)}:  $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=|G_P|/|\gamma^{G_P}|\cdot|\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}|/|\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}\cap C_2(P)|=240\cdot6/2=720$, $40\cdot6/2=120$, $32\cdot6/2=96$.  For $Co_3$ the corresponding data are determined in \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:co3}} below \textup{(finite computation, \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}\textup{)}}:  the two-point stabilizer has order $6531840$ \textup{(ordered)} and acts on the remaining $274$ points with suborbits of sizes $162,112$, and the three-point setwise stabilizers have orders $241920,349920$ with pointwise stabilizers $40320,58320$, both with image $S_3$, giving $\lambda=162,112$.  The values above are obtained from the explicit suborbit computations recorded here and in \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}}:  for $HS$ the occurring setwise stabilizer orders $720,120,96$ (all with image $S_3$) give $\lambda=12,72,90$, and for $Co_3$ the orders $241920,349920$ (image $S_3$) give $\lambda=162,112$.  The orbit numbers $r=3$ \textup{(}for $HS$\textup{)} and $r=2$ \textup{(}for $Co_3$\textup{)} are confirmed independently of the enumeration by the class-function count of \textup{Remark \ref{rem:char}} \textup{(}\textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}\textup{)}.

title: Remark

label: prop:hs2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:hs2}
Let $G=HS.2=\operatorname{Aut}(HS)$ act $2$-transitively on the $176$ points of the Higman--Sims graph.  The orbits of $G$ on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$ coincide with the three orbits of $HS$;  the three-point setwise stabilizers have orders
\[
|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=1440,\ 240,\ 192
\]
with $\lambda=12,72,90$ respectively, the pointwise stabilizers have orders $240,40,32$, and the induced image in $S_3$ is $S_3$ in each case.
head: environment
name: The overgroup $HS.2$ on 176 points

title: Proof
body_md: The block counts of the three $HS$-orbits are $|HS|/|HS_{\mathcal{O}}|=44352000/720=61600$, $44352000/120=369600$ and $44352000/96=462000$ \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:spor-correction})}, with $\lambda=12,72,90$ pairwise distinct.  Every $G$-orbit on triples is a union of $HS$-orbits, and $\lambda$ is a design parameter of the underlying block set, so orbits with distinct $\lambda$ cannot be fused by $G$;  hence $G$ has exactly the same three orbits on triples.  The orbit--stabilizer theorem then gives $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=|G|/\mathrm{blocks}=88704000/61600=1440$, $88704000/369600=240$, $88704000/462000=192$.  The induced image contains the $HS$-image $S_3$ and is contained in $S_3$, hence equals $S_3$, and the pointwise stabilizer orders are $1440/6=240$, $240/6=40$, $192/6=32$.  The arithmetic input is verified in GAP \textup{(Chapter \ref{sec:verify};  supplementary script \texttt{hs2\_orbits.g})}:  the three $HS$-orbits are computed directly with stabilizers $720,120,96$, each block count divides $|G|$ with quotient $1440,240,192$, and no nontrivial union of block counts divides $|G|$;  for the $\lambda=12$ and $\lambda=72$ orbits the normalizer of the \textup{(}center-free\textup{)} setwise stabilizer inside $\operatorname{Aut}(HS)$ is computed to have orders $1440$ and $240$, twice the $HS$-values, consistent with the orbit--stabilizer arithmetic.  The statement is a finite result for the degree-$176$ action;  no family claim is involved \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:open})}.

body_md:
\label{prop:co3}
Let $G=Co_3$ act $2$-transitively on the $276$ points \textup{(}point stabilizer $McL{:}2$, \cite{conway1985,wilson1996}\textup{)}.  Then $G$ has exactly two orbits on $\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$, with
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{orbit} & \lambda & |G_{\mathcal{O}}| & |G_{(\mathcal{O})}| & \overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}} & \#\text{blocks}\\
\hline
1 & 162 & 241920 & 40320 & S_3 & 2049300\\
2 & 112 & 349920 & 58320 & S_3 & 1416800

and $\binom{276}{3}=3466100=2049300+1416800$.

name: The sporadic group $Co_3$ on $276$ points

title: Proof
body_md: Take the degree-$276$ permutation representation of $Co_3$ from the Atlas \textup{(\texttt{Co3G1-p276aB0}, \cite{conway1985,wilson1996})}.  GAP \textup{(Chapter \ref{sec:verify};  supplementary script \texttt{co3\_orbits.g})} verifies $|G|=495766656000$, transitivity $2$, and the setwise two-point stabilizer order $|G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}|=13063680=2|G|/(276\cdot275)$;  its orbits on the remaining $274$ points have sizes $162$ and $112$.  The two representatives $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{1,2,4\}$ give distinct $G$-orbits on triples \textup{(the bijection of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:pair-orbits}} holds here, as for $HS$\textup{)}}.  For the two orbits the setwise stabilizers have orders $241920$ and $349920$, the pointwise stabilizers $40320$ and $58320$, and the induced image is $S_3$ in both cases;  the orbit--stabilizer theorem gives $2049300=495766656000/241920$ and $1416800=495766656000/349920$ blocks, summing to $\binom{276}{3}$, and $\lambda=6|G|/(|G_{\mathcal{O}}|\,276\cdot275)=162,112$ is integral.  The orbit count $r=2$ is confirmed independently by the class-function count of \textup{Remark \ref{rem:char}}:  $\sum_{g\in G}n(g)=991533312000=2|G|$ \textup{(Chapter \ref{sec:verify})}.  The statement is a finite result for the degree-$276$ action;  no family claim is involved \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:open})}.

label: lem:ext
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Extension lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Clear.  (2) Identifying $G$ with its image in $\operatorname{Aut}(S)$ (faithful, since $S$ is $2$-transitive and simple), we have $G\cap\operatorname{Inn}(S)=S$ and hence $G/S\le\operatorname{Out}(S)$.  The kernel of $G_{\mathcal{O}}\to G/S$ is $G_{\mathcal{O}}\cap S=S_{\mathcal{O}}$, so $|G_{\mathcal{O}}/S_{\mathcal{O}}|\le|\operatorname{Out}(S)|$ and the bound follows.  The isomorphism $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}/\overline{S}_{\mathcal{O}}\cong G_{\mathcal{O}}/(S_{\mathcal{O}}\cdot G_{(\mathcal{O})})$ follows from \eqref{eq:ses} and the third isomorphism theorem, since $S_{\mathcal{O}}\lhd G_{\mathcal{O}}$ and $G_{(\mathcal{O})}\lhd G_{\mathcal{O}}$.
(3) follows from the orbit-stabilizer theorem and the fact that $G= S\cdot(\text{outer part})$.
head: environment

label: prop:outer
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:outer}
Let $S\lhd G$ be a $2$-transitive extension acting on $\mathcal{P}$, and let $X\in\binom{\mathcal{P}}{3}$.  Then $S_X\le G_X$ and the quotient $G_X/S_X$ embeds into $G/S$.  Thus outer automorphisms can only enlarge the stabilizer and can fuse $S$-orbits, but the exact kernel, image, and orbit fusion must be computed for the particular extension.
head: environment
name: Outer extensions: general reduction

title: Proof
body_md: The inclusion $S_X\le G_X$ is immediate.  The map $G_X\longrightarrow G/S$ has kernel $G_X\cap S=S_X$, so the first isomorphism theorem gives an embedding $G_X/S_X\hookrightarrow G/S$.  If $X^S$ is an $S$-orbit, then the $G$-orbit of $X$ is a union of $S$-orbits because $S\lhd G$.  Whether several $S$-orbits fuse and whether an outer element acts trivially or nontrivially on $X$ is not determined by the abstract quotient alone.
