label: lem:affine
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The three-point stabilizer in affine groups

title: Proof
body_md: $(v,g_0)\in G_{\mathcal{O}}$ iff $\{v,\ g_0(u)+v,\ g_0(w)+v\}=\{0,u,w\}$.  The point $v$ must be one of $0,u,w$ (as $g_0$ is invertible, $v\ne g_0(u)+v$ etc.).  The four cases are obtained by matching the three images to the three points in all six ways;  (C) is the case $v=u$ with $g_0(u)+u=w$, $g_0(w)+u=0$, i.e.\ $g_0(u)=w-u$, $g_0(w)=-u$.  The affine element $(u,g_0)$ sends $0\mapsto u$, $u\mapsto g_0(u)+u=w$ and $w\mapsto g_0(w)+u=0$, so it permutes $\{0,u,w\}$ as the $3$-cycle $(0\,u\,w)$;  on the plane $\pi=\langle u,w\rangle$ the matrix of $g_0$ in the basis $(u,w)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose cube is the identity.  (The action of $g_0$ on a complement of $\pi$ is not constrained by (C), so $g_0$ may have order a multiple of $3$;  only the induced image on $\mathcal{O}$ matters.)
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:affine}} is the precise ``structure and solution'' of the three-point stabilizer announced in the Introduction:  computing $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ for the affine type is exactly solving the linear system \textup{(}T0\textup{)}--\textup{(}C\textup{)} inside $G_0$, together with the pointwise stabilizer \textup{(}1\textup{)}.  The solutions depend only on the $G_0$-orbit structure of pairs $\{u,w\}$ of nonzero vectors.
head: environment

label: rem:affine-six
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:affine-six}
Write the affine element as $g(x)=Ax+b$, $A\in G_0$, $b\in V$.  Since $g(0)=b\in X=\{0,u,w\}$, the image of $G_X$ in $Sym(X)$ is realized by the following six cases \textup{(}each row lists the induced permutation, the translation part $b$, and the images $A(u),A(w)$\textup{)}:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{permutation on }X & b & A(u) & A(w)\\ \hline
\mathrm{id} & 0 & u & w\\
(u\ w) & 0 & w & u\\
(0\ u) & u & -u & w-u\\
(0\ w) & w & u-w & -w\\
(0\ u\ w) & u & w-u & -u\\
(0\ w\ u) & w & -w & u-w
\end{array}
\]
For instance, $(0\ u\ w)$ requires $g(0)=u$, $g(u)=w$, $g(w)=0$, whence $b=u$, $A(u)=w-u$, $A(w)=-u$;  the other rows are obtained in the same way.  The pointwise stabilizer is therefore $G_{(X)}=\{A\in G_0: A(u)=u,\ A(w)=w\}$, embedded by $x\mapsto Ax$ (translation part zero), as in \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:affine}(1)}.  The two $3$-cycles are inverses of each other;  only one of them is an independent criterion, but listing both is convenient for checking computations and signs.
head: environment
name: The six permutations realized on a triple

label: thm:agl1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:agl1}
Let $G=AGL(1,p^d)=V\rtimes\mathbb{F}_{p^d}^{\times}$ \textup{(}$V=\mathbb{F}_{p^d}$, affine maps $t\mapsto at+b$\textup{)}, sharply $2$-transitive of degree $p^d$, $p^d\ge4$, and $\mathcal{O}=\{0,u,w\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G_{(\mathcal{O})}=1$ for all $\mathcal{O}$, and $G_{\mathcal{O}}\cong\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}\le S_3$.
\item A transposition \textup{(}fixing $0$ or $u$ or $w$\textup{)} exists iff $p$ is odd and one of the three points is the midpoint of the other two:
\[
\exists\ \text{transposition} \iff p\ \text{odd and } 2m=x+y\ \text{for }\{x,y,m\}=\mathcal{O}.
\]
In that case $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}=C_2$ \textup{(}unless a $3$-cycle also exists, giving $S_3$\textup{)}.
\item A $3$-cycle exists iff either
\[
\begin{gathered}
p
\ne3,\quad 3\mid p^d-1,\quad w=(a+1)u,\\
\text{where }a\in\mathbb{F}_{p^d}^{\times}\ \text{is a primitive cube root }(a^2+a+1=0,\ a
\ne1),
\end{gathered}
\]
or
\[
p=3\ \text{and } \mathcal{O}=\{x,x+u,x+2u\}\ \text{is an arithmetic progression}.
\]
\item Consequently \textup{(}with $q=p^d$\textup{)}:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $p=2$:  no transpositions exist \textup{(}$p$ even\textup{)};  a $3$-cycle exists iff $3\mid q-1$, i.e.\ iff $d$ is even \textup{(}since $3\mid2^d-1\iff d$ even\textup{)}.  Hence $G_{\mathcal{O}}=1$ for all $\mathcal{O}$ when $d$ is odd \textup{(}$q=8,32,128,\ldots$;  the smallest admissible example is $q=8$, since $q=2$ is excluded by $q\ge4$\textup{)}, while for $d$ even \textup{(}$q=4,16,\ldots$\textup{)} the triples of cube-root type have $G_{\mathcal{O}}\cong C_3$ and the remaining triples have $G_{\mathcal{O}}=1$;  in particular $AGL(1,4)\cong A_4$ has $G_{\mathcal{O}}\cong C_3$ for every $\mathcal{O}$ \textup{(}single orbit\textup{)};
  \item $p=3$:  $G_{\mathcal{O}}=S_3$ iff $\mathcal{O}$ is an arithmetic progression;  otherwise $G_{\mathcal{O}}=1$;
  \item $p
\ne2,3$:  $G_{\mathcal{O}}=C_2$ \textup{(}midpoint type\textup{)}, $C_3$ \textup{(}cube-root type\textup{)}, or $1$ \textup{(}generic\textup{)}, according to \textup{(}2\textup{)},\textup{(}3\textup{)};  in particular $G_{\mathcal{O}}$ is never $S_3$ for $p
\ne3$.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: $\AGL(1,p^d)$

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) sharply $2$-transitive:  the stabilizer of two points is trivial, so the pointwise stabilizer of three points is trivial.
(2) Solve (T0):  $g_0(t)=at+b$ with $\{b, au+b, aw+b\}=\{0,u,w\}$ and fixed point structure;  the transposition fixing $0$:  $b=0$, $a u=w$, $a w=u$:  $a^2=1$, $a
\ne1$ (as $u
\ne w$), so $a=-1$ (requires $p$ odd) and $w=-u$:  midpoint configuration $u+w=0$.  The transposition fixing $u$:  $b=w$, $a w + w = 0$:  $a=-1$ (p odd), $a u + w = u$:  $-u+w=u$:  $w=2u$:  so $\mathcal{O}=\{0,u,2u\}$:  $u$ is the midpoint of $0,2u$.  The transposition fixing $w$ is analogous and again reduces to the midpoint condition.
(3) (C):  $g_0(t)=at+b$, $b=u$, $a u+u=w$, $a w+u=0$:  $a u = w-u$, $a w = -u$:  substitute:  $a(w-u)=a w - a u = -u - (w-u) = -w$:  and directly $a^2 u = a(w-u) = -w$, $a^2 w = a(-u) = -a u = -(w-u)=u-w$:  so $a^2$ acts on $(u,w)$ as $u\mapsto -w$, $w\mapsto u-w$:  then $a^3$:  $a^3 u = a(-w) = -a w = u$:  so $a^3=1$ on the plane (as $a^3$ fixes $u$ and $w$):  $a^3=1$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$, $a
\ne1$:  $a$ a primitive cube root, $a^2+a+1=0$, which requires $p
\ne3$ and $3\mid q-1$.  Conversely if $a^2+a+1=0$, define $g_0(t)=at+u$;  check:  $g_0(0)=u$, $g_0(u)=a u+u=w$ (as $w=(a+1)u$), $g_0(w)=a w+u=a(a+1)u+u=(a^2+a)u+u=(-1)u+u=0$:  a $3$-cycle.  For $p=3$:  the translation $t\mapsto t+u$ is a $3$-cycle on $\{0,u,2u\}$ (arithmetic progression), and $t\mapsto t+u$ with $a=1$:  $g_0(0)=u$, $g_0(u)=2u$, $g_0(2u)=0$:  a $3$-cycle;  conversely a $3$-cycle with $a=1$:  $u+w$-type:  $g_0(0)=u$, $g_0(u)=u+u=2u=w$, $g_0(w)=w+u$ must be $0$:  $w=-u=2u$:  so $\mathcal{O}=\{0,u,2u\}$.
(4) follows from (2),(3) and the field arithmetic:  $3\mid p^d-1\iff p\equiv1\pmod3$ or ($p
\ne3$ and $d$ even with $p\equiv2\pmod3$);  for $p=2$:  $3\mid2^d-1\iff d$ even.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In characteristic $3$ the polynomial $a^2+a+1$ equals $(a-1)^2$, so the equation $a^2+a+1=0$ does not describe primitive cube roots there;  the $3$-cycle of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:agl1}(3)} in characteristic $3$ is the translation $t\mapsto t+u$ ($a=1$) on the arithmetic progression $\{x,x+u,x+2u\}$, not a cube-root case.  These two cases should not be conflated.
head: environment

label: thm:agamL1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:agamL1}
Let $G=A\string\Gamma L(1,p^d)=V\rtimes(\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}\rtimes C_f)$ \textup{(}affine maps $t\mapsto a\,\sigma(t)+b$, $\sigma\in C_f$ a subgroup of the field automorphisms of $\mathbb{F}_q$ \textup{(}$1\le f\le d$,\ $f\mid d$;\  $C_f$ is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p)\cong C_d$ of order $f$\textup{)};  the product $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}\rtimes C_f$ is a semidirect product because a field automorphism acts on the multipliers, $\sigma\,m_a\,\sigma^{-1}=m_{\sigma(a)}$\textup{)}, $q=p^d$, $\mathcal{O}=\{0,u,w\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The pointwise stabilizer consists of the \emph{twisted semilinear} maps
\[
x\longmapsto\frac{u}{\sigma(u)}\,\sigma(x),
\qquad \sigma\in C_f,\ \sigma(w/u)=w/u,
\]
one for each field automorphism fixing the ratio $r=w/u$ \textup{(}the multiplicative factor $a=u/\sigma(u)$ is then forced by $a\sigma(u)=u$\textup{)};  in particular
\[
|G_{(\mathcal{O})}|=\bigl|C_f(w/u)\bigr|=\frac{f}{[\,E(w/u):E\,]},
\qquad E=\mathrm{Fix}(C_f)=\mathbb{F}_{p^{d/f}},
\]
the order of the stabilizer of $r=w/u$ under $C_f$ \textup{(for the full group $C_f=\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p)$, i.e.\ $f=d$, this reduces to $|G_{(\mathcal{O})}|=d/[\mathbb{F}_p(w/u):\mathbb{F}_p]$;  for a proper subgroup $C_f$ the correct base field is the fixed field $E=\mathrm{Fix}(C_f)$)} \textup{(}a field automorphism $t\mapsto t^{p^k}$ fixes $w/u$ iff $k$ is a multiple of $[\mathbb{F}_p(w/u):\mathbb{F}_p]$\textup{)}.
\item A transposition in the induced action on $\mathcal{O}$ exists iff $\sigma(r)\in\{1-r,\ r^{-1},\ r/(r-1)\}$ for some $\sigma\in C_f$, and a $3$-cycle in the induced action exists iff $\sigma(r)\in\{1/(1-r),\ (r-1)/r\}$ for some $\sigma\in C_f$, where $r=w/u$ and $\sigma(r)$ denotes the image of $r$ under the field automorphism $\sigma$;  in each condition $\sigma$ ranges over $C_f$.  The three transposition values correspond respectively to the transpositions fixing $0$, $u$ and $w$;  the two $3$-cycle values are inverses of one another.  Here \textup{``the induced action contains a $3$-cycle''} is the precise statement:  when the pointwise kernel is nontrivial, the group element realizing the $3$-cycle need not itself have order $3$.
\item The full stabilizer order is
\[
|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=\sum_{\sigma\in C_f}\#\{\pi\in S_3:\ \sigma(r)=T_{\pi}(r)\},
\]
where $T_{\pi}$ ranges over the six anharmonic transformations of $r$ associated with the six permutations $\pi\in S_3$.  When computing the stabilizer one must count with multiplicity according to the six permutations and must not deduplicate the six values first:  for the midpoint type, the cube-root type and the characteristic-$3$ parameters, the values $T_{\pi}(r)$ can coincide.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: $\AaL(1,p^d)$

title: Proof
body_md: Direct from \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:affine}} and the structure of $\operatorname{\Gamma L}(1,q)$:  an affine semilinear map $x\mapsto a\sigma(x)+b$ fixes $\{0,u,w\}$ pointwise iff $b=0$, $a\sigma(u)=u$ and $a\sigma(w)=w$, i.e.\ iff $\sigma(w/u)=w/u$ and $a=u/\sigma(u)$;  by Galois theory the field automorphisms fixing $w/u$ are exactly those fixing $\mathbb{F}_p(w/u)$ pointwise, a cyclic group of order $f/[E(w/u):E]$ with $E=\mathrm{Fix}(C_f)=\mathbb{F}_{p^{d/f}}$ \textup{(reducing to $d/[\mathbb{F}_p(w/u):\mathbb{F}_p]$ for the full group $C_f=\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p)$)}.  For part\textup{ (2)}:  an element $(a,\sigma)\in G_0$ induces a permutation $\pi$ on $\mathcal{O}$ iff $\{a\sigma(0),\ a\sigma(u),\ a\sigma(w)\}=\{0,u,w\}$;  the condition $a\sigma(0)=0$ forces $b=0$, and solving for the multiplier $a$ shows that this holds exactly when $\sigma(r)=T_{\pi}(r)$, where $T_{\pi}$ is the anharmonic transformation attached to $\pi\in S_3$.  The six transformations are $r,\ 1-r,\ r^{-1},\ (1-r)^{-1},\ r/(r-1),\ (r-1)/r$;  the three transpositions correspond to $1-r$, $r^{-1}$, $r/(r-1)$ and the two $3$-cycles to $1/(1-r)$, $(r-1)/r$.  For part\textup{ (3)}:  for each $\sigma\in C_f$ there is at most one multiplier $a$ realizing a given $\pi$, so the count over $\sigma\in C_f$ and $\pi\in S_3$ with $\sigma(r)=T_{\pi}(r)$ is exact.

title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Non-collinear triples

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Direct from the structure of point stabilizers:  for $\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$ the pointwise stabilizer of the two vectors $u,w$ is the group of matrices $\begin{pmatrix}I_2&*\\0&*\end{pmatrix}$ with the bottom-right block in $\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)$ (order $q^{2(n-2)}|\operatorname{SL}(n-2,q)|$);  for $Sp$ fixing a nondegenerate plane pointwise is exactly $Sp$ of the perpendicular complement (order $|Sp(2a-2,q)|$).
(2) Let $g_0$ act on $\pi=\langle u,w\rangle$ by the matrix
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
i.e.\ $g_0(u)=w-u$, $g_0(w)=-u$.  With $\Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ the standard alternating form on $\pi$, $M^{\mathsf T}\Omega M=\Omega$ (direct multiplication) and $\det M=1$, so $g_0$ is an isometry of $(\pi,\beta|_\pi)$ and lies in $\operatorname{SL}(2,q)$.  For $H=\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$, $n\ge2$, we extend by the identity on a complement (for $n\ge3$;  for $n=2$, $\pi=V$).  For $H=Sp(2a,q)$:  if $\pi$ is nondegenerate, $V=\pi\perp\pi^{\perp}$ and the identity extension on $\pi^{\perp}$ works;  if $\pi$ is totally isotropic, the hyperbolic-basis extension of \textup{Remark \ref{rem:sp-isotropic}} applies.  In both cases the extended element lies in $Sp(2a,q)$.  By \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:affine}}(C) the affine element $(u,g_0)$ is a $3$-cycle on $\{0,u,w\}$.  Hence $3$-cycles exist on every non-collinear triple, for $H=\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$ ($n\ge2$), $Sp(2a,q)$ and $G_2'(q)\leSp(6,q)$ alike.
(3) The transposition fixing $0$ requires $g_0(u)=w,\ g_0(w)=u$, i.e.\ the matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on $\pi$;  $\det P=-1$, and $P^{\mathsf T}\Omega P=-\Omega$.  Hence, on a nondegenerate plane, the swap lies in $\operatorname{SL}$ (resp.\ $Sp$) iff $-1=1$, i.e.\ $q$ even.  The transpositions fixing $u$ or $w$ have matrices $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, both of determinant $-1$, so the same conclusion holds.  For $H=\operatorname{SL}(n,q)$ with $n\ge3$ the sign can be corrected in the complement (scale one complement basis vector by $-1$), so all transposition types exist for all $q$.  For $H=Sp(2a,q)$ on a totally isotropic plane the swap extends by $\mathrm{diag}(P,P)$ on a hyperbolic basis \textup{(Remark \ref{rem:sp-isotropic})}, so transpositions exist there for every $q$;  the two plane types therefore behave differently.
(4) The table follows from (1)--(3) and the splitting $G_{\mathcal{O}}=G_{(\mathcal{O})}\rtimes\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}$ (the image is realized inside $H$).

name: The $G_2'$ rows: orbits and pointwise stabilizers

title: Proof
body_md:
The order $|H_u|=q^6(q^2-1)$ is the classical parabolic-stabilizer value \textup{\cite{kleidmanliebeck}}:  $H_u=Q{:}L$ with $Q$ the unipotent radical of order $q^5$ and $L\cong\operatorname{SL}(2,q)$ of order $q(q^2-1)$;  together with the transitivity of $H$ on $V\setminus\{0\}$ this gives (1).  The orbit structure of (2) is the classical suborbit structure of the point stabilizer of $G_2(q)$ on the $6$-dimensional module, i.e.\ the split Cayley hexagon geometry \textup{\cite{cooperstein1979}}:  the hyperbolic ($h(u,w)
\ne 0$) and the two isotropic classes (long-root and short-root $2$-spaces) are the $H_u$-orbits listed, and the transitivity on each is part of that geometry;  the fixed points $\{\lambda u\}$ are fixed by (1).  The stabilizer orders in (2) are then computed from the orbit--stabilizer identity:  $q^6(q^2-1)/q^5=q(q^2-1)$;  $q^6(q^2-1)/(q(q^2-1))=q^5$;  $q^6(q^2-1)/(q^3(q^2-1))=q^3$.  For (3), the pointwise stabilizer of a collinear triple is $H_u$ by (1):  an element fixing $0,u,\lambda u$ pointwise fixes the line $\langle u\rangle$ pointwise and lies in $H_u$, and conversely every element of $H_u$ fixes the line pointwise \textup{(by linearity, (1)}\textup{)}.  No transposition exists by the characteristic-$2$ swap obstruction.  The collinear orbits are governed by the base-point moves:  translation by $u$ sends $\{0,u,\lambda u\}$ to $\{u,0,(\lambda+1)u\}=\{0,u,(\lambda+1)u\}$, and the identity $\{0,u,\lambda u\}=\{0,\lambda u,u\}$ identifies $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{-1}$;  hence the $\lambda$-classes are the orbits of $S_3\cong\langle s,i\rangle$ on $\mathbb{F}_q\setminus\{0,1\}$ as stated, whose number is $1+(q-4)/6$ for $f$ even \textup{(the two-point orbit $\{\omega,\omega^2\}$ plus the $(q-4)/6$ regular orbits}\textup{)} and $(q-2)/6$ for $f$ odd.  On the $\{\omega,\omega^2\}$-orbit the $3$-cycle is realized by the affine element $(u,\omega^2\cdot{})$ \textup{(the scalar $\omega^2$ on the line, available in the Levi factor of the point stabilizer, together with the translation by $u$}\textup{)}, so $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=3q^6(q^2-1)$;  on every other collinear orbit the image is $1$ and $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=q^6(q^2-1)$.  For the non-collinear orbits the decomposition $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=6|H_{u,w}|$ is the enumeration of $(v,g)$ described in the theorem \textup{(the six cosets realize $S_3$;  the occurrence of both linear parts for $v=u$ and $v=w$ uses that $w$ and $u+w$ are in the same $H_u$-orbit, which is part of the orbit list of (2)}\textup{)}.  The parameters $\lambda$ follow from \eqref{eq:lambda}:  $\lambda=6|G|/\bigl(|G_{\mathcal{O}}|\,v(v-1)\bigr)$ with $|G|=q^6|H|$, $v=q^6$:  the collinear $\{\omega,\omega^2\}$-orbit ($f$ even):  $6|H|/\bigl(3q^6(q^2-1)(q^6-1)\bigr)=2$;  the collinear image-$1$ orbits:  $6|H|/\bigl(q^6(q^2-1)(q^6-1)\bigr)=6$;  hyperbolic:  $6|H|/\bigl(6q(q^2-1)(q^6-1)\bigr)=q^5$;  isotropic:  $6|H|/\bigl(6q^5(q^6-1)\bigr)=q(q^2-1)$ and $6|H|/\bigl(6q^3(q^6-1)\bigr)=q^3(q^2-1)$, using $|H|=q^6(q^6-1)(q^2-1)$ throughout.  The numerical case $q=4$ (orbit lengths, stabilizer orders, images and $\lambda$ values $2,1024,60,960$, the collinear stabilizer $|G_{\mathcal{O}}|=184320=3q^6(q^2-1)$ with image $C_3$ and block size $5591040$, and the injectivity of the suborbit correspondence) is verified by the GAP computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} \textup{(supplementary script \texttt{g2\_full2.g})}.

label: lem:2homog-class
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:2homog-class}
Let $G$ be a finite $2$-homogeneous permutation group that is not $2$-transitive.  Then $G$ is affine one-dimensional, $G\leA\string\Gamma L(1,q)$ on $v=q=p^d$ points with $q$ odd, $G$ is solvable, and the point stabilizer $G_0$ has odd order.  In particular $|G|$ is odd, so $G$ contains no involution, and no almost simple example occurs.
head: environment
name: Classification of the $2$-homogeneous groups

title: Proof
body_md: The $2$-homogeneous groups were classified by Kantor \cite{kantor1985}; the only $2$-homogeneous groups that are not $2$-transitive are the affine one-dimensional groups $G\leA\string\Gamma L(1,q)$ with $q$ odd.  If $G_0$ contained an element of order $2$, then together with $2$-homogeneity this element would invert the action on the remaining points and make $G$ $2$-transitive (a classical observation of Livingstone--Wagner \cite{livingstone1965}):  an involution fixing one point of a pair acts transitively on the other, so transitivity on unordered pairs upgrades to transitivity on ordered pairs.  Hence $|G_0|$ is odd, and $|G|=v|G_0|$ is odd because $v=q$ is odd.  Since $|G|$ is odd, $G$ is solvable \cite{feit1963}, and no almost simple (non-solvable) group is $2$-homogeneous without being $2$-transitive.

label: thm:2homog
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:2homog}
Let $q\equiv3\pmod4$ be a prime power \textup{(so $q=p^d$ with $p\equiv3\pmod4$ and $d$ odd)}, let $V=(\mathbb{F}_q,+)$, let $M=(F_q^*)^2$ be the subgroup of squares, and let $G=V\rtimes M$ act on $V$.  Then $G$ is $2$-homogeneous but not $2$-transitive, $|G|=q(q-1)/2$ is odd, and the number of $G$-orbits on the three-point subsets of $V$ is
\[
\sigma_3(G)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{q+2}{3}, & q\equiv7\pmod{12},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{q-2}{3}, & q\equiv11\pmod{12},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{q}{3}, & q=3^d\ (d\ \text{odd}).
\end{cases}
\]
Every three-point orbit $X$ is a $2$-\mbox{$(q,3,\lambda_X)$} design with $\lambda_X\in\{1,3\}$, and the distribution is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{$q$ range} & \#\{X:\lambda_X=1\} & \#\{X:\lambda_X=3\}\\
\hline
q\equiv7\pmod{12} & 2 & (q-4)/3\\
q\equiv11\pmod{12} & 0 & (q-2)/3\\
q=3^d\ (d\ \text{odd}) & 1 & q/3-1
\end{array}
\]
The $\lambda=1$ orbits are Steiner triple systems (their number is $2$ for $q\equiv7\pmod{12}$, e.g.\ $q=7$ gives two distinct Fano planes, $1$ for $q=3^d$, and $0$ for $q\equiv11\pmod{12}$, consistently with the existence of $\mathrm{STS}(q)$ iff $q\equiv1,3\pmod6$), with setwise stabilizer of order $3$ and induced image $C_3$;  the $\lambda=3$ orbits have trivial setwise stabilizer and image $1$.  In particular no three-point orbit has induced image $C_2$ or $S_3$, since $|G|$ is odd.  The values are verified by direct enumeration for $q=7,11,19,23,31,43,47$ and $q=3$.
head: environment
name: Orbit data of the square-subgroup affine group

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Transitivity.}  The multiplier group $M$ has index $2$ in $F_q^*$ and, since $q\equiv3\pmod4$, $-1$ is not a square, so $-1
\notin M$;  hence $M$ is transitive on the $|F_q^*|/\{\pm1\}=(q-1)/2$ two-subsets $\{x,-x\}$, i.e.\ on unordered pairs of nonzero points, and $G$ is $2$-homogeneous.  $M$ is not transitive on $F_q^*$ ($|M|=(q-1)/2<q-1$), so $G$ is not $2$-transitive.

\emph{Orbit count (Burnside).}  The $q(q-1)/2$ elements of $G$ are the maps $g\colon x\mapsto mx+s$ with $m\in M$, $s\in\mathbb{F}_q$;  let $f(g)$ be the number of three-point subsets fixed by $g$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $g=\mathrm{id}$ ($m=1$, $s=0$):  $f=\binom q3$.
\item[(b)] $m=1$, $s
\ne 0$ (pure translation, order $p$):  if $p>3$ no three-point subset is fixed;  if $p=3$, $g$ is a product of $q/3$ three-cycles and fixes exactly $q/3$ three-subsets.
\item[(c)] $m
\ne1$:  $g$ has the unique fixed point $s/(1-m)$ and its cycles on the remaining points are the $|m|$-cycles;  it fixes a three-point subset exactly when $|m|=3$, in which case it fixes $(q-1)/3$ of them.
\end{itemize}
An element of $M$ has order $3$ iff $3\mid|M|=(q-1)/2$, i.e.\ iff $q\equiv1\pmod3$.  For $q\equiv7\pmod{12}$ ($q\equiv1\pmod3$ and $q\equiv3\pmod4$) $M$ contains exactly two elements of order $3$, each giving $q$ affine maps, whence
\[
\sigma_3=\frac{1}{q(q-1)/2}\left[\binom q3+2q\cdot\frac{q-1}{3}\right]=\frac{q+2}{3}.
\]
For $q\equiv11\pmod{12}$ ($q\equiv2\pmod3$) $M$ has no order-$3$ element and $p>3$, so
\[
\sigma_3=\frac{1}{q(q-1)/2}\binom q3=\frac{q-2}{3}.
\]
For $q=3^d$ the translations are three-cycles and $3
\nmid q-1$, so $M$ has no order-$3$ element, giving
\[
\sigma_3=\frac{1}{q(q-1)/2}\left[\binom q3+(q-1)\frac q3\right]=\frac q3.
\]

\emph{The $\lambda$-distribution.}  Each three-point orbit $X$ is a $2$-\mbox{$(q,3,\lambda_X)$} design by $2$-homogeneity;  its number of blocks is both $\lambda_X\cdot q(q-1)/6$ and $|G|/|G_X|$, whence $\lambda_X=3/|G_X|$ and $\lambda_X\in\{1,3\}$.  Let $a$ (resp.\ $b$) count the orbits with $\lambda=1$ (resp.\ $3$).  The sum of the $\lambda_X$ over all orbits equals $q-2$ \textup{(the number of three-subsets of the form $\{0,1,t\}$)}, i.e.\ $a+3b=q-2$;  together with $a+b=\sigma_3$ this yields $b=(q-2-\sigma_3)/2$ and $a=\sigma_3-b$, giving the displayed distributions.  In particular $a=0$ exactly for $q\equiv11\pmod{12}$, matching the non-existence of $\mathrm{STS}(q)$ for $q\equiv5\pmod6$;  for $q=7$ one obtains $a=2$ (two distinct Fano planes) and $b=1$, as checked.  Since $\lambda_X=3/|G_X|$, the $\lambda=1$ orbits have $|G_X|=3$ and induced image $C_3$, and the $\lambda=3$ orbits have $|G_X|=1$ and image $1$.

label: cor:blocktrans

head: environment
name: Block-transitive triple systems

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) If $|I|=1$, $\mathcal{T}$ is a $G$-orbit by construction, so $G$ is block-transitive.  If $|I|\ge2$, choose $i
\ne j$ in $I$; blocks of $\mathcal{T}_i$ and $\mathcal{T}_j$ lie in distinct $G$-orbits, so no element of $G$ maps one to the other, and $G$ is not block-transitive.
(ii) Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $2$-$(v,3,1)$ design and $G$ $2$-transitive.  Given blocks $X=\{a,b,c\}$ and $Y=\{a',b',c'\}$, $2$-transitivity gives $g\in G$ with $a^g=a'$, $b^g=b'$.  The block through $\{a,b\}$ is unique (namely $X$), and the block through $\{a',b'\}$ is unique (namely $Y$); hence $X^g=Y$, and $G$ is block-transitive.  By (i), $\mathcal{T}$ is a single orbit.  (The argument fails for $\lambda\ge2$, when $\lambda$ blocks pass through $\{a,b\}$ and $g$ may send $X$ to any of them.)
(iii) is immediate from (i).

label: cor:flagtrans
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Flag-transitive triple systems

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) A flag is an incident pair $(\alpha,X)$ with $\alpha\in X$.  Since $G$ is block-transitive on $\mathcal{T}_i$, it is flag-transitive exactly when the block stabilizer $G_{\mathcal{O}_i}$ is transitive on the three points of $\mathcal{O}_i$ (the standard block-transitive/flag-transitive reduction).  Via the exact sequence $1\to G_{(\mathcal{O}_i)}\to G_{\mathcal{O}_i}\to\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}_i}\to1$, this is transitivity of the image; among the subgroups of $S_3$, precisely $C_3$ and $S_3$ are transitive on three points, whereas $C_2$ (a single transposition) fixes one point and $1$ fixes all.
(ii) is obtained by reading the image attached to each orbit in \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}}, using the image computations in the cited theorems.  (Block's classical gcd criterion, that a block-transitive $2$-design with $\gcd(k,v)=1$ is flag-transitive, is a sufficient condition; here $k=3$, so it applies whenever $3
\nmid v$, but the image criterion above is both necessary and sufficient and also covers the case $3\mid v$.)

label: rem:sts
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sts}
A triple system with $\lambda=1$ is a Steiner triple system.  In the framework of \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:union-orbits}}, a nonempty union of three-point orbits is a Steiner triple system if and only if it consists of a single orbit with $\lambda_i=1$ \textup{(}each orbit parameter is a positive integer, so $\lambda_I=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1$ forces $|I|=1$ and $\lambda_i=1$\textup{)}.  The Steiner triple systems admitting a $2$-transitive automorphism group have been classified by M.~Hall \cite{hall1985}:  such a system is necessarily an affine space $\mathrm{AG}(r,3)$ \textup{(}$v=3^r$\textup{)} or a projective space $\mathrm{PG}(s,2)$ \textup{(}$v=2^{s+1}-1$\textup{)}, apart from the single exception of the $2$-transitive representation of $Alt(7)$ on the $15$ points of $\mathrm{PG}(3,2)$.  In the affine case the proof is due to J.~I.~Hall \textup{(}see \cite{hall1985}\textup{)}, and independently Kantor and Shult obtained similar results \textup{(}footnote in \cite{hall1985}\textup{)};  the wider context of $2$-transitive linear spaces is treated by Kantor \cite{kantor1985}.  For completeness we record the $\lambda=1$ rows of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:main}}, all consistent with Hall's classification and confirmed by the exhaustive computation of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} \textup{(}which, together with the integrality criterion \eqref{eq:lambda}, leaves no further $\lambda=1$ orbit in the tested degree range $v\le200$\textup{)}.  The projective-space systems:  the collinear triples of $\mathrm{PG}(n-1,2)$ \textup{(}$PSL(n,2)$, $n=3,4,5,6$\textup{)} give $\mathrm{STS}(7)$, $\mathrm{STS}(15)$, $\mathrm{STS}(31)$, $\mathrm{STS}(63)$.  The affine systems:  the characteristic-$3$ arithmetic-progression orbit of $AGL(1,q)$ \textup{(}$q\equiv0\pmod3$\textup{)} gives $\mathrm{STS}(q)$ for $q=3,9,27,81$ \textup{(}the affine space $\mathrm{AG}(r,3)$, $q=3^r$\textup{)}, and the collinear orbits of $ASL(n,q)$/$AGL(n,q)$ in characteristic $3$ give the affine spaces $\mathrm{AG}(2,3)$, $\mathrm{AG}(3,3)$, $\mathrm{AG}(4,3)$ \textup{(}that is, $\mathrm{STS}(9)$, $\mathrm{STS}(27)$, $\mathrm{STS}(81)$\textup{)}, together with a special non-collinear orbit of $ASL(2,9)$ which, by Hall's theorem, is abstractly isomorphic to $\mathrm{AG}(4,3)$.  The group $PSU(3,2)\cong3^2{:}Q_8$ of degree $9$, and its extensions, give the affine plane $\mathrm{STS}(9)$ \textup{(}the unitary case $q=2$ of Hall's analysis\textup{)}, and $Alt(7)\le\operatorname{GL}(4,2)$ on the $15$ nonzero vectors of $\mathbb{F}_2^4$ \textup{(}$a+b+c=0$\textup{)} gives $\mathrm{STS}(15)$, the same system as the collinear triples of $PSL(4,2)\congAlt(8)$ \textup{(}Hall's exception\textup{)}.  The groups $3^4{:}(2.S_5)$ and $ASp(4,3)$ of degree $81$ give further $\mathrm{STS}(81)$, which by Hall's theorem are abstractly isomorphic to $\mathrm{AG}(4,3)$.
head: environment
name: Steiner triple systems ($\lambda=1$

label: lem:orbital
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orbital}
Let $G\leSym(V)$ be transitive.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \cite[Proposition 6.3.1]{li2010}: the $G$-orbital graphs (one for each
self-paired orbital, otherwise pairs of complementary directed graphs) are
exactly the $G$-arc-transitive graphs with vertex set $V$; $G$ is primitive iff
every non-trivial orbital graph is connected (Higman's theorem,
\cite[Proposition 6.3.6]{li2010}).
\item[(ii)] \cite[Lemma 7.1.4]{li2010}: a $G$-arc-transitive graph $\Gamma$ is
vertex transitive and $G_v$ is transitive on $\Gamma(v)$; conversely a
connected $G$-vertex-transitive graph with $G_v$ transitive on $\Gamma(v)$ is
$G$-arc transitive.  In particular a graph $\Gamma$ is $G$-arc transitive iff
$G$ is transitive on the set of edges of $\Gamma$ \emph{and} $G_v$ is
transitive on $\Gamma(v)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Orbital graph criteria

label: def:inc
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:inc}
The \emph{incidence graph} $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ of $\mathcal{T}$ is the bipartite graph
with left part $\mathcal{P}$ (points), right part $\mathcal{T}$ (blocks), and edges the
point--block incidences $x\sim X$ iff $x\in X$.  The \emph{block graph}
$\overline{\Gamma}(\mathcal{T})$ has vertex set $\mathcal{T}$ and joins distinct blocks
$X,Y$ iff $X\cap Y
\ne\varnothing$.
head: environment

label: thm:incidence
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:incidence}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be an orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$, and let
$N$ be its $v\times b$ incidence matrix, $b=\lambda v(v-1)/6$,
$r=\lambda(v-1)/2$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is a connected bipartite graph with biparts of sizes
$v$ and $b$; every point has degree $r$ and every block has degree $3$,
i.e.\ $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is biregular with valencies $(3,r)$.  It is connected
with diameter at most $4$: any two points are at distance $2$ (every pair of
points lies in $\lambda\ge1$ blocks), and any two blocks are at distance
most $4$.
\item[(ii)] The adjacency matrix $A=A(\Gamma)$ satisfies
\[
NN^{\top}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J,
\]
and $A$ has spectrum
\[
\pm\sqrt{3r}\quad(1\text{ each}),\qquad
\pm\sqrt{r-\lambda}\quad(v-1\text{ each}),\qquad
0\quad(b-v\text{ each}),
\]
where the zero block has multiplicity $b-v$: since $3r>0$ and
$r-\lambda=\lambda(v-3)/2>0$, the matrix $NN^{\top}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$
is positive definite over $\mathbb{R}$, hence $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{R}}N=v$ and
the stated multiplicities hold over $\mathbb{R}$; (the $p$-rank over finite
fields is treated separately in the coding section, \textup{Section
\ref{sec:coding}}).
\item[(iii)] Each block $X=\{a,b,c\}$ spans a star $a-X$, $b-X$, $c-X$; the girth of $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is $4$ if $\lambda\ge2$ (two blocks share a pair
$\{a,b\}$, giving a $4$-cycle $a\sim X\sim b\sim Y\sim a$) and is exactly $6$ if
$\lambda=1$ and $v\ge7$: two blocks sharing a pair would force $\lambda\ge2$, so
no $4$-cycle exists, while a $6$-cycle always exists.  Indeed, for the unique
block $X=\{a,b,x\}$ containing the pair $\{a,b\}$ and any $d\notin\{a,b,x\}$,
let $Y=\{a,d,y\}$ and $Z=\{b,d,z\}$ be the unique blocks containing $\{a,d\}$
and $\{b,d\}$ respectively;  then $y\notin\{a,b,d,x\}$ (as $y=x$ would put
$\{a,x\}$, and $y=b$ would put $\{a,b\}$, in two blocks) and
$z\notin\{a,b,d,x,y\}$ (as $z=x$, $z=a$ or $z=y$ would likewise put a pair in
two blocks), so $a\sim X\sim b\sim Z\sim d\sim Y\sim a$ is a $6$-cycle.  Hence
every Steiner row of \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}} with $v\ge7$ has girth exactly $6$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Spectrum and structure of the incidence graph

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) The point degrees are $r$ by design; the block degree is $3$ by
definition.  Connectedness and the diameter bound: for points $a
\ne b$ there
are $\lambda\ge1$ blocks containing $\{a,b\}$, so $a$ and $b$ are joined via
such a block at distance $2$.  For blocks $X=\{a,x,y\}$ and $Y=\{b,u,w\}$ pick
any block $Z$ containing $\{a,b\}$; then
$X\sim a\sim Z\sim b\sim Y$ is a walk of length $4$.  Hence the graph is
connected, bipartite, and has diameter $\le4$; it is exactly $4$ unless all
blocks pairwise meet in points, i.e.\ unless the design is a projective plane
of order $2$ ($v=7$, the Fano plane), in which case the block--block distance
is $2$ through a common point.
(ii) The $(a,b)$-entry of $NN^{\top}$ is the number of blocks containing
$\{a,b\}$, hence $r$ on the diagonal and $\lambda$ off it, giving
$NN^{\top}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$.  The eigenvalues of the latter are
$3r=(r-\lambda)+\lambda v$ on the all-ones vector and $r-\lambda$ on
$\langle\mathbf1\rangle^{\perp}$.  For
$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&N\\ N^{\top}&0\end{pmatrix}$, a standard block
diagonalization of $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}NN^{\top}&0\\0&N^{\top}N\end{pmatrix}$
shows that the nonzero eigenvalues of $A$ are the square roots of the nonzero
eigenvalues of $NN^{\top}$ together with their negatives; since
$N^{\top}N$ has the same nonzero spectrum as $NN^{\top}$ plus $b-v$ zeros
(if $\operatorname{rank} N=v$), the displayed spectrum follows.
(iii) If $\lambda\ge2$, two distinct blocks contain a common pair
$\{a,b\}$, hence $a\sim X\sim b\sim Y\sim a$ is a $4$-cycle.  If $\lambda=1$
then any two blocks meet in at most one point, so no $4$-cycle exists;  for
$v\ge7$ the Steiner condition $v\equiv1,3\pmod6$ gives at least two blocks
through any point, and a $6$-cycle always exists:  fixing the unique block
$X=\{a,b,x\}$ of the pair $\{a,b\}$ and any $d\notin\{a,b,x\}$, the unique
blocks $Y=\{a,d,y\}$ and $Z=\{b,d,z\}$ satisfy $y,z\notin\{a,b,d,x\}$ and
$y\ne z$ (any coincidence would place a pair in two distinct blocks,
contradicting $\lambda=1$), so $a\sim X\sim b\sim Z\sim d\sim Y\sim a$ is a
$6$-cycle.  Hence the girth is exactly $6$, as stated.
head: environment

label: rem:integral
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:integral}
When $3r$ and $r-\lambda$ are both perfect squares, $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is an
\emph{integral} graph.  This happens, e.g., for the collinear orbit of
$PSU(3,3)$ on $28$ points ($3r=81$, $r-\lambda=25$) and for the
$\lambda=8$ non-collinear orbit of $PSU(3,3)$ ($3r=324$, $r-\lambda=100$);
see \textup{Table \ref{tab:as}}.  Integrality is a rare phenomenon and is read off
directly from the orbit data.
head: environment

label: thm:arc
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:arc}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system, and let
$S_a(\mathcal{T})=\{X\in\mathcal{T}:\ a\in X\}$ be the star of a point $a$.  The
incidence graph $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is $G$-arc transitive if and only if the
stabilizer $G_a$ is transitive on $S_a(\mathcal{T})$.  Equivalently, since
$G$ is $2$-transitive, $\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is $G$-arc transitive if and only if,
for a pair $P=\{a,b\}$, the two-point stabilizer $G_P$ is transitive on the
triples of $\mathcal{T}$ containing $P$ up to the action of $G_a$; more concretely,
the number of $G_a$-orbits on $S_a(\mathcal{T})$ equals the number of
$G_P$-suborbits on $\{c:\ \{a,b,c\}\in\mathcal{T}\}$ fused by $G_a$.
head: environment
name: Arc-transitivity criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
The bipartite parts are $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$, both $G$-invariant, so no element
of $G$ interchanges a point with a block.  Hence arcs $(a,X)$ are
$G$-transitive iff edges $\{a,X\}$ are, and by
\textup{Lemma \ref{lem:orbital}(ii)} this is equivalent to $G_a$ transitive on
$S_a(\mathcal{T})$.  The reformulation is the standard suborbital fusion: $G_a$
acts on the star, and a star element $\{a,b,c\}$ is determined by the pair
$\{b,c\}$, so the $G_a$-orbits on $S_a(\mathcal{T})$ correspond to the orbits of
$G_a$ on unordered pairs $\{b,c\}$ with $\{a,b,c\}\in\mathcal{T}$; fixing $b$,
these correspond to the $G_{\{a,b\}}$-suborbits of $c$, counted up to the
fusion induced by the action of $G_a$ on its star.
head: environment

label: cor:arc-families
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Arc-transitive families

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) For a $3$-transitive family, and for a $3$-homogeneous family whose
triple stabilizer induces $C_3$ or $S_3$, the image $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}}$
of the setwise stabilizer is $C_3$ or $S_3$, so the criterion of
\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:arc-image}} applies directly.  This is the
correct condition:  $3$-homogeneity alone is not enough, since $AGL(1,8)$
is $3$-homogeneous on $8$ points with trivial triple stabilizer, and its
unique orbit triple system is not flag-transitive.
(ii) For $G=PSL(2,q)$ acting on $\mathcal{P}=\mathbb{F}_q\cup\{\infty\}$ and
$a=0$, identify the remaining points with $\mathbb{F}_q$.  For
$q\equiv1\pmod4$ the two triple orbits are classified by the cross-ratio:
$\{0,1,t\}^{G}$ is determined by the class of
$t\in\mathbb{F}_q\setminus\{0,1\}$ modulo the square subgroup
$(\mathbb{F}_q^{\times})^2$ of index $2$; each orbit has
$\lambda=(q-1)/2$.  The stabilizer $G_0$ is the group of maps
$t\mapsto s^2t+b$ ($s\in\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$, $b\in\mathbb{F}_q$), which is
transitive on $\mathbb{F}_q$; fixing $b$, the subgroup fixing both points
acts as multiplication by squares on the remaining points and is transitive
on each set $\{c:\ c/b\ \text{lies in a fixed square class}\}$.  Hence $G_0$
has exactly one orbit on the star of a fixed orbit $\mathcal{T}$, so
$\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$ is $G$-arc transitive.  The argument for the single orbit in
the $3$-homogeneous case is the same, with all of $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$
acting.  (iii) A star element $\{a,u,v\}$ is mapped by $G_a=\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}$
(multiplication about $a$) to $\{a,su,sv\}$, so the ratio $v/u$ is a $G_a$-
invariant; the star orbits are therefore in bijection with the ratio classes
occurring among the blocks of the orbit.  The assertion follows.  In each
case the criterion of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:arc}} applies.
head: environment

label: prop:arc-image
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Arc-transitivity via the stabilizer image

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii): an arc $(\alpha,X)$ of $\Gamma(\mathcal{T}_i)$ is by
definition a flag of $\mathcal{T}_i$, and conversely.  (ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv):
by \textup{Corollary \ref{cor:flagtrans}(i)}, flag-transitivity is equivalent
to $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}_i}\in\{C_3,S_3\}$.  (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv): the
transitive subgroups of $S_3$ on three points are exactly $C_3$ and $S_3$
(the subgroups of $S_3$ are $1$, the three conjugates of $C_2$, $C_3$ and
$S_3$;  among these precisely $C_3$ and $S_3$ act transitively on the three
points), so transitivity of $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}_i}$ on $\mathcal{O}_i$ is
equivalent to $\overline{G}_{\mathcal{O}_i}\cong C_3$ or $S_3$.  Finally, by
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:arc}}, arc-transitivity of $\Gamma(\mathcal{T}_i)$ is
equivalent to transitivity of $G_\alpha$ on the star
$S_\alpha(\mathcal{T}_i)$, which is precisely flag-transitivity (ii), completing
the cycle.

label: prop:arc-classification
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:arc-classification}
Throughout, $\lambda$ denotes the design parameter (the number of blocks
through a pair of points, i.e.\ the \emph{index}) of an orbit triple
system, given by \eqref{eq:lambda} (this is \emph{not} the replication
number $r=\lambda(v-1)/2$, the number of blocks through a point;  note that $\lambda=6/|G_{\mathcal{O}}|$ holds only in the
two-point-regular case, the general formula involving the two-point
stabilizer);  no second meaning is attached to the symbol $\lambda$ in this
monograph.  Reading the image column of \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}} through
\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:arc-image}}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $PSU(3,q)$, $d=\gcd(3,q+1)$, exactly the following orbit triple
systems have $G$-arc-transitive incidence graphs:  the collinear orbit
($\lambda=q-1$, image $S_3$) for every $q$;  the $\lambda=(q^2-1)/d$ orbits
(image $S_3$, $q$ odd, $d$ of them) and the $\lambda=2(q^2-1)/d$ orbits
(image $C_3$) whenever they occur;  the $\lambda=6(q^2-1)/d$ orbits (image
$1$, $(q+1)/3$ of them when $d=3$ --- for $q$ odd by \textup{Proposition
\ref{prop:psu-odd}} and for $q$ even ($q=2^{2m+1}$) by \textup{Proposition
\ref{prop:psu-even}}, e.g.\ three $\lambda=126$ orbits for $q=8$;  none occurs
for $d=1$) are not arc transitive.  In particular for $q=3$ all three orbits are arc transitive
(image column $S_3,C_3,S_3$, one orbit of each type), confirming the
computational census of \textup{Table \ref{tab:magma}}.
\item For $Sz(q)$, $q=2^{2m+1}>2$ \textup{(the exceptional $Sz(2)$ is not
simple and is excluded)}, no orbit triple system has arc-transitive incidence
graph:  the circle orbit has image $C_2$ and every generic orbit image $1$.
\item For $Ree(q)$, $q=3^{2m+1}>3$, the $\lambda=2(q-1)$ orbits (image $C_3$)
and the two $\lambda=q-1$ orbits (collinear image $C_3$, non-collinear image
$S_3$) are arc transitive, while the $\lambda=6(q-1)$ (image $1$) and
$\lambda=3(q-1)$ (image $C_2$) orbits are not;  the small case $q=3$
(${}^2G_2(3)\congP\string\Gamma L(2,8)$ on $28$ points) is covered separately by the
computed census of \textup{Table \ref{tab:verify}} \textup{($\lambda=6,4,6,2,6,2$)}.
\end{enumerate}

label: thm:stblock
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:stblock}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The block graph $\overline{\Gamma}(\mathcal{T})$ is $G$-vertex
transitive and regular of degree
\[
k=3\lambda\frac{v-3}{2}=3r-3\lambda,
\]
because a block $X=\{a,b,c\}$ meets $\lambda(v-3)$ blocks through $a$, and
each of the other blocks through $b$ or $c$ has been counted twice over.
\item[(ii)] If $\lambda=1$ and $v\ge9$, then $\overline{\Gamma}(\mathcal{T})$ is
strongly regular with parameters
\[
srg\Bigl(\frac{v(v-1)}6,\ \frac{3(v-3)}2,\ \frac{v+3}2,\ 9\Bigr).
\]
For $v=7$ (the Fano plane, $\operatorname{GL}(3,2)=PSL(3,2)\congPSL(2,7)$ acting on the
$7$ points) the block graph is the complete graph $K_7$, not strongly regular
with the above parameters.
\item[(iii)] If $v\ge9$ and $\lambda\ge2$, the block graph is regular but
generally not strongly regular; its adjacency spectrum is not controlled by
the pair data alone (the block--block intersection numbers depend on the
suborbits of the two-point stabilizers).
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Block graph: general and Steiner cases

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) $G$ is transitive on blocks, so vertex transitivity is clear.  For the
degree, fix $X=\{a,b,c\}$ and let $N_1$ be the number of blocks meeting $X$
in exactly one point and $N_2$ the number meeting $X$ in exactly two points.
The latter are the blocks through a pair of $X$ other than $X$ itself: there
are $\lambda-1$ through $\{a,b\}$, $\lambda-1$ through $\{a,c\}$, and
$\lambda-1$ through $\{b,c\}$, all distinct, so $N_2=3(\lambda-1)$.  The
former are the blocks through $a$ containing neither $b$ nor $c$: their
number is $r-1-2(\lambda-1)=\lambda(v-1)/2-2\lambda+1$, and similarly for
$b,c$, with the three families disjoint.  Hence
\[
k=N_1+N_2=3\Bigl(\frac{\lambda(v-1)}2-2\lambda+1\Bigr)+3(\lambda-1)
=\frac{3\lambda(v-3)}2.
\]
The blocks avoiding $X$ altogether are the remaining ones, so
\[
N_0=b-1-k=\frac{\lambda v(v-1)}6-1-\frac{3\lambda(v-3)}2,
\]
and the three layers $N_0,N_1,N_2$ partition the block set.  Note that the
count is uniform in $\lambda$: for $\lambda\ge2$ two blocks may meet in $0$, $1$
or $2$ points, and the computation above accounts for both the $\lambda-1$
blocks through a fixed pair and the blocks through a fixed point avoiding the
other two, without ambiguity.
(ii) Let $\lambda=1$.  Adjacent blocks $X=\{a,b,c\}$, $Y=\{a,d,e\}$
share exactly one point, say $a$.  A common neighbor $Z$ of $X,Y$ is either a
block through $a$ (other than $X,Y$): there are $r-2=(v-5)/2$ of these; or a
block determined by one point of $X\setminus\{a\}$ and one of
$Y\setminus\{a\}$: there are $2\times2=4$ such blocks
$Z=\{b,d,w\}$ with $w
\ne a$, and they are distinct from the blocks through
$a$ and from each other (two of them sharing two points of $X$ would force
them equal, contradicting $\lambda=1$).  Hence
$\lambda_{\overline\Gamma}= (v-5)/2+4=(v+3)/2$.  For nonadjacent blocks
$X,Y$ (disjoint, since $\lambda=1$): any common neighbor $Z$ meets each of
$X,Y$ in exactly one point, so it is determined by a pair of points
$(x\in X,\ y\in Y)$; all $3\cdot3=9$ such blocks exist and are distinct,
giving $\mu_{\overline\Gamma}=9$.  Since $v\ge9$ guarantees the existence of
disjoint pairs of blocks and of intersecting pairs, the claimed strongly
regular parameters follow.
(iii) This is the generic situation; the failure of strong regularity is
visible already for $\lambda=2$: the number of common neighbors of two
blocks meeting in two points depends on the number of further blocks through
that pair, i.e.\ on $\lambda-1$ data, whereas for disjoint blocks it depends
on the suborbits of the two-point stabilizers.
head: environment

label: rem:blocklayers
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:blocklayers}
For $\lambda\ge2$ the edge set of $\overline{\Gamma}(\mathcal{T})$ splits into two
$G$-invariant layers: the pairs of blocks meeting in exactly one point and the
pairs meeting in exactly two points (the intersection size is $G$-invariant,
so each layer is a union of $G$-orbits on unordered block pairs).  The
corresponding per-vertex degrees are exactly the numbers $N_1$ and $N_2$ of
the proof above, $N_1=3(r-2\lambda+1)$ and $N_2=3(\lambda-1)$, so the total
degree is $k=N_1+N_2$.  Strong regularity fails precisely when the
common-neighbor count distinguishes the two layers: the common neighbors of
two blocks meeting in two points are controlled by the $\lambda-1$ further
blocks through the common pair, while for blocks meeting in one point they
are controlled by the two-point stabilizer suborbits, and these two data are
independent in general (see \textup{Proposition \ref{prop:blockgraph-srg}}).  For $\lambda=1$ the
second layer is empty and one recovers the strongly regular regime of
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)}; this is the only case in which the block graph
is determined by the pair data alone.
head: environment
name: Edge layers of the block graph for $\lambda\ge2$

label: prop:blockgraph-srg
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:blockgraph-srg}
Let $\mathcal{T}_i$ be a single orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$
and block graph $\overline\Gamma_i$, and let $G_X$ be the setwise stabilizer
of a block $X\in\mathcal{T}_i$ in $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Criterion.}  $\overline\Gamma_i$ is strongly regular if and only
if, for the fixed block $X$, the common-neighbor count
$c(X,Y)=\#\{Z\in\mathcal{T}_i:\ Z\cap X
\ne\varnothing
\ne Z\cap Y\}$ takes a single value on the whole set of blocks meeting $X$ in
exactly $2$ points, a (possibly different) single value on the whole set of
blocks meeting $X$ in exactly $1$ point, and a single value on the whole set
of blocks disjoint from $X$;  equivalently, constancy on the whole adjacency
set and on the whole non-adjacency set.  (Constancy on each individual
$G_X$-orbit alone would be automatic for any $G_X$-invariant function and is
\emph{not} sufficient:  the criterion requires the same value across all
$G_X$-orbits within each of the three intersection layers.  By
block-transitivity the value is then constant over all block pairs, as
required by strong regularity.)  A sufficient condition is that each of the
three layers is a single $G_X$-orbit, together with the required equality of
the common-neighbor values on the two adjacent layers;  when all three
layers are nonempty single $G_X$-orbits the rank of $G$ on $\mathcal{T}_i$ is
$4$, not $3$, and the equality of the common-neighbor values on the
one-point and two-point layers (both adjacent to $X$) must still be
verified.  The criterion is necessary since $G_X$ preserves the
intersection size and the common-neighbor count, and the three layers are
nonempty for $v\ge9$, $\lambda\ge1$ \textup{(for $\lambda=1$ the two-point
layer is empty and the condition on it is vacuous)}.
\item For $\lambda=1$ and $v\ge9$ the criterion holds and yields the strongly
regular parameters of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)};  this settles the
Steiner case family-wide.
\item For $PSU(3,3)$ \emph{none} of the three block graphs is strongly
regular (computed by exhaustive enumeration of all block pairs):  the
collinear orbit ($v=28,\lambda=2$, block number $252$) has constant counts
$33$ on the one-point layer and $50$ on the two-point layer, but the
zero-point layer takes the two values $15$ and $18$;  the non-collinear
orbits ($\lambda=8$, block number $1008$, and $\lambda=16$, block number
$2016$) split already on the two-point layer, with the two values $212,214$
resp.\ $428,430$.
\item For $PSU(3,3)$ the three block graphs fail the criterion, as
computed in (3).  For the unitary, Suzuki and Ree rows beyond $PSU(3,3)$
the criterion is \emph{not} settled family-wide here:  a split of an
intersection layer into several $G_X$-orbits does not by itself force
distinct common-neighbor values, and the full common-neighbor counts have
not been computed for every parameter value.  The strongly regular block
graphs \emph{established} in this monograph are therefore the Steiner cases
of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)} and the $PSU(3,3)$ failures of
(3);  the remaining unitary, Suzuki and Ree rows are left as a
case-by-case computational question rather than a closed classification.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Strong regularity of the block graph

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) The block graph is $G$-vertex transitive.  For a pair of vertices
$X,Y$ the number $c(X,Y)$ of common neighbors is a $G_X$-invariant
function of $Y$, hence constant on $G_X$-orbits;  it is moreover constant on
each intersection layer whenever that layer is a single $G_X$-orbit, which
gives the sufficient direction, while the necessary direction is obtained by
noting that a strongly regular graph has, by definition, a single
$\lambda$-value on adjacent pairs and a single $\mu$-value on non-adjacent
pairs, and each of the three intersection layers consists either of adjacent
or of non-adjacent pairs (a block meeting $X$ in $2$ points is adjacent to
$X$;  meeting it in $1$ point is adjacent;  meeting it in $0$ points is
not).  If $G$ has rank at most $3$ on $\mathcal{T}_i$, then $G_X$ has at most two
orbits off $X$, namely the one- and two-point layers, whence both are single
orbits and the sufficient condition of (1) applies.
(2) is \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)} recast in the language of (1).
(3) is the computed statement above;  the counts are obtained by exhaustive
enumeration of the $\binom{b}{2}$ unordered block pairs, which is feasible
for $b\le2016$.
(4) For $PSU(3,3)$ the statement is the computation of (3).  The
suborbit data of \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:prelim}} supply the $G_X$-orbit
decomposition of the blocks off $X$ through the two-point stabilizers
(\textup{Proposition \ref{prop:pair-orbits}}), but a split of a layer into
several $G_X$-orbits does not by itself imply distinct common-neighbor
values;  a family-wide claim for the unitary, Suzuki and Ree rows would
require the full common-neighbor counts, which are not computed here.
head: environment

label: ex:pg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:pg}
[The Fano block graph and $\operatorname{PG}(n-1,2)$]
For the projective geometry $\operatorname{PG}(n-1,2)$, the points are the
$v=2^n-1$ nonzero vectors of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and the blocks are the
$b=(2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)/3$ triples $\{x,y,x+y\}$.  This is an STS$(v)$
invariant under $\operatorname{GL}(n,2)$, so by \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)} the block
graph is $srg\bigl((2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)/3,\ 3(2^{n-1}-2),\ 2^{n-1}+1,\ 9\bigr)$
for $n\ge4$ \textup{(the parameter formula of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)}
requires $v\ge9$, and $v=2^n-1\ge9$ exactly for $n\ge4$)}.  The Fano case
$n=3$ ($v=7$) is singled out:  the block graph is $K_7$, reflecting that in
the Fano plane any two triples meet.  For $n=4$ ($v=15$, the STS$(15)$ on
$\mathbb{F}_2^4$), the block graph is
$srg(35,18,9,9)$, which is the well-known complement of the
Tutte--Coxeter / Kneser-type graph parameter; in particular it is strongly
regular with the parameters of the $(35,18,9,9)$ graph.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The strongly regular block graph of an STS is the classical connection between
Steiner triple systems and strongly regular graphs (see \cite{cameron1999}).
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)} upgrades the classical statement: the
\emph{orbit} triple systems of a $2$-transitive group with $\lambda=1$
necessarily yield these parameters, and the $2$-transitive rows of
\textup{Table \ref{tab:main-lambda}} with $\lambda=1$ are exactly the $AGL(1,q)$ orbits with
$q\equiv0\pmod3$, i.e.\ the affine Steiner triple systems STS$(q)$,
together with the Hering exceptional rows containing $\lambda=1$:  the $Alt(7)$-on-$15$ row $(\mathrm{STS}(15))$ and the degree-$81$ row $3^4{:}(2.S_5)$ $(\mathrm{STS}(81))$ \textup{(cf.\ Remark \ref{rem:sts})}.  The geometric
STS's $\operatorname{PG}(n-1,2)$ of \textup{Example \ref{ex:pg}} are orbit systems of the
$2$-transitive group $PSL(n,2)=\operatorname{GL}(n,2)$ on the points of
$\operatorname{PG}(n-1,2)$ (\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:psln}}), with $\lambda=1$;  they are
included here as an illustration of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:stblock}(ii)}
alongside the affine and Hering Steiner rows.
head: environment

label: def:cw
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cw}
The \emph{constant-weight code} of $\mathcal{T}$ is
\[
C_{cw}(\mathcal{T})=\{\,\mathbf1_X:\ X\in\mathcal{T}\,\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^{v},
\]
the set of characteristic vectors of the blocks, viewed as a binary code of
length $v$ and weight $3$.
head: environment

label: thm:cwdist
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cwdist}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The constant-weight code $C_{cw}(\mathcal{T})$ has parameters
$(v,\,|\mathcal{T}|,\,d\,;\,3)$ with $d=6-2m$, $m=\max_{X
\ne Y}|X\cap Y|$.
\item[(ii)] If $\lambda\ge2$ then $m=2$ and $d=2$: two distinct blocks
containing the same pair realize distance $2$ (for $v\ge7$), while blocks
meeting in exactly one point realize distance $4$.
\item[(iii)] If $\lambda=1$ then $m=1$ and $d=4$ (for $v\ge7$, the Steiner
triple system condition $v\equiv1,3\pmod6$): blocks meet in at most one
point, and two blocks through a point realize distance $4$.
\item[(iv)] $m=0$ occurs if and only if the blocks of $\mathcal{T}$ are pairwise
disjoint, which for a $2$-transitive orbit forces the degenerate case
$|\mathcal{T}|\le1$ or $v<6$; in particular $d=6$ never occurs for the nontrivial
families of \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}}.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Minimum distance of orbit codes

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) and the formula for $d$ are immediate.  (ii): $\lambda\ge2$ means that a
point pair $\{a,b\}$ lies in at least two blocks of $\mathcal{T}$, so the two distinct
blocks containing $\{a,b\}$ realize $|X\cap Y|=2$; since $m\le2$ always, the
maximum is attained inside the orbit and $m=2$.  (iii): $\lambda=1$
means no pair of blocks shares two points, so $m\le1$.  If $v\ge7$, the
Steiner condition $r=(v-1)/2\ge3$ gives at least two blocks through any point $a$,
and any two such blocks intersect in $\{a\}$ exactly, so $|X\cap Y|=1$ is
attained inside $\mathcal{T}$; hence $m=1$ and $d=4$.  In both cases the extremal
intersection is realized by explicit blocks of the orbit, not merely inferred
from the replication number.  (iv): $m=0$ forces all
blocks pairwise disjoint; since $G$ is transitive on $\mathcal{T}$ and $2$-transitive
on $\mathcal{P}$, each point lies in $r$ blocks, and pairwise disjointness gives
$3|\mathcal{T}|=vr$ together with $\lambda=0$, contradicting
$\lambda\ge1$ unless $|\mathcal{T}|=1$ (then $v=3$ and $r=1$) or no such orbit
exists; the table families all have $v\ge5$ and $\lambda\ge1$, so $d=6$ is
excluded.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For every nontrivial $2$-transitive orbit triple system,
$d\in\{2,4\}$, with
\[
d=2\iff\lambda\ge2,\qquad d=4\iff\lambda=1.
\]
In particular the orbit codes of the families of \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}} are
all of distance $2$, except exactly the Steiner rows
$\lambda=1$: the $AGL(1,q)$ orbits with $q\equiv0\pmod3$ and the Hering
exceptions with $\lambda=1$, which have distance $4$.
head: environment
name: Classification of the binary orbit codes

label: thm:johnson
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:johnson}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-invariant Steiner triple system on $v$ points
($\lambda=1$), and let $C_{cw}(\mathcal{T})=\{\mathbf1_X:X\in\mathcal{T}\}\subseteq\mathbb F_2^v$
be the constant-weight orbit code of \textup{Section \ref{sec:coding}}.  By
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:cwdist}(iii)} it has parameters $(v,|\mathcal{T}|,4;3)$.  The
Johnson bound for binary constant-weight codes states
$A(n,2\delta,w)\le\lfloor\frac nw\,A(n-1,2\delta,w-1)\rfloor$; for
$(n,w,\delta)=(v,3,2)$:
\[
|\mathcal{T}|=A(v,4,3)=\frac{v(v-1)}6,
\]
and equality holds because $|\mathcal{T}|=v(v-1)/6$ by the design count
(\textup{Lemma \ref{lem:lambda}}), which equals the bound.  Hence the code is
optimal among constant-weight codes of the given length, weight and minimum
distance: it attains the Johnson bound.
head: environment
name: Steiner orbit codes meet the Johnson bound

title: Proof
body_md:
By \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:cwdist}(iii)} the code has parameters
$(v,|\mathcal{T}|,4;3)$, and $|\mathcal{T}|=v(v-1)/6$ by the design count
(\textup{Lemma \ref{lem:lambda}}).  The Johnson bound gives
\[
A(v,4,3)\le\Big\lfloor\frac v3\,A(v-1,4,2)\Big\rfloor
=\Big\lfloor\frac v3\Big\lfloor\frac{v-1}2\Big\rfloor\Big\rfloor
=\frac{v(v-1)}6
\]
since $v\equiv1,3\pmod6$:  for $v\equiv3\pmod6$ one has $3\mid v$ and $2\mid(v-1)$, while for $v\equiv1\pmod6$ (e.g.\ $v=7,13$) the factor $(v-1)/2$ is a multiple of $3$, so $\bigl\lfloor\frac v3\lfloor\frac{v-1}2\rfloor\bigr\rfloor=\frac v3\cdot\frac{v-1}2=\frac{v(v-1)}6$ in both cases.  Hence
$A(v,4,3)=|\mathcal{T}|$.
head: environment

label: ex:mj
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:mj}
The $3$-homogeneous row $v=12$ has $\lambda=10$, so the constant-weight code
has parameters $(12,220,2;3)$.  The Steiner rows of
\textup{Table \ref{tab:main}} produce the optimal codes
$(q, q(q-1)/6, 4; 3)$ for STS$(q)$ under $AGL(1,q)$, $q\equiv0\pmod3$:
for $q=9$ this is a $(9,12,4;3)$ code, and for $q=27$ a
$(27,117,4;3)$ code.
head: environment
name: Optimal Steiner orbit codes

label: def:descode
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:descode}
Let $N$ be the $v\times b$ incidence matrix of $\mathcal{T}$ over a field $F$ (rows indexed by points, columns by blocks).  The \emph{design code} of $\mathcal{T}$ over $F$ is
\[
C_{q}(\mathcal{T})=\operatorname{RowSpan}_{F}(N)\subseteq F^{b},\qquad q=|F|,
\]
the span of the point rows $\mathbf r_\alpha$ of weight $r$.
(If $F=\mathbb{F}_2$ we write $C_2(\mathcal{T})$.)
head: environment

label: thm:descode
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:descode}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$,
$r=\lambda(v-1)/2$, and let $F=\mathbb{F}_q$ with $\operatorname{char}F=p$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If $p
\nmid3r$ and $p
\nmid(r-\lambda)$, then
$\operatorname{rank} N=v$ and $\dim_F C_q(\mathcal{T})=v$.
\item[(ii)] The all-ones word $\mathbf1\in C_q(\mathcal{T})$ whenever $p
\ne3$
(the sum of the $v$ rows equals $3\mathbf1$).
\item[(iii)] For $p=2$: $C_2(\mathcal{T})$ \textup{(the point-row code of \textup{Definition \ref{def:descode}}}
\textup{)} is self-orthogonal (with respect to the
standard inner product) if and only if $r$ and $\lambda$ are both even: the row
self-products equal $r$ and the distinct-row products equal $\lambda$, so all
inner products vanish in $\mathbb F_2$ exactly when both are even.  This
criterion is independent of (i): a full-rank Gram matrix $NN^{\top}$ does not
by itself imply self-orthogonality, and self-orthogonality is tested directly
on the row inner products, not on the rank.  In
particular:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] the $PSL(2,q)$ orbits with $q\equiv1\pmod4$
($\lambda=(q-1)/2$ even) are self-orthogonal exactly for $q\equiv1\pmod8$:
indeed $r=(q-1)q/4$ is even iff $(q-1)/4$ is even;
\item[(b)] among the $3$-homogeneous rows, the unique orbit with $\lambda=v-2$ is
self-orthogonal exactly when $r$ and $v-2$ are both even, e.g.\ $M_{22}$ on
$22$ points ($r=210$, $\lambda=20$), while $M_{11},M_{12},M_{23},M_{24}$ and
$Alt(v),Sym(v)$ are not in general;
\item[(c)] all non-collinear $PSU(3,q)$ orbits are self-orthogonal: for $q$ odd,
$\lambda\in\{(q^2-1)/d,2(q^2-1)/d,6(q^2-1)/d\}$ is even (for odd $q$
one has $8\mid q^2-1$, and division by $d\in\{1,3\}$ does not remove the
factor $2$, so $(q^2-1)/d$ is even) and $r=\lambda q^3/2$ is even;
for $q$ even the existing non-collinear types
($\lambda=2(q^2-1)/d$, $6(q^2-1)/d$) are even again and $r$ is even;
\item[(d)] the collinear $PSU(3,q)$ orbits are self-orthogonal exactly for
$q\equiv1\pmod4$ ($r=(q-1)q^3/2$ is even iff $q\equiv1\pmod4$);
\item[(e)] the trivial $Sz(q)$ orbits ($\lambda=6(q-1)$, $r=3(q-1)q^2$) are
self-orthogonal, while the circle orbits
($\lambda=3(q-1)$, $q$ even) are not;
\item[(f)] the $Ree(q)$ orbits with $\lambda\in\{6(q-1),2(q-1)\}$ are
self-orthogonal, those with $\lambda\in\{3(q-1),q-1\}$ are not;
\item[(g)] the second $Sp(2n,2)$ orbits ($\lambda_1=2^{2n-2}$ even, $r$ even) are
self-orthogonal, the first ones are not.
\end{itemize}
\item[(iv)] The minimum weight of $C_q(\mathcal{T})$ is at most
\[
\min\{\,r,\ 2(r-\lambda)\,\},
\]
realized by the point rows (weight $r$) and by the \emph{difference} of
two rows belonging to a pair (weight $2(r-\lambda)$;  in characteristic $2$
the difference equals the sum).
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Rank, all-ones word, self-orthogonality

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) $NN^{\top}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$ has eigenvalues $3r$ and $r-\lambda$;
if both are nonzero in $F$, then $NN^{\top}$ is nonsingular, so
$\operatorname{rank} N\ge\operatorname{rank} NN^{\top}=v\ge\operatorname{rank} N$, and $\operatorname{rank} N=v$.
(ii) The $j$-th entry of the sum of all rows is the number of points in block
$j$, namely $3$; dividing by $3$ (possible for $p
\ne3$) gives $\mathbf1$.
(iii) $C_2(\mathcal{T})$ is self-orthogonal iff the rows of $N$ are pairwise
orthogonal, iff $NN^{\top}=0$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, iff (reading the diagonal
and off-diagonal entries of $(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$) $r\equiv\lambda\equiv0
\pmod2$.  The family-by-family statements follow by substituting the orbit
parameters from \textup{Table \ref{tab:main}}; e.g.\ for
$PSL(2,q)$, $q\equiv1\pmod4$: $\lambda=(q-1)/2$ is even and
$r=\lambda q/2=(q-1)q/4$ has the parity of $(q-1)/4$, so the code is
self-orthogonal exactly for $q\equiv1\pmod8$; for
non-collinear $PSU(3,q)$, $q$ odd, $d=1$ or $3$, the parameters
$\lambda\in\{(q^2-1)/d,2(q^2-1)/d,6(q^2-1)/d\}$ are even (as $8\mid
q^2-1$ for odd $q$ and division by $d\in\{1,3\}$ does not remove the factor
$2$) and
$r=\lambda(q^3)/2$ is even (as $q^3$ is odd and $\lambda/2$ even by the same
divisibility), so self-orthogonality holds; the collinear $PSU(3,q)$ orbit
has $r=(q-1)q^3/2$, which is odd exactly for $q\equiv3\pmod4$, giving the
claimed parity.
(iv) The rows have weight $r$; for two points $\alpha,\beta$ lying in a
common block, the difference $\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta$ of their
rows has weight $2(r-\lambda)$ (the coordinates of the $\lambda$ common
blocks become $0$);  over characteristic $2$ the difference equals the sum.
Both words lie in $C_q(\mathcal{T})$, hence the minimum weight is at most the
smaller one.
head: environment

label: prop:rank-minweight
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rank-minweight}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a single orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$,
$r=\lambda(v-1)/2$ and $v\ge5$, with incidence matrix $N$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Criteria.}  Two independent criteria hold.  First,
$\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_2}N=v$ if and only if there is no nonempty subset
$S\subseteq\mathcal{P}$ meeting every block in an even number of points
\textup{(an \emph{even transversal}:  $|S\cap X|$ even for every
$X\in\mathcal{T}$)}\textup{)}.  Second, the minimum weight $d$ of $C_2(\mathcal{T})$
equals $r$ if and only if no word of weight $<r$ occurs among the nontrivial
combinations $xN$, $0\ne x\in\mathbb{F}_2^v$;  (the row space of $N$ is spanned by the
  point rows, whose weight is the generator weight $r$, while the minimum distance $d$ is the
  minimum weight over all nonzero codewords, i.e.\ over all nontrivial combinations $xN$;
  the two notions are distinguished explicitly)  the inequality $d\le r$ holds
unconditionally (the point rows have weight $r$), and for $v\ge5$ the upper
bound of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(iv)} tightens to the single value
$r$ (as $\min\{r,2(r-\lambda)\}=r$, i.e.\
$\lambda(v-1)/2\le\lambda(v-3)$), so the criterion for $d=r$ reduces to the
absence of combinations of weight $<r$;  the finite searches of (2) below
verify this absence only for combinations of at most five rows, so they bound
the minimum weight from below in that range without determining the complete
minimum distance.
\item \emph{Computed values.}  For $PSU(3,3)$ (all three orbits,
$\lambda=2,8,16$) and $PSU(3,5)$ (all six orbits, $\lambda=4,8,48$) the
$\mathbb{F}_2$-rank of $N$ is $v$ ($28$ resp.\ $126$):  the design codes of
these orbit triple systems have \emph{full} $\mathbb{F}_2$-rank, and no even
transversal exists.  Moreover for $PSU(3,3)$ every combination of at most five point rows has
weight at least $r$ ($27,108,216$) --- in particular none has weight $<r$;
the complete minimum distance is not determined by this finite search, as
stated.
(This is a finite search result in that range only;  a determination of the
true minimum distance would require a complete traversal of all $2^v-1$
combinations, a reliable minimum-distance algorithm or a theoretical lower
bound, and is not claimed here.)  The conjectured values $v-2$ or $v-3$
recorded in the literature are not attained by the full-rank codes in the
cases computed.
\item \emph{Consequences.}  In every case of (2) the all-ones word lies in
$C_2(\mathcal{T})$ \textup{(} $p=2$, $\mathbf1=\sum_{\alpha}\mathbf r_\alpha$,
as $3\equiv1\pmod2$ \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(ii)}\textup{)}, and in
the self-orthogonal cases
\textup{(Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(iii)(c))} the inclusions
$C_2(\mathcal{T})\subseteq C_2(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ with $\dim C_2(\mathcal{T})=v$ give
$\dim C_2(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}=b-v$, consistent with $b\ge2v$
\textup{($b=\lambda v(v-1)/6\ge2v$ for $v\ge13$, which holds in all cases
above)}\textup{)}.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Full rank and minimum weight of the unitary design codes

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) $\operatorname{rank} N=v$ means the $v$ point rows are independent over
$\mathbb{F}_2$, i.e.\ $xN=0$ has only the trivial solution;  the $j$-th
coordinate of $xN$ is $|S\cap X_j|$ with $S=\mathrm{supp}(x)$, so a nonzero
solution is exactly an even transversal.  The second statement is the
definition of the minimum weight of the row space.  The equality
$\min\{r,2(r-\lambda)\}=r$ for $v\ge5$ is the elementary inequality
$(v-1)/2\le v-3$.
(2) The ranks are computed with GAP on the standard unital permutation
representations used throughout \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}}:
\textup{AtlasGroup("U3(3)")} of degree $28$ and the primitive group of degree
$126$ and order $126\,000$ \textup{(} $PSU(3,5)$, found in the GAP
primitive-group library\textup{)};  the incidence matrix of each orbit is
assembled from the orbit file and row-reduced over $\mathbb{F}_2$.  The
implementation is checked against the Fano plane \textup{STS}(7), whose design
code has the classical rank $4$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.  The minimum-weight
values for $PSU(3,3)$ are obtained by exhaustive search of the combinations
$xN$ with $x$ of support at most $5$, together with the upper bound $r$ of
(1);  the search establishes the absence of weight-$<r$ words in that range
only, as stated.
(3) follows from \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(ii),(iii)(c)} and the rank
values of (2).
head: environment

label: prop:dual
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dual}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system with parameters $(v,3,\lambda)$ and
$r=\lambda(v-1)/2$, and let $F=\mathbb{F}_q$ with $\operatorname{char}F=p$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] (\emph{Exact generators of $C_q(\mathcal{T})$.)}  $C_q(\mathcal{T})$ is spanned
by the point rows $\mathbf r_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\mathcal{P}$.  If $p
\ne3$, then the
all-ones word has the exact expression
\[
\mathbf1=3^{-1}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbf r_\alpha\in C_q(\mathcal{T}),
\]
and, provided moreover $p\nmid v$, one has
$C_q(\mathcal{T})=\langle\,\mathbf1,\ \mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta:
\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{P}\,\rangle$ (one fixed $\beta$ suffices;  the natural
condition here is $p\nmid v$, not $p\nmid r$).
\item[(ii)] (\emph{Membership of $\mathbf1$ in the dual.)}
$\mathbf1\in C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ if and only if $p\mid r$.  For $p=2$ the
all-ones word therefore lies in $C_2(\mathcal{T})\cap C_2(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ if and
only if $r$ is even; in particular this holds in every self-orthogonal case
of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(iii)}, e.g.\ the $M_{22}$ row ($r=210$) and the
non-collinear $PSU(3,q)$ rows.
\item[(iii)] (\emph{Exact description of the dual.)}
\[
C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}=\bigl\{\,u\in F^b:\ \sum_{X\in\mathcal{T},\ \alpha\in X}u_X=0
\text{ for every }\alpha\in\mathcal{P}\,\bigr\},
\]
i.e.\ $u\in C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ iff the point-block incidence equations
$Nu^{\top}=0$ hold entrywise.  When the rank criterion of
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(i)} applies, $\dim C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}=b-v$.  For
$p=2$, $C_2(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ is spanned by the characteristic vectors of the
\emph{even covers} of $\mathcal{P}$: indeed the entrywise condition says exactly that
the support of $u$ covers every point an even number of times, and conversely
every even cover satisfies the entrywise equations.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: All-ones word and the dual code

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) The first assertion is the definition.  For $p
\ne3$, summing the rows
gives $\sum_\alpha\mathbf r_\alpha=3\mathbf1$ coordinatewise (block $X$ has
$3$ points), hence the displayed expression.  For the spanning assertion
assume additionally $p\nmid v$.  If $u=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\mathbf
r_\alpha$ has zero coordinate sum, then
$0=\sum_Xu_X=3\sum_\alpha c_\alpha$, so (as $p\ne3$) $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha=0$ and
$u=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta)\in
\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta\}$.  Thus
$C_q(\mathcal{T})\cap\{\text{zero coordinate sum}\}$ equals the span of the
differences.  It remains to place $\mathbf r_\beta$ itself in
$\langle\mathbf1,\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta\rangle$.  Summing
the coordinatewise identity $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbf r_\alpha=3\mathbf1$
in the quotient
$F^b/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta\}$ gives
$v[\mathbf r_\beta]=3[\mathbf1]$, hence, since $p\nmid v$,
$\mathbf r_\beta-(3/v)\mathbf1\in
\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta\}$ \textup{(equivalently,
by $3b=vr$, the coordinate sum of $\mathbf r_\beta-(r/b)\mathbf1$ is $0$,
so the same conclusion follows from the first part)}.  Therefore
$\mathbf r_\beta=(3/v)\mathbf1+
(\mathbf r_\beta-(3/v)\mathbf1)\in
\langle\mathbf1,\mathbf r_\alpha-\mathbf r_\beta\rangle$.  The reverse
inclusion is immediate.
(ii) $\mathbf1\cdot\mathbf r_\alpha=\sum_{X
\ni\alpha}1=r$ for every
$\alpha$, so $\mathbf1\in C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ iff $r=0$ in $F$, i.e.\ iff
$p\mid r$.  For $p=2$ one has $p
\ne3$ automatically, so
$\mathbf1\in C_2(\mathcal{T})$ by (i) and $\mathbf1\in C_2(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ iff
$r$ is even.
(iii) $u\in C_q(\mathcal{T})^{\perp}$ iff $u\cdot\mathbf r_\alpha=0$ for all
$\alpha$, which is exactly the entrywise condition displayed.  The dimension
claim follows from $\dim C_q(\mathcal{T})=v$ under the criterion of
\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(i)}.  For $p=2$ the displayed condition is
equivalent to the support of $u$ being an even cover, so the dual is spanned
by their characteristic vectors.
head: environment

label: rem:not-selforth
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:not-selforth}
Two conventions for the linear code of a design coexist in the literature, and the distinction is kept throughout this monograph.  The standard design code of Assmus--Key is the span of the \emph{block vectors} in $\mathbb F_2^v$;  since every block of a triple system has weight $3$, that code is never self-orthogonal over $\mathbb F_2$.  In this monograph the design code $C_q(\mathcal{T})$ of \textup{Definition \ref{def:descode}} is the row space of the $v\times b$ incidence matrix (the span of the \emph{point rows} $\mathbf r_\alpha$ in $\mathbb F_2^b$), and its self-orthogonality is governed by the parity of $(r,\lambda)$, not by the block size;  in particular the design codes of the non-collinear $PSU(3,q)$ orbits with $q$ odd are self-orthogonal over $\mathbb F_2$.  The constant-weight code $C_{cw}(\mathcal{T})$ of \textup{Section \ref{sec:coding}} is the (nonlinear) set of block vectors of weight $3$ in $\mathbb F_2^v$, for which self-orthogonality is not defined.  The two linear objects, the point-row code in $\mathbb F_2^b$ and the block code in $\mathbb F_2^v$, have the same dimension $\operatorname{rank} N$, but their self-orthogonality criteria are opposite in nature (parity of $r,\lambda$ versus the parity of the block size $3$);  the statements of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(iii)} refer to the point-row code.
head: environment
name: Block vectors versus point rows; two conventions

label: thm:module
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:module}
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $G$-orbit triple system and $N$ its point-by-block incidence
matrix, so that the design code $C_q(\mathcal{T})$ of \textup{Definition \ref{def:descode}}
is the row space of $N$ in the block-coordinate space $\mathbb F_q^{\mathcal B}$
(with the induced permutation action of $G$ on the block coordinates).  Let $F$
be a field of characteristic $p$ with $p
\nmid|G|$ and $p
\nmid3r,\ r-\lambda$.
Then
$C_q(\mathcal{T})\cong F^{\mathcal{P}}$ as $G$-modules, where $F^{\mathcal{P}}$ is the
point-permutation module and the isomorphism is the $G$-equivariant
point-row map $\varphi$ of the proof.  Over $\mathbb{C}$,
\[
C_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{T})\cong 1_G\oplus\pi
\]
with $\pi$ an irreducible $G$-module of dimension $v-1$, the unique
$v-1$-dimensional constituent of the permutation module; in particular the
design code decomposes into exactly two irreducible constituents.  We stress
that the design code $C_q(\mathcal{T})$ itself lives in the block-coordinate space
$F^{\mathcal{B}}$; the decomposition $1_G\oplus\pi$ describes its module structure
\emph{via the point--block isomorphism $\varphi$} of the proof, and in
particular it always carries the natural $G$-invariance under the induced
action on the block coordinates.  The irreducible decomposition is asserted
only under the stated assumptions on the $\ell$-rank of $N$, which guarantee that $\varphi$ is an
isomorphism.
head: environment
name: Structure of the design code as a $G$-module

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $\varphi\colon C_q(\mathcal{T})\to F^{\mathcal{P}}$ sending the point row
$\mathbf r_\alpha$ to the basis vector $e_\alpha$ is well defined and injective
because $\operatorname{rank} N=v$ under the stated assumptions (\textup{Theorem \ref{thm:descode}(i)}),
and it is $G$-equivariant: the identity $P_gN=NQ_g$ noted after
\textup{Definition \ref{def:descode}} intertwines the point and block permutation
actions, so $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of $G$-modules.  The decomposition
$1_G\oplus\pi$ is the classical structure of the permutation module of a
$2$-transitive group on $\mathcal{P}$: its permutation character is $1+\chi$ with
$\chi$ irreducible of degree $v-1$ (the unique nontrivial constituent), so over
$\mathbb C$ the module is the direct sum of the trivial module and this
irreducible; see \cite{dixon1996, li2010}.

body_md:
\label{rem:ver}
The entries marked ``$\checkmark$'' are proved: the $3$-homogeneous rows by
\textup{Corollary \ref{cor:arc-families}(i)}, and the $PSL(2,q)$ rows by
\textup{Corollary \ref{cor:arc-families}(ii)}.  The entries marked ``c'' are verified
by direct computation on the stated representations: for $PSU(3,3)$ each of
the three orbits has a single star orbit (hence is arc transitive, marked
``$\checkmark$'' in \textup{Table \ref{tab:as}}); for $Sz(8)$ the circle orbit has
$2$ star orbits and the trivial orbit $3$ (hence neither is arc transitive);
for $AGL(1,7)$ the $\lambda=2$ orbit has $1$ star orbit and the $\lambda=3$
orbit $2$.  The scripts (recorded in \textup{Chapter \ref{sec:verify}} together with the
verification data) reproduce each entry.  We do not claim unproved
arc-transitivity: for the unitary, Suzuki, Ree and sporadic rows the criterion
of \textup{Theorem \ref{thm:arc}} is the statement, and the computational entries are
explicitly bounded by the checked parameters.
